Join Microsoft’s Doug Burger and guests as they dig into the fundamental truths about AI and how it will reshape the future.

Listen now
Opens in a new tab

How TokenEconomizer works

After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2.

Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. TokenEconomizer identifies recurring patterns across sessions and proposes corresponding notes. They are added to the agent’s starting context only after several sessions have confirmed the pattern, and retires the note if later evidence contradicts it.

Tool pruning removes tools that repository history suggests the agent is unlikely to use, while always retaining core tools for running commands and editing files. Removed tools can be restored if needed.

Failure-loop intervention watches for an agent that keeps hitting the same failure. A judge model decides whether the agent is truly stuck or still making progress. If it is stuck, the agent gets a short note suggesting a different approach. In the open-source plugin, if the agent is still stuck after the note, TokenEconomizer alerts the developer rather than stopping the work itself.

The controller is designed to revise its decisions as new evidence arrives. Reported savings also account for the cost of TokenEconomizer’s own model calls.

Saving costs in every repository

We evaluated TokenEconomizer on 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories, using five different AI coding agent and model combinations. For each repository, TokenEconomizer started with no prior session history. 

TokenEconomizer lowered the average cost by 18.4–30.9%, as shown in Figure 3, and saved the most in all 30 repository-combination pairs without performance loss. By contrast, lowering the model’s reasoning effort saved similar or larger amounts but led to substantial performance degradation.

Savings grow as experience accumulates. Early tasks can cost more while TokenEconomizer learns, but cumulative costs fell below the default in every repository by the sixth task, shown inFigure 4. Each mechanism contributes savings on its own, and combining all three delivers the largest reduction.

The savings also carried over to sequential web development, with costs 16.0–21.2% lower on Web-Bench. On security auditing, where every task is in a new repository, costs were 6.4–19.6% lower.

Looking ahead

TokenEconomizer opens a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively. Its lightweight controller shows how experience can improve efficiency without changing the underlying agent or model.

The open-source plugin makes these directions accessible to developers and researchers. It is designed to run alongside existing AI coding agents without modifying their underlying models, requires no API key of its own, and keeps what it learns on the developer’s machine. We invite the community to use it as a starting point for exploring agents that become more resourceful with experience, adapting how they work, as well as what they know.

items.title: Lambda Boosts AI Factory Resiliency and Efficiency With NVIDIA Photonics
items.summary: To train an AI model, thousands of GPUs have to work together, requiring a network that’s fast, efficient and resilient. Lambda is tackling the network piece of the puzzle with NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics (CPO) switches. The cloud provider is using the switches to connect NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks with more than 10,000 GPUs, delivering […]
items.content:
To train an AI model, thousands of GPUs have to work together, requiring a network that’s fast, efficient and resilient.

Lambda is tackling the network piece of the puzzle with NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics (CPO) switches. The cloud provider is using the switches to connect NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks with more than 10,000 GPUs, delivering lower power, higher resiliency and longer mean time between interruptions (MTBI) to an AI factory at scale.

“Networking has to keep pace with the demands of increasingly large AI clusters,” said Dave Ward, president of cloud services at Lambda. “Bringing co-packaged optics into a deployment of this scale is an important step toward building the infrastructure needed to support the next generation of AI.” 

 

Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26

 

In the company’s tests using the switches, network latency — the time needed for moving data — dropped by about 4% at rack scale and by up to about 10% at pod scale. Across rack, scalable unit and pod configurations, the network maintains the same throughput as conventional pluggable optics.

Delivering Power Efficiency and Resiliency at Scale

Improving power efficiency and resiliency matters because the network sits at the center of AI factory productivity. 

In a large training job, one interrupted link can stall thousands of GPUs. With agentic inference, one network disruption can introduce cascading latency effects on many agents. Every interruption costs time, and every watt spent on networking is a watt not available for compute. 

NVIDIA Photonics addresses both power efficiency and resiliency. By replacing pluggable transceivers with co-packaged optical engines on the switch package, it delivers up to 5x better power efficiency and up to 15x higher reliability than conventional pluggable optics. It also uses 4x fewer lasers, which means fewer components that can fail.

Cooler Optics, Replaceable Light Sources Increase Resiliency

Lambda’s deployment uses NVIDIA Photonics switches, each with 144 ports running at 800Gb/s. Liquid cooling carries heat away from the switch chip and optical engines. 

The company reports a median optics temperature of 36°C, compared with 51°C for conventional pluggable optics, and its tests find more stable signal integrity.

NVIDIA Photonics also brings the electrical-to-optical conversion closer to the switch chip. Each switch has 18 removable external light sources, which supply light to the optical engines. Optical engines sit alongside the chip on the same package and convert electrical signals into light that carries data over fiber between parts of the cluster. 

Technicians can replace the light-source modules in the field, unlike traditional pluggable optics, which require replacing the entire module if a laser fails.

Co-packaging shortens the electrical path from inches to millimeters, which reduces signal loss. It also removes the need for retimer chips, cutting both power draw and the number of parts in the signal path.

Explore NVIDIA Photonics and read Lambda’s deployment announcement.

items.title: NVIDIA Expands Slurm to Bring Quantum Computing Into Supercomputing
items.summary: Quantum processor deployments at supercomputing centers have grown nearly sevenfold over the past five years, with nearly 30 supercomputing centers around the world now in the process of deploying over 50 quantum processors.  Many of these centers use Slurm to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows […]
items.content:
Quantum processor deployments at supercomputing centers have grown nearly sevenfold over the past five years, with nearly 30 supercomputing centers around the world now in the process of deploying over 50 quantum processors. 

Many of these centers use Slurm to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows and tools, enabling computational chemists, nuclear physicists and materials scientists to bring quantum computing into their research domains without friction.

In a new release, Slurm builds on previous work with IBM, Pasqal and the wider quantum computing community to allow QPU builders to create a single interface to their hardware for every supercomputing center, through a simple file. This makes it easier than ever for HPC centers and QPU builders to integrate and serve their hardware. 

The expansion is already being adopted by Alice & Bob, IBM, IQM, Pasqal, Quantinuum and MQSC and supports the widely used QRMI and QDMI interfaces.

Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26

 

Beating the Bottleneck

Until now, integrating a QPU into a supercomputing center meant a new software challenge for every new QPU or supercomputing center. By building on existing quantum-HPC interfaces such as QRMI and QDMI, the Slurm expansion allows QPU builders to reuse their integrations across all their deployments. It also means that supercomputing centers can add new quantum processors to their existing scheduling and resource-management workflows without developing bespoke QPU-specific solutions.

For quantum computing to advance science, it needs to be used by scientists. Now scientists can run quantum-classical applications developed with platforms such as NVIDIA CUDA-Q with Slurm coordinating access to all the processing they need.

Slurm 26.11 will be available later this month. 

Orchestrating Resources in an Open Quantum-GPU Platform

The Slurm expansion adds a community-developed orchestration layer to NVIDIA’s open platform for quantum-GPU supercomputing, which centers around the CUDA-Q open platform for hybrid quantum-classical computing. At SC26, new releases expand all aspects of the platform:

CUDA-Q QEC allows researchers developing quantum error correction to rapidly prototype and test new ideas, including with a new decoder server. A new TCBP-JOBS decoder is 13,000x faster than the industry standard.

CUDA-Q gets an expanded layer of fault-tolerant primitives that application builders can use to realistically compile their ideas. Fermilab has already used CUDA-Q to perform studies in three weeks that would normally have taken five months.

CUDA-Q Algorithms provides reusable components for builders of quantum applications, including new capabilities in helping design the loading data into quantum circuits and tools specifically for chemistry and materials applications

CUDA-Q Pulse gives quantum hardware builders a layer for shaping the ‘pulses’ needed to control qubits on a QPU, including tools to GPU accelerate their generation.

The quantum ecosystem around the world is continuing to build with this platform. Quantum Motion integrated its QUICHE chemistry framework with CUDA-Q. Altera and Oxford Quantum Circuits designed an FPGA-based controller connecting qubit control and readout to GPUs through NVQLink.

At supercomputing scale, QunaSys used cuQuantum and 1,024 NVIDIA Hopper GPUs on ABCI-Q to simulate more than 300 million quantum operations, reaching chemical accuracy for a four-hydrogen-atom model. NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER to simulate 104 qubits under realistic noise, testing fault-tolerant designs before they’re built.

Learn more about NVIDIA quantum computing technologies.

items.title: NVIDIA Sweeps MLPerf Training and Endpoints as Vera Rubin Debuts With Leading Performance
items.summary: In its MLPerf benchmarks debut, with results released today, the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform delivers leading performance across training, post-training and agentic inference.  NVIDIA swept every MLPerf Training v6.1 benchmark and, in its first MLPerf Endpoints submission, delivered more than 10x generational gains in throughput per watt for agentic AI — measuring how much agentic […]
items.content:
In its MLPerf benchmarks debut, with results released today, the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform delivers leading performance across training, post-training and agentic inference. 

NVIDIA swept every MLPerf Training v6.1 benchmark and, in its first MLPerf Endpoints submission, delivered more than 10x generational gains in throughput per watt for agentic AI — measuring how much agentic work a system delivers with each watt of power. 

These results are just the beginning. Vera Rubin performance will keep climbing through continuous optimization of NVIDIA’s CUDA-powered software stack, so the infrastructure that customers invest in today delivers more value over time.

NVIDIA Sweeps MLPerf Training v6.1

AI agents are now everywhere, writing code, running business workflows, answering customer questions and, as this week’s SC26 conference highlights, advancing scientific research. 

Faster training means smarter agents can reach users sooner, drug discovery models can keep pace with new lab data and fraud-detection models can adapt to new threats faster.

MLPerf Training measures how fast a system can train a range of AI models to a target level of accuracy. 

The NVIDIA platform was the only one with results on every benchmark this round, spanning large language models, image generation, recommender systems and reinforcement learning post-training. In its debut, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivered up to 2x more performance per GPU than the highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 system — early results that show the pace of generation-over-generation innovation. 

NVIDIA also demonstrated performance at scale. On the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 scaled from 256 to 1,024 GPUs with about 97% efficiency: quadrupling the GPUs cut time to train from 16 minutes to about four. 

NVIDIA also ran the benchmark on 10,240 GPUs with GB300 systems, representing the largest scale in this round. Microsoft Azure matched that scale with 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 systems. 

Results at this scale matter because adding GPUs only speeds up training if they can work together efficiently. NVIDIA NVLink scale-up networking connects the GPUs within each system so they act as one, while NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand and Spectrum-X Ethernet scale-out networking link those systems across the data center. Combined with optimized software, this keeps thousands of GPUs working in concert, helping developers build more intelligent models while cutting training times.

NVIDIA Vera Rubin Leads Agentic Inference on MLPerf Endpoints

An AI agent for travel that plans and books a whole trip — or an IT agent that finds and fixes a problem before anyone files a ticket — may reason, call tools and check its work many times to finish a single task. 

Each of those steps generates tokens. Because AI data centers are limited by power, the more tokens a system can generate each second for every watt of power, the more agents it can serve and the more value it creates. 

MLPerf Endpoints tests systems on real agentic coding and enterprise workflows, and checks that the agents still complete their tasks correctly. NVIDIA Vera Rubin leads across all of its agentic benchmarks.

For example, in a provisional result for Kimi K3, a large open model built for agentic workflows, Vera Rubin NVL72 systems deliver more than 10x the throughput per watt of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 at the same response speed. 

Every AI service has to balance serving many users at once against responding quickly to each one. Vera Rubin shifts that entire curve, serving more users while responding faster. 

Leadership Across Benchmarks and Workloads

NVIDIA partners participated extensively in MLPerf Training, with submissions from 20 organizations: ASUS, Azure, Cisco, CoreWeave, Crusoe, Dell Technologies, Firmus, Giga Computing, Google Cloud, HPE, Inventec, Krai, Lambda, Nebius, Oracle, Quanta Cloud Technology (QCT), Supermicro, TTA and the University of Florida. 

Their submissions show how NVIDIA’s programmable platform, with open source libraries and frameworks, lets a vast ecosystem of partners innovate and optimize AI training performance.

The lead extends beyond MLPerf. 

Vera Rubin also delivers leading performance on independent benchmarks including SemiAnalysis AgentX and Artificial Analysis AgentPerf, showcasing how the same NVIDIA infrastructure can productively run everything from pretraining and post-training to agentic inference, as well as workloads beyond AI, such as the high-performance computing showcased at SC26 this week. 

Dive deeper into the results in the MLPerf Training and MLPerf Endpoints technical blogs.

items.title: NVIDIA CUDA-X Libraries Give Agents the Tools to Accelerate Scientific Discovery
items.summary: With expanded NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including cuPhoton, cuPotential and cuSpa, researchers can sift through vast amounts of data to accelerate research, from astrophysics and materials science to single-cell biology. The speedups are helping scientists analyze larger datasets and model more complex systems. The new libraries give AI agents the tools to help researchers make discoveries […]
items.content:
With expanded NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including cuPhoton, cuPotential and cuSpa, researchers can sift through vast amounts of data to accelerate research, from astrophysics and materials science to single-cell biology.

The speedups are helping scientists analyze larger datasets and model more complex systems.

The new libraries give AI agents the tools to help researchers make discoveries faster than ever.

 

Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26

 

Bringing Black Holes Into Focus

Seeing a black hole takes a telescope the size of Earth. The Event Horizon Telescope links radio dishes worldwide, generating petabytes of data that can take months to process.

With NVIDIA cuPhoton.xBeam, a module within the cuPhoton Toolkit, black hole observations from the Event Horizon Telescope can now be correlated orders of magnitude faster than ever. Analysis that once took over a month now takes eight minutes.

By combining global radio dishes into Earth-sized aperture, cuPhoton delivers unprecedented astronomical imaging resolution. cuPhoton successfully correlated observations of powerful black hole jets J1924 and 3C279 in the night sky — making it a reality to reconstruct a Messier 87* black hole galaxy in real time. 

The entire pipeline, from data loading and processing to visualization, runs on distributed multi-GPU systems or a compact NVIDIA DGX Spark system, helping scientists study how gas spirals inward under a black hole’s powerful gravitational pull.

Steering Fusion Simulations

Sustaining plasma at millions of degrees is essential to achieving stable, continuous fusion energy. But simulating its behavior is costly: on petascale systems, a single time step can take days, with simulations running for weeks. Experiments also generate data faster than traditional pipelines can process it, often leaving scientists waiting until experiments end to analyze results.

Pacific Fusion researchers used NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module to extract insights while plasma simulations run, helping them visualize what’s happening as results emerge. 

The NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module extracts insights while plasma simulations run, helping researchers understand what’s happening as results emerge. Researchers can couple the entire pipeline with an NVIDIA Nemotron-powered agent running locally on the same system, enabling interactive analysis that can help steer simulations in real time to inform fusion reactor target and chamber design.

Exploring Potential Medicines

Molecular simulations help scientists evaluate drug designs before costly laboratory experiments. NVIDIA cuPotential, built on work by researchers at Simons Foundation’s Flatiron Institute and D. E. Shaw Research, accelerates existing simulation software by up to 3x while improving calculation stability and accuracy. It expedites synthetic data creation for generative AI models, finding previously unknown molecular binding sites and calculating the strength of molecular interactions.

NVIDIA is working with Schrödinger and the AMBER, NAMD, GROMACS, LAMMPS and Open Molecular Software Foundation communities to bring cuPotential acceleration to molecular dynamics engines and workflows.

Cadence, Fathom Therapeutics, Topos Bio, Genesis Molecular AI and Terray Therapeutics are adopting it for drug discovery.

Accelerating Materials Research

Daviator, a collection of batched GPU kernels for the widely used Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package, is coming to NVIDIA ALCHEMI — delivering quantum-mechanical calculations up to 22x faster and at up to 75% lower cost. With Daviator, researchers building simulation models can now use GPU acceleration across atomistic systems of all sizes to generate the millions of calculations of atomic interactions needed for model training and inference, including for small systems that previously ran faster on CPUs.

At Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, the NVIDIA DAQIRI networking library connects a high-speed electron microscopy detector to GPU processing, moving analysis into the experiment itself. Researchers can identify useful signals, discover previously unknown regions of interest and decide what to measure next while measurements are being taken. 

The workflow supports atomic-resolution materials studies that can distinguish elements, laying the groundwork for future automated experiments.

Revealing Biology at Scale

The newly open source cuSpa accelerates cell polygon calculations, enabling developers to generate massive spatial graphs for next-generation patient and cancer models at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, with a 900x speedup compared with using CPUs. 

Codeveloped with scverse, the rapids-singlecell framework accelerates single-cell analysis — and is now available in a single, agent-ready container. Using the tool, Therna Biosciences processed data 200x faster for therapeutic design. 10x Genomics integrated rapids-singlecell in its new Sentira platform, helping academic researchers, biopharma teams and foundation model builders accelerate the path from large-scale spatial data to biological insights. 

And the NVIDIA GPU-accelerated HMMER library, also open source, accelerates the annotation of predicted protein sequences, supporting data preparation for biological foundation models. At Basecamp Research, benchmark searches ran up to 84x faster than with standard HMMER, reducing the time required to annotate the large biological datasets used to train the company’s therapeutic design models.

Explore NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries. Learn more in this technical blog on GPU-powered black hole reconstruction.

items.title: CUDA at 20: How the Platform Transformed Scientific Computing
items.summary: This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of CUDA by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI.  CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers […]
items.content:
This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of CUDA by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI. 

CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers building on their work today. 

At the platform’s core is this developer community whose experiments, tools and persistence expanded what accelerated computing could do.

From SC06 to SC26

NVIDIA announced CUDA in November 2006 and brought it to the scientific community at SC06, giving scientists and developers a familiar, high-level programming model for using GPUs. It fundamentally extended accelerated computing beyond graphics use cases to accelerate demanding applications for science, simulation and more.

In the two decades since, developers have used CUDA to advance Nobel Prize-winning AI research, accelerate scientific applications on supercomputers and support visual effects in Oscar-winning films. 

Today, more than 11 million developers build on CUDA across the computing stack. 

 

Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26

 

Honoring the Architects of Progress

Now, at SC26, NVIDIA is looking back at some of the CUDA luminaries who’ve spearheaded breakthroughs in science and AI:

At the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, biophysicist Klaus Schulten’s team helped connect GPU computing with molecular biology through Nanoscale Molecular Dynamics and Visual Molecular Dynamics, tools for molecular simulation and visualization. In 2013, researchers at Illinois, the University of Pittsburgh and Vanderbilt University used CUDA-accelerated tools to help resolve the HIV capsid’s atomic structure. They combined experiments with simulations on Blue Waters, one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers at the time.

In a critical breakthrough in AI, University of Toronto researchers Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton used CUDA to train AlexNet on just two NVIDIA GPUs. Their image-recognition system won the 2012 ImageNet competition, helping demonstrate the potential of GPU computing for deep learning. 

That connection between computing and scientific discovery is seen with AlphaFold, which predicts protein structures. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein structure prediction. Their team’s publicly released AlphaFold 2 software uses CUDA for GPU execution.

These are just a few of many examples that show how one generation’s work creates opportunities for the next. With 1,000+ NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, developers are now reshaping industries and giving machines the power to see, learn and reason — from discovering new medicines and designing next-generation factories to advancing autonomous vehicles, modeling financial markets and unlocking quantum computing — and more.

Start building with the CUDA Toolkit and visit the 20-Year CUDA Celebration Event Wall at NVIDIA’s booth at SC26.

items.title: NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics
items.summary: Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows.  As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next […]
items.content:
Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows. 

As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design.

The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink interconnect technology.

 

Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26

 

Scientists and engineers rely on simulation to understand complex systems before committing to experiments or physical prototypes. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps.

“For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.” 

Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery

Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing workloads take a similar shape: an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers a handful of scattered values, calculates a result and repeats this on an enormous scale. 

To help address the challenge, Rubin HPC will offer a balanced design, scaling data movement and compute together rather than increasing compute alone. 

That balance is what optimizes Rubin HPC for scientific computing. It keeps the GPU’s record number of CUDA cores supplied with data, so they spend their time computing rather than waiting. This accelerates recurring patterns of every simulation workload — from sparse matrix operations to stencil computations to sorting and reductions. 

These patterns are prevalent across data analytics, science and engineering workloads, which is why a purpose-built GPU delivering the broadest acceleration can help unlock cross-industry breakthroughs.

NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries offer a growing set of optimized implementations of complex algorithms for agents to use, including those most relevant to simulation and analytics. Used together with Rubin HPC, the libraries can give agents the fastest glide path to reasoning outcomes. 

And faster agent-invoked simulations mean faster feedback — shortening the loop of hypothesis, simulation and refinement, so researchers and engineers can choose next steps sooner and point lab work at the most promising candidates.

Rubin HPC is expected to be available in 2028.

items.title: Advancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams
Agent Security Meets Regulatory Reality -- A Practitioner Systematization of Autonomous-Agent Threats and Controls in Regulated Financial Systems
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.29142v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language model agents are entering regulated financial systems, yet research on their attack surface remains predominantly laboratory-based, and practitioner guidance is neither peer-reviewed nor connected to a formal threat model. Using production evidence, we map six agentic threat categories, namely prompt injection, identity and authorization, action auditability, tool abuse, data residency, and boundary policy enforcement, to the specific control obligations imposed by US and EU financial regulation (ECOA and Regulation B, EU AI Act, GDPR Article 22, and FINRA's 2026 agent guidance), showing how legal accountability increases their operational significance. We distill these obligations into five runtime control invariants with reference algorithms that enforce them at auditable architectural boundaries. We develop a formal model expressing each invariant as a predicate over a case-bound event chain and prove the audit reconstruction gate is sound and complete with respect to these invariants: compliance is decidable from the case identifier alone. We show that two of the invariants constrain audit cost and throughput rather than constituting pure operational overhead. We document four architectural patterns from a production Know Your Customer (KYC) deployment for a consumer credit product that reduced multi-day manual processing to same-day automated resolution for approximately four in five cases. Finally, we report three negative results, two identified through internal audit or production observation rather than adversarial testing. We conclude that securing agents in regulated environments depends less on novel attack classes than on rendering auditability, least-privilege authorization, and boundary policy enforcement, with verifiable compliance and bounded audit cost at scale.
items.author: Krishna Mohan Guda Nagavenkata Srinivasa, Satya Phanindra Kalaga, Karthik Guda Vishnu

items.title: Reproducibility in the Age of Agentic AI: Context Engineering at the Timescale of a Codebase
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.11728v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reproducible research practices are context engineering for AI coding agents. I argue that agents lower the cost of maintaining tests, commit histories, repository structure, instructions, and decision records while making their benefits immediate. Researchers remain responsible for verifying these artifacts and the scientific judgments they encode.
items.author: Lorena A. Barba

items.title: A Governance Methodology Layer for AI-Assisted Software Development: Defect Taxonomy, Controlled Ablation, and a Test of Process-Over-Capability
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.04218v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Autonomous coding agents produce output that passes syntactic checks -- compilation, type safety, CI -- at high velocity. Yet syntactic correctness does not imply semantic correctness: design boundaries, security invariants, and maintainability contracts remain structurally invisible to automated pipelines. This paper makes four contributions. First, we present a defect-class taxonomy grounded in five AI agent permission and governance modules, separating defects structurally detectable by static analysis from those requiring semantic review. Second, we describe a runtime-decoupled governance gate -- a file-based protocol that reads generator output and emits a structured verdict without API coupling, hence portable across generators. Third, we formalize methodology-as-code: expressing a verification protocol as a version-controlled, executable artifact whose two layers separate portable methodology from host automation. Fourth, we report a controlled ablation experiment (E-ablation, N=5 artifacts, 8-item independent ground truth) comparing harness-structured review against a token-matched unstructured prompt. The structured condition records 62% lenient recall against 50%, with 25% strict against 0%. A severity-grade differential reported earlier does not survive blind re-grading and is withdrawn (Sec. 6.6). An independent-session re-test with blind scoring does not replicate that contrast: the conditions differ by one strict hit in 24 (6/24 against 5/24), the structured aggregate again 25% and the unstructured 0% not recurring (Sec. 6.7). Both conditions miss document-quality defects identified by a human QA reviewer, indicating complementarity between structured AI review and human process inspection. A later pre-registered test varying model tier (184 runs) did not support process design as the dominant factor: under strict scoring the tier effect was larger (Sec. 6.8).
items.author: Sungjin Kwon

items.title: Drive the Thoughts: Runtime Monitoring of VLA Reasoning-Trajectory Consistency
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.29583v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: While machine learning models help autonomous vehicles (AVs) navigate complex environments, their black-box nature complicates validation and verification (V&V). Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a unique opportunity: alongside trajectories, they generate an explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) explaining their decisions. We posit that this CoT can serve as a candidate specification to cross-check trajectories and expose unsafe behavior. To assess this, we curate DriveAlignBench, a dataset of 150 CoT-trajectory pairs from NVIDIA's Alpamayo 1.5 VLA, manually annotated for CoT reliability, CoT-trajectory consistency, and trajectory safety. We find that 33.3% of CoTs are unreliable, and among reliable CoTs, 26% have inconsistent trajectories. To detect these cases, we propose integrating a CoT-trajectory consistency check into a runtime monitor. This check is nontrivial because CoTs express open-vocabulary, scene-relative maneuvers, while trajectories are low-level ego-motion sequences whose semantics depend on road geometry and motion context. To bridge this gap, we develop a family of automated consistency monitors. The strongest, the lane-aware monitor, adds lane-relative evidence to the input of the judge model scoring consistency. This raises F1 across all four evaluated judges from 0.56-0.62 with raw waypoints to 0.65-0.82, showing that evidence representation improves detection across judges. Moreover, for reliable CoTs, inconsistency is associated with unsafe behavior: 27% of human-labeled inconsistent trajectories are unsafe compared to 3% of consistent ones, and the lane-aware monitor flags most of these unsafe cases. We release DriveAlignBench, the monitor implementations, and per-run results at https://github.com/less-lab-uva/drive-the-thoughts.
items.author: Tian Yu, Lu Feng, Sebastian Elbaum

items.title: Identifying and Mitigating API Misuse in Large Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2503.22821v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: API misuse in code generated by large language models (LLMs) presents a serious and growing challenge in software development, as although LLMs demonstrate impressive code generation capabilities, their interactions with complex library APIs are often error-prone and can lead to software failures and vulnerabilities. In this paper, we conduct a large-scale study of API misuse patterns in LLM-generated code by analyzing both method selection and parameter usage across Python and Java, using three representative LLMs: StarCoder-7B, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, and GitHub Copilot. Based on extensive manual annotation of 3,209 method-level and 3,492 parameter-level misuses, we identify and categorize four recurring misuse types by building on and refining prior API misuse taxonomies. Our evaluation of the three LLMs reveals persistent challenges in API usage, particularly hallucination and intent misalignment. To address these issues, we propose Dr.Fix, an LLM-based automatic repair approach guided by our taxonomy, which improves repair accuracy compared to baseline prompting and existing repair methods, achieving gains of up to 38.4 BLEU and up to 72 more exact matches on benchmark datasets. This work offers important insights into the current limitations of LLMs in API usage and points to directions for improving automated misuse repair in code generation systems.
items.author: Terry Yue Zhuo, Junda He, Jiamou Sun, Zhenchang Xing, David Lo, John Grundy, Xiaoning Du

items.title: A Taxonomy of Real Faults in Hybrid Quantum-Classical Architectures
items.summary:
arXiv:2502.08739v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: With the popularity of Hybrid Quantum-Classical architectures, particularly noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) architectures, comes the need for quality assurance methods tailored to their specific faults. In this study, we propose a taxonomy of faults in Hybrid Quantum-Classical architectures accompanied by a dataset of real faults in the identified categories. To achieve this, we empirically analysed open-source repositories for fixed faults. We analysed over 5000 closed issues on GitHub and pre-selected 529 of them based on rigorously defined inclusion criteria. We selected 133 faults that we labelled around symptoms and the origin of the faults. We cross-validated the classification and labels assigned to every fault between two of the authors. As a result, we introduced a taxonomy of real faults in Hybrid Quantum-Classical architectures. Subsequently, we validated the taxonomy through interviews conducted with eleven developers. The taxonomy was dynamically updated throughout the cross-validation and interview processes. The final version was validated and discussed through surveys conducted with an independent group of domain experts to ensure its relevance and to gain further insights.
items.author: Avner Bensoussan, Gunel Jahangirova, Mohammad Reza Mousavi

items.title: Meta Build Systems as Logic Programs
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17672v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Meta build systems such as CMake, Meson and Bazel derive command graphs from project descriptions, user choices and machine facts. Imperative scripts, search paths and special cases make routine decisions interact poorly: search order can choose compatible packages without an explicit project choice, packagers must patch author flag preferences, and cross-builds need annotations or nested build trees for tools run during the build.
  Our central insight is to express configuration as relational inference: objects follow from sources, flags and libraries from dependencies, and language standards from transitive requirements. We introduce buildlog, a meta build system whose stratified logical core isolates build derivation from impure environmental probes. It rejects ambiguity in toolchain or package selection and explains derived facts through provenance. Author constraints and user preferences use distinct, statically checked input relations. Libraries can ship consumer rules, including Qt's moc/rcc rules, using the same facts for installed and built code. Using a compiled program in a build rule lets buildlog infer its build-machine configuration.
  We evaluate buildlog on eleven case studies of ten projects, validating configurations through execution and artifact checks while reporting remaining flag differences and platform limits. In Halide, generators link an LLVM-based compiler and run during the build to emit WebAssembly or Android code; where CMake requires nested builds, buildlog derives build-machine and target-platform configurations in one graph. A supporting formal account establishes termination, within-round probe-order independence, and agreement between fresh and validated cached runs under explicit finiteness and probe obligations. The results show that confining impurity to fact discovery yields a small, uniform and explainable configuration semantics.
items.author: Alex Reinking

items.title: Everything is an Operational View: UI as a Projection over Context in Agentic Systems
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17355v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The emergence of generative AI has enabled Generative User Interfaces (GenUI) that dynamically construct interfaces from user intent, yet existing approaches rely on request-response pipelines that fragment context and limit transparency and control. This paper proposes AFS-UI, which reconceptualises UI as projections over context built on an agentic file-system abstraction that organizes data, capabilities, and interaction state within a unified, persistent workspace. In particular, AFS-UI addresses key limitations in current systems, including heterogeneous resource discoverability, incompatible operation semantics, tangling projection and context, rigid source composition and substitution, and limited evolvability. Within this framework, interfaces become dynamic, inspectable views over shared resources, supporting both human and agent interaction through a common operational surface.
items.author: Jieshan Chen, Robert Mao, Xiwei Xu, Xuewu Gu, Yechao Li, Zhenchang Xing

items.title: HerAgent: A Block-Level Checkpointing Harness for Coding-Agent Environment Setup
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18443v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern coding agents rely on establishing executable software environments before they can perform software engineering tasks such as testing, debugging, and patch validation. Existing setup agents typically control progress at either single-command or whole-script granularity, making recovery either too local to remove polluted state or too coarse to preserve useful progress. We present HerAgent (Harness EnviRonment Setup Agent), a block-level harness for coding-agent environment setup. HerAgent's main contribution is semantic setup blocks: a single progress-control abstraction used for execution, validation, checkpointing, repair, and rollback. Evaluated against six prior agents on four environment-setup datasets, HerAgent improves setup success in every comparison, achieving the largest gains on Installamatic-Bench (52.0% to 85.0%) and SetupBench (46.3% to 70.4%). It also reduces setup costs by up to 94.5%, showing that block-level progress control improves reliability and efficiency.
items.author: Xiang Li, Siyu Lu, Federica Sarro, Claire Le Goues, He Ye

items.title: DesignSpecs: A DESIGN.md Dataset of Visual Design Specifications for AI Agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17713v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While AI agents increasingly generate and modify user interfaces, they rarely rely on a visual design specification for a certain project. The DESIGN.md format, which originated from Google's AI design tool Stitch and which was open-sourced in April 2026, addresses this gap by describing a visual identity through design tokens (such as named colors, text styles) and Markdown prose. To our knowledge, no large-scale research dataset of such design specification files exists. We present DesignSpecs, a dataset of 36,906 DESIGN.md files from 15,794 public, non-fork GitHub repositories, representing 17,240 unique file contents. We collected 613,207 files named DESIGN.md in October 2026. Because the same file name also denotes architectural plans and other design documents, we filtered those with YAML front matter, a design-system name, at least one recognized design token, and zero errors under the official linter. Our JSON Lines dataset provides file-level and deduplicated views of the original Markdown, links files to repositories, paths, and commits, and is released with related scripts. We outline research opportunities on visual design knowledge and design-aware AI agents. Dataset is available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Jl-wei/DesignSpecs
items.author: Jialiang Wei, Walid Maalej

items.title: SZZBench: Controlled Git Histories with Explicit Oracles for Diagnosing SZZ Implementations
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17669v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The SZZ algorithm traces a bug-fixing commit back to the commits that introduced the bug. Its labels underlie defect-prediction data sets and many mining software repositories studies. SZZ implementations are mostly evaluated against oracles mined from real projects. Such oracles are realistic, but each case mixes the history factors that make an implementation succeed or fail, and an aggregate score cannot show why. We present SZZBench, a tool that shows why: it generates ordinary Git repositories from declarative scenarios with explicit oracles, scores the predictions of any SZZ implementation under declared evaluation policies, and reads each result against 26 naive baselines, such as always answering the second commit. SZZBench also checks the declarations of new scenarios, such as the tier, against the results of the naive baselines. Currently, SZZBench ships 279 scenarios in 17 categories and adapters for four SZZ tools. Running these tools in nine configurations without changing their code, we find that PyDriller passes 161 scenarios and a rule that always answers the second commit passes 160, yet only 97 scenarios are passed by both: the two succeed on different scenarios, which the number of passed scenarios hides and the per-scenario results reveal. SZZBench is available at https://github.com/higolab/SZZBench.
items.author: Yoshiki Higo, Inase Kondo, Masanari Kondo, Yasutaka Kamei

items.title: Beyond Source Code: Evaluating Natural Language Specifications for LLM-Based C-to-Rust Translation
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17581v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promising results for C-to-Rust translation, yet existing approaches primarily rely on source code as input, leaving natural-language specifications of program behavior underexplored as an alternative or complementary representation. We hypothesize that direct code translation encourages LLMs to preserve C-specific implementation choices, producing Rust that may be functionally correct but unnecessarily verbose, reliant on unsafe constructs, and less idiomatic. We investigate this hypothesis by comparing three translation settings: code-only, specification-only, and code-and-specification. Using 300 C programs from the IBM CodeNet dataset, we evaluate GPT-5.2 and GPT-4o-mini on functional correctness, maintainability, complexity, idiomaticity, unsafe construct usage, and cost. Code-only translation achieves the highest test pass rate (98.6%) but often mirrors C's implementation patterns. In contrast, specification-only translation produces the most idiomatic and compact Rust, reducing unsafe blocks by approximately 6x and Clippy style warnings by 2.4x. However, using specifications without validation yields test pass rates as low as 86% with our best performing model. Adding an iterative test-based validation and refinement step for specifications raises this to a 95.3% test pass rate. Overall, specification-based translation consistently improves code quality relative to code-only translation, while code-and-specification offers the best balance between correctness (98.3% test pass rate) and maintainability. Our study systematically compares these translation settings, highlighting the trade-offs among specification quality, translation correctness, code quality, and computational cost.
items.author: Biruk Tadesse, Lawrence Arkoh, Marcelo D'Amorim, Wesley K. G. Assun\c{c}\~ao

items.title: Some complete $\omega$-powers of a one-counter language in the difference hierarchy
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.16473v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Fix a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ having at least two letters, and natural numbers $n,k\geq 1$. We denote by $D_n(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$ the class of differences of $n$ subsets of the Cantor space $\Sigma^\omega$ in $\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k$, and by $D^-_n(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$ the class of complements of sets in $D_n(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$. We prove, for any natural numbers $n,k\geq 1$, the existence of a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ having at least two letters and a finitary language $U_{n,k}$ over $\Sigma$ accepted by a one-counter automaton such that the $\omega$-power $$U_{n,k}^\infty:=\{ w_0w_1\cdots\in\Sigma^\omega\mid\forall i\in\omega ~~w_i\in U_{n,k}\}$$ is $D_{2n-1}(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$-complete. We also prove a conditional result for the dual classes $D^-_{2n}(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$: under the assumption that there exists a finitary language $V_{n,3}$ accepted by a one-counter automaton, such that its $\omega$-power $V_{n,3}^\infty$ is $D^-_{2n}(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_3)$-complete, there would also exist, for any integer $k > 3$, a finitary language $V_{n,k}$ accepted by a one-counter automaton, such that its $\omega$-power $V_{n,k}^\infty$ is $D^-_{2n}(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$-complete. Finally we add another conditionnal result about Wadge degrees of rational $\mathbf{\Delta}^0_2$ omega powers, which completes the recent results of [FGL26].
items.author: Jacques Duparc (UNIL), Olivier Finkel (IMJ-PRG), Dominique Lecomte (IMJ-PRG)

items.title: From Reading Code to Reading Spec: A Verified Layer for LLM-Driven Codebase Maintenance
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.06383v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The rapid growth of LLM-generated code increases software complexity and the maintenance burden on engineers. While LLMs offer a potential automated alternative, this structural complexity hinders their ability to manage codebases directly. We introduce the Provable Representation Of Original Functionality (PROOF), which manages codebases indirectly via structured specifications. To enable full-lifecycle codebase management strictly through these specifications, PROOF abstracts codebase topology into a hierarchical natural-language representation. To establish absolute trust, the system proves semantic equivalence by reconstructing source code exclusively from this specification. This verified foundation drives maintenance requests, executing code modifications while synchronously updating itself to prevent semantic drift. Experiments on real-world repositories confirm the effectiveness of these specifications.
items.author: Xinhao Zhang, Jingjie Lu, Kunpeng Liu, Fei Xie

items.title: HackWorld: Evaluating Computer-Use Agents on Exploiting Web Application Vulnerabilities
items.summary:
arXiv:2510.12200v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Web applications are prime targets for cyberattacks as gateways to critical services and sensitive data. Traditional penetration testing is costly and expertise-intensive, making it difficult to scale with the growing web ecosystem. While language model agents show promise in cybersecurity, modern web applications demand visual understanding, dynamic content handling, and multi-step interactions that only computer-use agents (CUAs) can perform. Yet, their ability to discover and exploit vulnerabilities through graphical interfaces remains largely unexplored. We present HackWorld, the first framework for systematically evaluating CUAs' capabilities to exploit web application vulnerabilities via visual interaction. Unlike sanitized benchmarks, HackWorld includes 36 real-world applications across 11 frameworks and 7 languages, featuring realistic flaws such as injection vulnerabilities, authentication bypasses, and unsafe input handling. Using a Capture-the-Flag (CTF) setup, it tests CUAs' capacity to identify and exploit these weaknesses while navigating complex web interfaces. Evaluation of state-of-the-art CUAs reveals concerning trends: exploitation rates below 12% and low cybersecurity awareness. CUAs often fail at multi-step attack planning and misuse security tools. These results expose the current limitations of CUAs in web security contexts and highlight opportunities for developing more security-aware agents capable of effective vulnerability detection and exploitation.
items.author: Xiaoxue Ren, Penghao Jiang, Kaixin Li, Zhiyong Huang, Xiaoning Du, Jiaojiao Jiang, Zhenchang Xing, Jiamou Sun, Terry Yue Zhuo

items.title: From Survey Histories to Interpretable Digital Twins: Auto-Discovering Task-Specific Personas and Behavioral Mechanisms
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.20344v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLM-based "digital twins" aim to simulate how an individual would behave in new environments or respond to novel questions, given some representation of that individual's prior responses. We ask whether long survey histories can be transformed into compact, task-specific personas that remain predictive for unseen respondents and products within the same task while making simulated decisions more interpretable. We introduce an iterative auto-discovery pipeline that constructs persona representations and learns how persona evidence influences simulated responses. We evaluate the procedure on the 40-item Product Preferences--Pricing task of Twin-2K-500 (Toubia et al., 2025), learning from 20 respondents and 20 products and evaluating the frozen representation and mechanism on 30 unseen respondents and 20 unseen products. The holdout answers come from two survey waves, and every prediction is scored against each wave separately. For gpt-5.4-nano, replacing the full survey transcript with the learned channel representation and mechanism improves exact accuracy from 0.573 to 0.623 and from 0.558 to 0.626 in the two waves. Larger and cross-provider simulators (gpt-5.4, gpt-5-mini, qwen3-8b) using the full transcript do not achieve statistically significant improvements over the baseline in both waves, and none significantly outperforms the learned representation in either wave. This pattern shows that the learned representation produces consistent gains against human responses collected in both waves while retaining an explicit mapping from respondent evidence to predicted decisions.
items.author: Tianze Deng, Iris Ye, Ozan Candogan

items.title: Characterizing Treatment-Context Medication Evidence Across Clinic Notes and Structured EHR Medication History
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.01570v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Clinic notes may describe medication changes that are not reflected in structured electronic health record (EHR) medication history at the same encounter. Differences in terminology and documentation timing further complicate the interpretation of these discrepancies. We evaluated medication normalization in clinic notes and examined how semantic and temporal matching affected overlap with structured history. A note-grounded reference was constructed from large language model (LLM)-proposed mentions, deterministic canonical projection, and existing targeted correction records; random-audit records were summarized separately. On 5,360 reference mention rows from held-out patients, conditional canonical agreement increased from 81.25% with surface matching to 93.58% after lexical cleanup and curated aliases. Candidate-reference mention alignment was evaluated separately, yielding an F1 score of 0.6547. Across 27,552 reference rows, exact same-visit overlap was 16.71%. Overlap reached 90.22% when ingredient and broad-category matches were permitted at the same visit or within 30 days before or after the note. Incomplete mapping of note-derived labels contributed to residual nonoverlap in ontology-backed comparisons. Exact-label comparison captured only part of the related medication information across sources; broader matches do not establish equivalent medication use or treatment events.
items.author: Mingyang Jiang, Congning Ni, Weixin Liu, Zhijun Yin

items.title: Comparing Human and Automatic Recognition of Dutch Dysarthric Continuous Speech: A Case Study
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.30237v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In our goal to develop personalised dysarthric speech recognition (DSR) models, this study compared the recognition performances of human listeners and those of three state-of-the-art, off-the-shelf ASR systems (Whisper-large-V3, Google Chirp 3, and Omnilingual) on the recognition of Dutch continuous read and spontaneous speech from a single speaker with severe dysarthria. Results showed that both humans listeners and the three off-the-shelf ASR systems exhibit word error rates (WER) exceeding 70% on average, indicating that DSR is highly challenging for both humans and ASR systems. Fine-tuning on the dysarthric speech significantly reduced WER. Although overall WERs are still quite high (>23%), the personalised DSR models outperformed the human listeners, and performance is getting closer to being useful for supporting day-to-day communication of dysarthric speakers. Future research should focus on improving personalized DSR on spontaneous speech and longer utterances in the case of read speech, with a specific focus on particular phonemes.
items.author: Yuanyuan Zhang, Dimme de Groot, Jorge Martinez, Odette Scharenborg

items.title: From Facts to Insights: A Persona-Driven Dual Memory Framework and Dataset for Role-Playing Agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.25693v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: While role-playing agents excel in short-term interactions, long-term conversations overwhelm context windows, motivating external memory frameworks. Current systems typically rely on persona-agnostic summarization, which records facts without persona-specific interpretation, yielding generic responses that compromise persona fidelity. To bridge this gap, we introduce RoleMemo, a dataset featuring four reasoning tasks where the factual fragments must be interpreted through the persona to reach the correct answer. Evaluation on RoleMemo exposes critical limitations of persona-agnostic frameworks. We thus propose DualMem, which decouples memory into two streams: factual cognition and persona-conditioned insight. Trained through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL), our framework with a 4B-parameter model outperforms zero-shot persona-agnostic frameworks powered by DeepSeek-V3.2 for sustained persona fidelity. Our resources are available at https://github.com/Collab-Gen/RoleMemo.
items.author: Rongsheng Zhang, Ruofan Hu, Weijie Chen, Jiji Tang, Junnan Ren, Wanying Wu, Xunuoyan Chen, Tangjie Lv, Tao Jin, Zhou Zhao

items.title: SpecHop: Continuous Speculation for Accelerating Multi-Hop Retrieval Agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.21965v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models increasingly use external tools such as web search and document retrieval to solve information-intensive tasks. However, multi-hop tool use in complex tasks introduces substantial latency, since the model must repeatedly wait for tool observations before continuing. We study how to accelerate such trajectories without changing the final trajectory the model would have taken without acceleration, assuming access to faster but less reliable speculator tools. We develop a theoretical framework for lossless speculation in multi-hop tool-use settings, characterizing the optimal achievable latency gain. We propose SpecHop, a continuous speculation framework that maintains multiple speculative threads, verifies predicted observations asynchronously as target tool outputs arrive, commits correct branches, and rolls back incorrect ones. This preserves accuracy while reducing wall-clock latency. We show that SpecHop can approach oracle latency gains with enough active threads. Empirically, on retrieval-augmented multi-hop tasks, SpecHop closely matches theoretical predictions and reduces latency by up to 40\% in some settings. Code: https://github.com/mehrdadsaberi/spechop
items.author: Mehrdad Saberi, Keivan Rezaei, Soheil Feizi

items.title: RECOVER: Robust Entity Correction via agentic Orchestration of hypothesis Variants for Evidence-based Recovery
items.summary:
arXiv:2603.16411v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Entity recognition in Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) is challenging for rare and domain-specific terms. In domains such as finance, medicine, and air-traffic control, these errors are costly. If an entity is entirely absent from the ASR output, text-only post-correction has little signal to recover it. To address this, we introduce RECOVER, an agentic post-ASR entity-correction framework. It leverages multiple hypotheses as evidence from ASR, retrieves relevant entities, proposes Large Language Model (LLM) correction under constraints, filters them through deterministic guardrails and uses an LLM critic that judges each surviving edit and can trigger a targeted feedback round to recover an entity the first pass missed. The hypotheses are used by one of several strategies, namely 1-Best, Entity-Aware Select, Recognizer Output Voting Error Reduction (ROVER) Ensemble, LLM-Select and Adaptive Routing. Evaluated across five diverse datasets over a Whisper-large-v3 baseline, it achieves up to 49% relative reduction in entity-phrase word error rate (E-WER) and increases entity recall by up to 14 percentage points while preserving the overall word error rate (WER), with LLM-Select the strongest strategy.
items.author: Abhishek Kumar, Aashraya Sachdeva

items.title: Beyond Trajectory Similarity: Evaluating Surgical Planning by Protocol Adherence
items.summary:
arXiv:2601.10455v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Surgical planning is commonly evaluated by trajectory similarity to a single observed execution, a paradigm borrowed from activity anticipation benchmarks such as Ego4D. This conflates two distinct concepts: task completion and protocol adherence and assumes similarity to a completed surgical trajectory implies a valid plan. In surgery, this assumption is flawed: the clinically relevant target is protocol adherence rather than mere completion, and the reference trajectory is only one observed execution that may itself deviate from the protocol. We therefore introduce an evaluation framework grounded in expert-defined protocol rules that directly measures protocol adherence. Under this framework, similarity-based metrics systematically fail: they penalize protocol-adherent plans that deviate from the reference trajectory, while rewarding protocol-violating plans that remain superficially similar to it. Evaluating Video-LLMs further reveals two separable failure modes: unreliable video-to-state grounding and under-constrained planning. Neither is resolved by model scaling alone, whereas structural knowledge injection provides consistent gains. Our results motivate a shift from trajectory similarity toward protocol adherence as the evaluation standard for surgical planning.
items.author: Ruochen Li, Kun Yuan, Yufei Xia, Yue Zhou, Qingyu Lu, Weihang Li, Youxiang Zhu, Nassir Navab

items.title: Investigating LLM Capabilities on Long Context Comprehension for Clinical Question Answering
items.summary:
arXiv:2510.18691v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Despite the impressive reported performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on medical Question-Answering (QA), evaluation still overrelies on multiple-choice and extractive settings primarily assessing textbook knowledge, with limited work on open-ended QA over patient records. We present a comprehensive study investigating LLM long-context (LC) comprehension on longitudinal, patient-centric Electronic Health Records (EHRs) across multiple datasets, models and metrics, covering extractive, multiple-choice, and open-ended generative QA under different context formulation and Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) settings. We show that medically fine-tuned models offer no measurable benefit over base counterparts, smaller models exhibit stronger memorization, and longitudinal supplementary notes aid generative QA. Reasoning models gain on complex multi-note QA under LLM Correctness but not stricter reference-aligned metrics, while hybrid RAG with reranking outperforms Full-Context (FC) prompting. A question-category analysis and multi-faceted metric evaluation further reveal where RAG and FC excel and struggle, with RAG falling behind in longitudinal reasoning, thus uncovering systematic failures pointing to the need for reasoning-appropriate metrics.
items.author: Feras AlMannaa, Talia Tseriotou, Jenny Chim, Maria Liakata

items.title: Beyond Gold Standards: Epistemic Ensemble of LLM Judges for Formal Mathematical Reasoning
items.summary:
arXiv:2506.10903v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Statement autoformalization plays a crucial role in formal mathematical reasoning by enabling the automatic translation of natural language statements into formal languages. While recent advances using large language models (LLMs) have shown promising capabilities in autoformalization, methods for automatically evaluating autoformalization remain underexplored. LLM-as-a-judge presents a promising approach for automating such evaluation, however, existing methods typically employ coarse-grained and generic evaluation criteria, which limit their effectiveness for advanced formal mathematical reasoning, where quality hinges on nuanced, multi-granular dimensions. In this work, we take a step toward addressing this gap by introducing a systematic, automatic method to evaluate autoformalization tasks. The proposed method is based on an epistemically and formally grounded ensemble (EFG) of LLM judges, defined on criteria encompassing logical preservation (LP), mathematical consistency (MC), formal quality (FQ), and formal validity (FV), resulting in a transparent assessment that accounts for different contributing factors. We validate the proposed framework to serve as a proxy for autoformalization assessment within the domain of formal mathematics. Overall, our experiments demonstrate that the EFG ensemble of LLM judges is a more suitable emerging proxy for evaluation than a coarse-grained model. These findings suggest that LLM judges, especially when guided by a well-defined set of atomic properties, could offer a scalable, interpretable, and reliable support for evaluating formal mathematical reasoning.
items.author: Lan Zhang, Marco Valentino, Jordan Meadows, Andr\'e Freitas

items.title: On Robustness of Prompt-based Semantic Parsing with Large Pre-trained Language Model: An Empirical Study on Codex
items.summary:
arXiv:2301.12868v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Semantic parsing is a technique aimed at constructing a structured representation of the meaning of a natural-language question. Recent advancements in few-shot language models trained on code have demonstrated superior performance in generating these representations compared to traditional unimodal language models, which are trained on downstream tasks. Despite these advancements, existing fine-tuned neural semantic parsers are susceptible to adversarial attacks on natural-language inputs. While it has been established that the robustness of smaller semantic parsers can be enhanced through adversarial training, this approach is not feasible for large language models in real-world scenarios, as it requires both substantial computational resources and expensive human annotation on in-domain semantic parsing data. This paper presents the first empirical study on the adversarial robustness of a large prompt-based language model of code, \codex. Our results demonstrate that the state-of-the-art (SOTA) code-language models are vulnerable to carefully crafted adversarial examples. To address this challenge, we propose methods for improving robustness without the need for significant amounts of labeled data or heavy computational resources.
items.author: Terry Yue Zhuo, Zhuang Li, Yujin Huang, Fatemeh Shiri, Weiqing Wang, Gholamreza Haffari, Yuan-Fang Li

items.title: Rethinking Round-Trip Translation for Machine Translation Evaluation
items.summary:
arXiv:2209.07351v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Automatic evaluation on low-resource language translation suffers from a deficiency of parallel corpora. Round-trip translation could be served as a clever and straightforward technique to alleviate the requirement of the parallel evaluation corpus. However, there was an observation of obscure correlations between the evaluation scores by forward and round-trip translations in the era of statistical machine translation (SMT). In this paper, we report the surprising finding that round-trip translation can be used for automatic evaluation without the references. Firstly, our revisit on the round-trip translation in SMT evaluation unveils that its long-standing misunderstanding is essentially caused by copying mechanism. After removing copying mechanism in SMT, round-trip translation scores can appropriately reflect the forward translation performance. Then, we demonstrate the rectification is overdue as round-trip translation could benefit multiple machine translation evaluation tasks. To be more specific, round-trip translation could be used i) to predict corresponding forward translation scores; ii) to improve the performance of the recently advanced quality estimation model; and iii) to identify adversarial competitors in shared tasks via cross-system verification.
items.author: Terry Yue Zhuo, Qiongkai Xu, Xuanli He, Trevor Cohn

items.title: WaferTetris: Efficient Freeform Mapping on Wafer-Scale Accelerators
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18527v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Wafer-scale accelerators offer massive compute capacity through hundreds of thousands of processing elements (PEs) interconnected across a single wafer, but realizing this potential requires efficient application mapping. Their scale makes programming these systems and mapping applications onto them challenging. Existing approaches rely on template-based mappings to maintain productivity, but these templates restrict the mapping design space. In particular, they impose fixed geometric layouts over the PE grid, often leaving compute and memory resources underutilized.
  In this work, we present WaferTetris, a system that removes these geometric restrictions through freeform mapping. Its Tetris-like strategy flexibly packs computation across the wafer, improving PE utilization and usable memory capacity while preserving PE-task code. We develop a recurrence-based throughput model that captures branch-and-join dependencies to guide spatial parallelism, and an architecture model with per-color gates that enable existing FPGA place-and-route algorithms to enforce WSE routing constraints.
  We evaluate WaferTetris on Cerebras WSE-3 using LLM decoding and scientific stencil benchmarks. For LLM decoding, it achieves up to $4.42\times$ the system throughput of a template-based automatic mapping baseline on the same fabric size. Compared with the manually optimized WaferLLM, WaferTetris supports $1.8\times$ the context length for LLaMA3.1-8B (80k versus 44k), while delivering equal or higher per-user throughput at matched context lengths, up to $1.10\times$.
items.author: Dayou Du, Congjie He, Andrew Boutros, Luo Mai, Vaughn Betz, Jianyi Cheng

items.title: Marimba: A System One Model for Speech
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18330v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Speech applications require decisions about term presence, turn completion, and language within an audio window. We present Marimba, an interface for typed speech decisions built on frozen Qwen3-ASR 0.6B features. Lexical questions use zero-shot scoring of ASR transcripts; non-lexical questions use a question-conditioned head and a separate layer-18 turn-end readout. Language identification uses the ASR model's own language scores. On private conversational test sets, decoder AUROC is 0.80-0.92; on public read speech it is 0.92-0.97. Speech Commands four-way accuracy is 0.93; binary lexical ECE is at most 0.08. Personal-information detection, which passes the greedy transcript to a private, curated PII pipeline, reaches item-level F1 0.904 on synthetic Brazilian Portuguese speech (1.000 on reference transcripts). Layer-12 speaker readouts detect speaker change with AUROC 0.966-0.980 on AMI and VoxConverse, above an ECAPA baseline, and count speakers (0, 1, 2, or 3+) more accurately than pyannote 3.1. The turn-end readout reaches AUROC 0.930 versus Smart Turn v3.2 at 0.982 on Smart Turn's own test set. On a subset of ICSI meetings labeled by next speaker, AUROC is 0.716 versus 0.712; the paired confidence interval includes zero.
items.author: Solano Amadori

items.title: PerfArena: Ranking LLMs by Code Performance
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18030v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Industry now relies on LLMs to write a large share of production code. Although that code is mostly, but not always, correct, correctness alone does not determine whether it is fit for repeated and extensive use, which depends on what the code costs in time, memory and energy. Most code-generation benchmarks nonetheless evaluate correctness in isolation, and most performance-oriented benchmarks cover few languages and rarely measure energy consumption. To address this gap, we present PERFARENA, an open-source, reproducible arena that ranks LLMs by the performance of their generated code across multiple languages and competitions. PERFARENA executes the solutions of each LLM on a Unix-like host and reports correctness together with latency, peak memory, and energy consumption. Correctness oracles, performance oracles, profilers, and code-generation workflows are pluggable in PERFARENA, enabling the integration of new judging backends and measurement tools without changing the pipeline. We evaluate PERFARENA on two competitions: CLBGComp, 10 compute-intensive benchmarks from the Computer Language Benchmarks Game, and LeetCodeComp, 99 LeetCode problems whose accepted solutions differ measurably in latency. Currently, PERFARENA holds 9,455 correct and measured solutions from 13 state-of-the-art LLMs across 7 programming languages. Across both competitions, got-6-astra is the only LLM that no other LLM beats significantly in latency, energy consumption, or peak memory, solving 99.7% of LeetCodeComp and 100% of CLBGComp. All PERFARENA leaderboards and measured solutions are publicly available, providing a continuously updated reference that helps developers choose an LLM per language and metric, instead of relying only on correctness rates or pricing.
items.author: Rui Rua, Hailemariam Mersha, Joao Paulo Fernandes, Karim Ali

items.title: AmbiSteer: Selectively Eliciting Ambiguity-Aware Responses in Vision-Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17900v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often exhibit overconfidence, providing firm answers even when visual evidence is insufficient. A prominent case is referential ambiguity in Visual Question Answering (VQA), where multiple entities in an image are plausible referents of a question. Addressing such cases requires recognizing when ambiguity is present: ambiguous questions can be handled by asking for clarification or enumerating plausible referents, while unambiguous questions should receive a direct answer. Current VLMs struggle with this distinction, often defaulting to a single interpretation. To investigate whether activation steering can serve as an inference-time mechanism to elicit such behaviors, we introduce AmbiSteer, a lightweight framework to selectively elicit ambiguity-aware behavior. Across three VLMs, we find that steering alone has limited and model-dependent effects, while prompting is generally more effective. Combining prompting and steering substantially increases clarification and enumeration behaviors, but also elicits them on unambiguous cases. AmbiSteer addresses this using a linear classifier to predict input ambiguity and condition the steering direction accordingly, increasing the proportion of inputs handled appropriately from 59.0% to 77.0% on average across models. Our work sets the ground for lightweight approaches to reduce model overconfidence in uncertain multimodal settings.
items.author: Monica Riedler, Samuele Antonelli, Barbara Plank, Raffaella Bernardi

items.title: Agentic induction of common data elements and information extraction from sarcoma case report abstracts
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18506v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Common data elements (CDEs) support clinical data comparability but are usually defined manually. We investigated whether large language model agents could derive a CDE schema from sarcoma case report abstracts and apply it at scale. An agent proposed 72,909 candidate CDEs from 24,588 PubMed abstracts; agentic consolidation yielded 1,570 CDEs. We retained 53 supported by at least 50 abstracts and attempted evidence-linked extraction across the corpus. Processing succeeded for all retained CDEs in 79.2% of abstracts, including responses indicating non-mention. Two human reviewers approved 83.0% of retained CDEs for relevance, 67.9% for clarity, and 56.6% for correctness. In 100 sampled abstracts, exact agreement with the value extracted by the LLM was 94.9% among 1,116 pairs with a non-empty answer (abstract-level bootstrap 95% CI, 93.0-96.4%). Errors concentrated in anatomical and temporal fields. These findings support agent-assisted schema drafting followed by expert curation before large-scale extraction.
items.author: Daniel Reichenpfader (Institute for Patient-Centered Digital Health, Bern University of Applied Sciences, Bern, Switzerland, Faculty of Medicine, University of Geneva, Geneva, Switzerland), Kwaku Appiagyei (F. Hoffmann-La Roche AG, Basel, Switzerland), Manovah Nadarajah (Kantonsspital Aarau, Aarau, Switzerland), Ahmed Reda Bahr (University of Alexandria, Alexandria, Egypt), Irina Filchenko (Department of Neurology, Inselspital, Bern University Hospital and University of Bern, Bern, Switzerland), Fabio Dennst\"adt (Data Semantics and Decision Making Institute, Department of Digital Medicine, Inselspital, Bern University Hospital and University of Bern, Bern, Switzerland)

items.title: LitArc-Bench: Disentangling Text-Specific Reader-Response Dynamics from Position and Lexical Affect
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18412v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When model predictions track an unfolding human affect trajectory, alignment may reflect narrative position, affective words, or text-specific reader-response dynamics. We introduce LitArc-Bench to separate these explanations: 39 Chinese-language literary excerpts segmented into seven checkpoints, with 430 questionnaires from 81 adults in two classroom groups (9,020 VAD ratings).
