A fundamental challenge is that, for any given scenario, this discrepancy cannot be observed directly, since both systems are accessible only through finite samples, often of heterogeneous sizes across scenarios. Standard predictive inference methods are therefore ill-suited, as they quantify uncertainty in observable outputs rather than latent population parameters. To address this, we construct confidence sets for these latent parameters and use them to derive a robust proxy for the sim-to-real discrepancy. We then estimate the quantile function of this proxy to obtain a distribution-level risk profile of the simulator, which supports a broad range of statistical summaries, including statistical inference for the real output distribution in a new scenario, the calculation of risk measures like Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR), and principled comparisons across simulators. Our method is model-agnostic and handles general output spaces, such as categorical survey responses and continuous multi-dimensional data. We demonstrate the practical utility of this method by evaluating the alignment of four major LLMs with human populations on the WorldValueBench dataset.
items.author: Garud Iyengar, Yu-Shiou Willy Lin, Kaizheng Wang

items.title: E0: Expressive Fine-Grained Discrete Action Prediction for Vision-Language-Action Models via Tweedie Discrete Diffusion
items.summary:
arXiv:2511.21542v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a unified framework for robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and control generation. However, existing VLA systems still struggle to generalize across diverse tasks, scenes, and camera viewpoints, and often produce coarse or unstable actions. We argue that these limitations are closely tied to the structural properties of actions in VLA settings, including the inherent multi-peaked nature of action distributions, the token-based symbolic reasoning of pretrained VLM/VLA backbones, and the effective finite resolution imposed by real-world robotic control. Motivated by these properties, we introduce E0, a tweedie discrete diffusion framework that formulates action generation as iterative denoising over quantized action tokens. By operating in a discrete action space with a principled diffusion process, E0 naturally aligns with token-based reasoning, supports fine-grained yet executable action control, and avoids the distributional mismatch of masking-based discrete diffusion. Experiments on LIBERO, VLABench, ManiSkill, and a real-world Franka arm demonstrate that E0 achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse environments, outperforming strong baselines by 8.1% on average.
items.author: Zhihao Zhan, Jiaying Zhou, Likui Zhang, Qinhan Lyu, Hao Liu, Weizheng Li, Jusheng Zhang, Ziliang Chen, Tianshui Chen, Ruifeng Zhai, Keze Wang, Liang Lin, Guangrun Wang

items.title: BigCodeArena: Unveiling More Reliable Human Preferences in Code Generation via Execution
items.summary:
arXiv:2510.08697v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Crowdsourced model evaluation platforms, such as Chatbot Arena, enable real-time evaluation from human perspectives to assess the quality of model responses. In the coding domain, manually examining the quality of LLM-generated content is extremely challenging, as it requires understanding long chunks of raw code and deliberately simulating code execution. To this end, we introduce BigCodeArena, an open human evaluation platform for code generation backed by a comprehensive and on-the-fly execution environment. Built on top of Chatbot Arena, BigCodeArena enables the execution of LLM-generated code and allows humans to interact with the execution process and outcomes. We collected over 14,000 raw code-centric conversation sessions across 10 widely used LLMs, spanning 10 languages and 8 types of execution environments. Among these conversations, we identified more than 4,700 multi-turn samples with pairwise human preferences. Further analysis uncovers underexplored preferences of LLMs in fine-grained domains characterized by tasks, languages, and frameworks. To systematically examine code understanding and generation capabilities of frontier LLMs, we curated two benchmarks based on the collected data, namely BigCodeReward and AutoCodeArena. For BigCodeReward, we post-processed the 4,700 conversations and evaluated the consistency between reward models and human preferences. The evaluation shows that most LLMs have superior performance in judging coding preferences when the execution results are available. Inspired by these findings, we propose AutoCodeArena, an automatic Elo rating benchmark designed to assess the coding quality of LLMs without human involvement. We find that proprietary LLMs like GPT-5, Claude-Sonnet-4, and Claude-Opus-4 still lead in code generation performance among recent emerging models.
items.author: Terry Yue Zhuo, Xiaolong Jin, Hange Liu, Juyong Jiang, Tianyang Liu, Chen Gong, Bhupesh Bishnoi, Vaisakhi Mishra, Marek Suppa, Noah Ziems, Saiteja Utpala, Ming Xu, Guangyu Song, Kaixin Li, Yuhan Cao, Bo Liu, Zheng Liu, Sabina Abdurakhmanova, Wenhao Yu, Mengzhao Jia, Jihan Yao, Kenneth Hamilton, Kumar Shridhar, Minh Chien Vu, Dingmin Wang, Jiawei Liu, Zijian Wang, Qian Liu, Binyuan Hui, Meg Risdal, Ahsen Khaliq, Atin Sood, Zhenchang Xing, Wasi Uddin Ahmad, John Grundy, David Lo, Banghua Zhu, Xiaoning Du, Torsten Scholak, Leandro von Werra

items.title: Graph Your Own Prompt
items.summary:
arXiv:2509.23373v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We propose Graph Consistency Regularization (GCR), a novel framework that injects relational graph structures, derived from model predictions, into the learning process to promote class-aware, semantically meaningful feature representations. Functioning as a form of self-prompting, GCR enables the model to refine its internal structure using its own outputs. While deep networks learn rich representations, these often capture noisy inter-class similarities that contradict the model's predicted semantics. GCR addresses this issue by introducing parameter-free Graph Consistency Layers (GCLs) at arbitrary depths. Each GCL builds a batch-level feature similarity graph and aligns it with a global, class-aware masked prediction graph, derived by modulating softmax prediction similarities with intra-class indicators. This alignment enforces that feature-level relationships reflect class-consistent prediction behavior, acting as a semantic regularizer throughout the network. Unlike prior work, GCR introduces a multi-layer, cross-space graph alignment mechanism with adaptive weighting, where layer importance is learned from graph discrepancy magnitudes. This allows the model to prioritize semantically reliable layers and suppress noisy ones, enhancing feature quality without modifying the architecture or training procedure. GCR is model-agnostic, lightweight, and improves semantic structure across various networks and datasets. Experiments show that GCR promotes cleaner feature structure, stronger intra-class cohesion, and improved generalization, offering a new perspective on learning from prediction structure. [Project website](https://darcyddx.github.io/gcr/) [Code](https://github.com/Darcyddx/graph-prompt)
items.author: Xi Ding, Lei Wang, Piotr Koniusz, Yongsheng Gao

items.title: Chi-Square Wavelet Graph Neural Networks for Heterogeneous Graph Anomaly Detection
items.summary:
arXiv:2505.18934v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Graph Anomaly Detection (GAD) in heterogeneous networks presents unique challenges due to node and edge heterogeneity. Existing Graph Neural Network (GNN) methods primarily focus on homogeneous GAD and thus fail to address three key issues: (C1) Capturing abnormal signal and rich semantics across diverse meta-paths; (C2) Retaining high-frequency content in HIN dimension alignment; and (C3) Learning effectively from difficult anomaly samples with class imbalance. To overcome these, we propose ChiGAD, a spectral GNN framework based on a novel Chi-Square filter, inspired by the wavelet effectiveness in diverse domains. Specifically, ChiGAD consists of: (1) Multi-Graph Chi-Square Filter, which captures anomalous information via applying dedicated Chi-Square filters to each meta-path graph; (2) Interactive Meta-Graph Convolution, which aligns features while preserving high-frequency information and incorporates heterogeneous messages by a unified Chi-Square Filter; and (3) Contribution-Informed Cross-Entropy Loss, which prioritizes difficult anomalies to address class imbalance. Extensive experiments on public and industrial datasets show that ChiGAD outperforms state-of-the-art models on multiple metrics. Additionally, its homogeneous variant, ChiGNN, excels on seven GAD datasets, validating the effectiveness of Chi-Square filters. Our code is available at https://github.com/HsipingLi/ChiGAD.
items.author: Xiping Li, Xiangyu Dong, Xingyi Zhang, Kun Xie, Yuanhao Feng, Bo Wang, Guilin Li, Wuxiong Zeng, Xiujun Shu, Sibo Wang

items.title: AbFlowNet: Optimizing Antibody-Antigen Binding Energy via Diffusion-GFlowNet Fusion
items.summary:
arXiv:2505.12358v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Complementarity Determining Regions (CDRs) are critical segments of an antibody that facilitate binding to specific antigens. Current computational methods for CDR design utilize reconstruction losses and do not jointly optimize binding energy, a crucial metric for antibody efficacy. Rather, binding energy optimization is done through computationally expensive Online Reinforcement Learning (RL) pipelines rely heavily on unreliable binding energy estimators. In this paper, we propose AbFlowNet, a novel generative framework that integrates GFlowNet with Diffusion models. By framing each diffusion step as a state in the GFlowNet framework, AbFlowNet jointly optimizes standard diffusion losses and binding energy by directly incorporating energy signals into the training process, thereby unifying diffusion and reward optimization in a single procedure. Experimental results show that AbFlowNet outperforms the base diffusion model by 3.06% in amino acid recovery, 20.40% in geometric reconstruction (RMSD), and 3.60% in binding energy improvement ratio. ABFlowNet also decreases Top-1 total energy and binding energy errors by 24.8% and 38.1% without pseudo-labeling the test dataset or using computationally expensive online RL regimes.
items.author: Abrar Rahman Abir, Haz Sameen Shahgir, Md Rownok Zahan Ratul, Md Toki Tahmid, Greg Ver Steeg, Yue Dong

items.title: LEGAL-UQA: Testing Constitutional Question-Answering Systems for Urdu Speakers with a Parallel English-Urdu Benchmark
items.summary:
arXiv:2410.13013v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Legal information assistants could help Urdu speakers understand their constitutional rights, but building reliable systems requires test data and evaluation methods suited to the language. We present LEGAL-UQA, a parallel English-Urdu benchmark of 619 question-answer pairs linked to passages from Pakistan's Constitution. Each example includes the question, reference answer, and source passage in both languages. We evaluate two components separately: answering Urdu questions when the source passage is supplied, and retrieving the passage from which each question was generated. We also compare JEV, a decision model used as an automated judge, with human grades. The findings show that model rankings depend on how answer similarity is measured, while a simple word-matching method retrieves source passages more effectively than the embedding methods tested. At the evaluated cutoff, JEV agrees with human grades less often than a baseline that gives every answer full credit. An audit also identifies cases where generated references omit information supported by the source. Together, these findings highlight the need to test retrieval and answering separately, include simple retrieval baselines, and validate automated judges and reference answers with human review when engineering legal QA software for Urdu speakers.
items.author: Faizan Faisal, Umair Yousaf, Muhammad Hassnain, Zeerak Babar

items.title: Benign Overfitting for Regression with Trained Two-Layer ReLU Networks
items.summary:
arXiv:2410.06191v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study the least-square regression problem with a two-layer fully-connected neural network, with ReLU activation function, trained by gradient flow. Our first result is a generalization result, that requires no assumptions on the underlying regression function or the noise other than that they are bounded. We operate in the neural tangent kernel regime, and our generalization result is developed via a decomposition of the excess risk into estimation and approximation errors, viewing gradient flow as an implicit regularizer. This decomposition in the context of neural networks is a novel perspective of gradient descent, and helps us avoid uniform convergence traps. In this work, we also establish that under the same setting, the trained network overfits to the data. Together, these results, establishes the first result on benign overfitting for finite-width ReLU networks for arbitrary regression functions.

items.title: Using AI in Research | Stanford CS193T Guest Panel with Mark Algee-Hewitt, Megan Ma & Markus Covert
items.summary:
Explore AI courses and programs from Stanford Online: https://stanford.io/4BYTekh 

How do Stanford researchers use AI in their own fields? In this Stanford CS193T: Thinking with AI guest panel recording, hosted by Senior Lecturer Cynthia Bailey, guests from three different corners of campus (English, Law, and Bioengineering) share innovative applications of AI in their respective disciplines, what responsible use of AI means in their academic communities, and how they protect the core of what makes them successful from atrophy. Professor Mark Algee-Hewitt leads Stanford's Digital Humanities program, using computational methods to explore language and meaning-making. Megan Ma is the Executive Director of the Stanford Legal Innovation through Frontier Technology (LIFT) Lab, creating AI tools for the practice of law and studying the future of legal education and training under shifting attorney labor market pressures due to AI. Professor Markus Covert is the Chair of the Department of Bioengineering, and for over two decades has pioneered the development of computational models of complex biological processes.

Key questions answered in this lecture recording:
Q: Should professors use AI to write recommendation letters?
A: Markus Covert has decided not to write letters with AI; he uses it only to hold and recall information about a student, and asks how AI could raise a letter's quality rather than save time.

Q: Should universities and journals ban AI?
A: Mark Algee-Hewitt argues blanket bans push people to use AI without saying so. Journals in his field instead require disclosure and define acceptable uses, such as coding with Claude Code but not writing the paper.

Q: How is AI being used to train lawyers?
A: Megan Ma describes LIFT Lab's open-source deposition simulator, which turns a witness statement into an AI witness with adjustable personalities (combative, evasive, forgetful) so junior attorneys can practice.

Q: What skills should students not lose to AI?
A: Mark Algee-Hewitt names critical thinking, Megan Ma names judgment built from real experience and storytelling, and Markus Covert names scientific taste, intellectual courage, and curiosity.

Q: How can I use AI to write without losing my own voice?
A: Markus Covert writes each paragraph himself, then asks Claude for missing citations, the strongest counterarguments, and analogies from other fields, checking every paper himself.

Q: Are rubrics or preference rankings better for evaluating legal AI?
A: In LIFT Lab's JudgmentBench research, Megan Ma reports that preference rankings far outperformed rubrics because they capture lawyer intuition.

About the speakers:
Mark Algee-Hewitt leads Stanford's Digital Humanities program. His work combines critical and quantitative approaches to the analysis of literature. As director of the Stanford Literary Lab, he has led projects on the literature of suspense, the history of racialized language in American literature, and an analysis of the reports of the OECD's anti-bribery convention.

Megan Ma is the Executive Director of the Stanford Legal Innovation through Frontier Technology (LIFT) Lab. She also teaches courses in computational law at the Law School and Department of Computer Science.

Markus Covert is the Chair of the Department of Bioengineering at Stanford. His research focus is building computational models of complex biological processes, and using these models to guide an experimental program. Biological systems of interest include metabolic, regulatory and signaling networks as well as cell-cell interactions.

items.title: AI Memory, RAG & Prompt Injection Explained | Stanford CS193T Lecture 3 with Cynthia Bailey
items.summary:
Explore AI courses and programs from Stanford Online: https://stanford.io/4BYTekh 

What else is sharing your AI's context window besides your prompt? In this Stanford CS193T: Thinking with AI lecture recording, Senior Lecturer Cynthia Bailey focuses on context, information, and prompt instructions that persist beyond a single chat session: settings, remembered facts, uploaded files, and retrieved web pages. Examples include how to use these tools to reduce sycophancy and "AI style," understanding what your chat history is (and isn't) used for, saving your best prompts as reusable Skills or Gems, and strategic withholding, where the smartest prompt leaves something out. She introduces retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for grounding AI in your own documents when they would overflow the context window, and the documented ways trust in a RAG store can fail. The lecture closes on a cybersecurity note with prompt injection: why an AI can't always tell your instructions apart from malicious text on the internet.

Key questions answered in this lecture recording:
Q: Does ChatGPT learn from my conversations?
A: A released model's weights are frozen, so memories change behavior only through the context window. But a company that sees your chat history could use it to train future models; Stanford's licensed AI tools prohibit that, while personal accounts may not.

Q: What is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)?
A: RAG is a user-curated document store, much larger than the context window, that the tool searches to place only relevant documents into the context. Because RAG content gets extra weight, Bailey warns that bad sources can poison results.

Q: What is the adaptive chameleon vs stubborn sloth problem in LLMs?
A: Citing the paper "Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth," Bailey explains that models sometimes accept bad information in your RAG too eagerly and sometimes ignore your sources in favor of training data. Either behavior can help or hurt.

Q: How do I get more honest feedback from ChatGPT or Claude?
A: Use strategic withholding: ask the AI to evaluate "this essay," not "my essay," or frame your resume as a candidate's, and use a temporary chat so memories don't reveal it's yours.

Q: What is prompt injection?
A: The system prompt, your prompt, and retrieved web pages are one continuous stream of tokens, so hidden text on a web page can issue instructions the model may obey. The risk grows when AI has connectors to email or files.

Q: Do Claude Skills or Gemini Gems fine-tune the model?
A: No. Bailey says skills and gems are one more piece of text in the context window, functioning between the system prompt and your prompt, and they do not change the model's weights.

About the speaker:
Cynthia Bailey is a Senior Lecturer in the Computer Science Department at Stanford University. In 2023-2024, she served as an AI Policy Fellow in the United States Senate through the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS). Her scholarship focuses on computer science education, AI/machine learning, and the social impacts of technology, including creating courses such as Equity and Governance for Artificial Intelligence and Race and Gender in Silicon Valley. Her teaching and research awards include the Lloyd W. Dinkelspiel Award for exceptional contributions to undergraduate education at Stanford, the Lasting Impact Award from the International Computing Education Research conference, a "Top 10 Papers of All Time" award at the 50th anniversary of the ACM SIGCSE Technical Symposium, and the Stanford Society of Women Engineers' Professor of the Year. She has consulted for Apple, NASA, law firms, and machine learning startups. She holds a Ph.D. in Computer Science from UC San Diego.

items.title: Your PR Says the Tests Passed. Prove It. - Stephen Chin & Cassandra Chin
items.summary:
A pull request can claim that checks passed even when the recorded commands do not establish that the submitted change was tested. Cassandra Chin built Tracetoon to recover the context behind a branch, write a better pull request description and optionally explain it with a comic. Together with Stephen Chin, she follows one troublesome review through repeated revisions, missing evidence and rising token costs. The problem is more specific than producing fluent prose: the writer needs to connect a change to its rationale, the commands that ran, their timing and the version of the code they actually checked.

Their next iteration uses Relate, an embedded graph database written in Rust, to assemble that evidence before the writing begins. A connected brief gives the writer and reviewers the same sources, reducing repeated searches through session logs. The speakers explain why they kept a stronger writer while using less expensive reviewers to check claims against the brief, and show results from their own PR Bench development comparisons. Those reported results combine improved description quality with roughly half the token usage; they describe this project's evaluation, not a guarantee for other codebases. The practical pattern is to preserve provenance and relationships outside the model's conversation, make uncertainty visible, and give reviewers evidence tied to the submitted content. The comic provides the story, but the useful engineering artifact is the reviewable chain behind each claim.

items.title: Every Correction You Give Your Agent Is Data - Brian Douglas, Paper Compute
items.summary:
A Rust program can compile and still violate the decisions an experienced teammate would catch immediately. Brian Douglas finds that missing knowledge in moments when engineers push back on their coding agents. At Paper Compute, he captures agent sessions, labels corrections and uses those traces to recover the reasoning that otherwise disappears inside a local coding harness. His example starts with a gap in his own Rust expertise: accepting plausible generated code leads to objections later, when a teammate reviews the pull request. Those earlier objections become useful training material only if someone preserves and labels them.

Brian demonstrates session capture with Tapes and Paper Console, then runs a Twin Review prototype against a pull request using examples of a teammate's feedback. He discusses labels for pushback, successful sessions and regressions, and shows how the same records can support skills, evaluations or model adaptation. The prototype is a demonstration, not a measured comparison against an independent evaluation set, and Brian corrects himself during the recording to clarify that Twin Review is not publicly released because its data is sensitive. His practical starting point is simpler than training a model: collect the traces you already generate, find the corrections that encode your team's conventions, and turn those into a skill you can test. The durable asset is the connection between a decision, the expert's objection and the resulting outcome.

items.title: Your Agent Hates Your CLI - Ayush Bhardwaj, Allos AI
items.summary:
An agent can hide a failed test behind a successful shell pipeline. It can also trim away the error message and confidently report that everything worked. Ayush Bhardwaj examined roughly 20,000 tool calls from his own coding sessions and found a product roadmap in the commands agents wrote immediately afterward. Repeated uses of head, tail, grep and Python showed where tools returned too much information, exposed the wrong fields, or made the agent reconstruct the same query again. The examples come from his own traces and his chat history CLI, which lets agents retrieve context from earlier coding sessions.

The fixes are small and concrete: return the messages around a search match, offer compact search results, inspect several sessions in one call, and put a useful failure summary at the end of the output. But implementing a flag does little if the skill file still teaches the old interface. In Ayush's case study, agents kept passing a flag that did nothing until the instructions changed. He also explains how to turn recorded calls into replay tests, reserve examples for evaluation, and check whether better output actually improves answers and reduces turns. Smaller responses alone do not establish a faster or cheaper workflow. The useful feedback is already in the transcript: what the agent tried, what it discarded, and what it had to ask again.

items.title: Give Your On-Call Its Own AI Teammate - Swaapnika Motapothula, Chinmay Gandhi & Vlad Tsvang, Meta
items.summary:
Twelve alerts fire at 2 a.m., and a useful assistant can still leave the engineer coordinating every step. Meta's on call team uses that illustrative scenario to explain a different design: one AI teammate per rotation, with shared context, its own identity, persistent memory and explicit limits on what it can do. Swaapnika Motapothula, Chinmay Gandhi and Vlad Tsvang describe a system that connects alerts, tickets, incident history and code changes instead of leaving each automation with its own isolated view. The goal is to bring a human a decision with supporting evidence and a proposed action.

Their autonomy ladder starts with investigation, advances to drafting fixes for approval, and permits selected lower criticality work only when mistakes are cheap to detect and the agent has earned trust on that action. Critical production decisions stay with people, and code changes still go through normal review and continuous integration. The team explains the automation loops for triage, recovery from stuck runs, and shift handoffs, plus how team specific skills and memory carry expertise between engineers. Corrections reopen work and become new evidence, while memory entries can be promoted or retired. The examples show the intended experience rather than a measured time savings result: the speakers explicitly reserve that claim for a rigorous study. Their next steps focus on accepted mitigations, better feedback and earning further autonomy.

items.title: You Can't Tell What an Agent Skill Will Do by Reading It - Roey Ben Chaim, Zenity
items.summary:
An official diagnostic skill can read cloud credentials, contact identity services and probe an instance metadata endpoint. Those same actions can resemble an information stealer. Roey Ben Chaim of Zenity and the MATS Fellowship uses that ambiguity to explain why reading a SKILL.md file cannot establish what an agent will actually do. Instructions can fetch more instructions, installation scripts can pull in packages, and those packages can create processes whose effects never appear in the agent's own trace. The missing evidence is runtime behavior, collected inside a controlled environment.

Roey walks through the evolution of an agent detonation chamber: a sandbox, a world builder that supplies the services a skill expects, an operator that exercises different paths, and instrumentation for processes, filesystem activity and network traffic. He then follows concrete cases involving chained skill installation, a misleading package name, persistence, hooks and remotely fetched prompts. One investigation traces a lookalike project through a downloaded payload to credential harvesting, showing why the complete chain matters more than the entry file. The examples illustrate both malicious behavior and legitimate activity that can trigger suspicion; they are not a claim that one scanner can classify every skill correctly. The engineering takeaway is to treat skills as software dependencies, inspect what they load, restrict their access, and preserve evidence of what executes beyond the model's visible conversation.

Jonathan Cohen, vice president of applied research at NVIDIA, showed how enterprises can build agents they own and control. Breakout sessions featured speakers from Coupang Intelligent Cloud, Doosan Robotics, LG AI Research, LG Electronics, NAVER Cloud, SK Telecom and Upstage.

“It was a genuinely enjoyable time to have candid conversations,” said Hyunho Yang, research engineer for omnimodal foundation models at SK Telecom. “Seeing the passion of fellow AI developers was a real source of inspiration for me.”

The Agentic AI 10x Bootcamp Community Day brought together Pseudo Lab, Python Korea, PyTorchKR, HAERAE, Hugging Face KREW, Graph User Group, Womxn Who Code Korea, Dnol (Datayanolja) and other developer communities. Five finalists from the Hangul Day hackathon, co-hosted with Fastcampus, built agents trained on the Korean language and culture with the OpenShell runtime. The winning team, FlyGate, received an NVIDIA DGX Spark system.

More than 500 developers also took part in full-day NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute workshops and NVIDIA Certification exams in Korean. Workshops covered deploying and optimizing AI inference at scale, building end-to-end robotics workflows with the NVIDIA Isaac platform and developing secure AI agents. Certification included the new AI Model and Application Development exam. 

The Physical AI Startup Connect event included pitches from 10 NVIDIA Inception startups: AIM Intelligence, Avikus, GoLe Robotics, MOVIN, Neubility, ROAI, ROBROS, TESOLLO, TwelveLabs and XYZ. The AI for Science Forum brought together the Korea Institute of Science and Technology Information, Korean universities and NVIDIA Research.

items.title: Goal Engineering: How to Design Goals
items.summary:
The scope of tasks that agents can take on has increased drastically over the past few years. They have gone from simple text generation to tool calling and decision making to executing full tasks. The future of agents is them taking on open ended goals and driving towards completion of those goals. Launches like that of Hone give us a glimpse into that future.

In this world, designing the scope of agents is crucial. Point them in the wrong direction, and you’ll get a lot of wasted tokens. A key part of the Hone agent set up is defining metrics for them to optimize.

How to design goals

As we’ve worked on similar styles of agents, we’ve realized something about designing the scope for agents: you want to design the scope of an agent such that it makes it as easy as possible to give feedback as the agent operates within that scope.

Why is this?

When agents mess up, a big reason they mess up is lack of right context. In order to fix this, you need to give the agent the right context. There are different types of context. Some types of context are things like access to the right documents or APIs - that is relatively easy to fix. The trickiest context to give the agent is context that is not written down anywhere already. This context needs to be given to the agent as feedback from a human expert.

This is especially important as agents expand beyond doing verifiable tasks and start taking on subjective work alongside humans within an organization. For example, if you want an agent to help optimize a business metric (like improving your ads to optimize marketing performance), there are so many nuances beyond just factual context that you want to govern how the agent behaves. You probably have a certain taste around what sounds and looks good. You have opinions about how provocative or out-there your brand can be. An agent that can’t effectively get feedback to learn these things quickly becomes useless.

If the scope of your agent makes it really easy to give lots of high quality feedback on the agent’s work, that will help you immensely in building an agent that can reliably pursue a long-horizon goal.

A related learning is that you want to invest a lot in an intuitive and delightful UX for reviewing agent work. The bottleneck for agents performing is often them learning from feedback. Therefore, you should seek to optimize ease and quality of feedback collection! Investing in a clear UX for that is a worthwhile investment.

Case Study: Actively AI

Let’s look at an example from Actively AI, which builds agents for sales teams.

Actively’s first goal-oriented agent experience was designed in a way where they had an agent per account (a prospective customer a sales team wants to sell to). The agent was tasked with the goal of moving the account forward and produced actions for sales reps to approve. Intuitively, this made sense - this was a relatively constrained and directed goal with a solid outcome. Naively, it seemed like the context about the account was the most important context for the agent to have, so you should orient an agent around that.

As the agents worked, they found that there was another source of important context the agent needed: how to do its job efficiently. Specifically, how to outbound, how to reply, how to strategize about deals, how aggressive to be, how to navigate a large org, etc. This type of context was spread across multiple agents - if you learn something about outbounding in one account, you very frequently want to transfer that learning to other accounts as well.

Actively found that when the agent was tackling a single account, it was tough for salespeople to efficiently use - and provide feedback to - the agent. There are many different jobs the agent has to do when progressing a single account, and those can often be spread out over time. They found that (a) there was a lot of context switching between agents (since there was only a few things that needed review at any point in time for a single agent) and (b) it was an awkward UX to share learnings across agents (which was needed, since they were learning the same thing).

The second version of Actively’s agent experience fixed this. Their new goal-oriented agents (built on Deep Agents!) are called “motions”. A motion is a particular job to be done - like outbounding or early-stage deal progression. How to do that job is not well defined and a lot of it even relates to an individual sales rep’s preferences. Lots of knowledge is in the seller's head that needs to be given as feedback to the agent in charge of that motion for it to learn. Since a motion is a bunch of similar tasks, it is pretty easy for a salesperson to review them all together. Any feedback learned from one task in a motion intuitively transfers to other tasks in the motion.

This aligns feedback (both scope of feedback, and ease of giving feedback) with the agents themselves, which makes it far easier to create powerful agents.

This isn’t to say that account context isn’t important - it obviously is! But that account context is often already written down and much more objective. So Actively has context-gathering agents that run in the background and assemble context on each account, but the actual work of progressing accounts down the funnel is now handled by motions that work across many accounts. They own the slice of a sales motion, learn much more quickly from feedback, and pull in each account’s context as needed.

In the future

In the future, agents will advance to the point where you just give them a goal, and they go out and work to optimize that goal.

Human review of work these agents are doing takes a lot of time - but it is so valuable. That is how you teach these agents what to do, and adapt them for your domain. This knowledge that is only in peoples heads is so important to extract in a form that is easy to pass to agents.

In order to best do this, you will want to align an agent’s goals to what is easiest for humans to review. This allows you to create a delightful review UX, extract the most information possible, and enable your agents to continually learn so they can be increasingly useful and autonomous over time.

Prompt engineering and context engineering will disappear, but goal engineering will remain.

  • Fixed sessions on many third-party gateways and Foundry stopping with a context length error on every turn instead of compacting

  • Fixed shell commands running in the launch directory after the working directory was deleted; the command now fails with a message and can be re-issued

  • Fixed a saved sonnet[1m] model setting being rewritten on a new install to a model id the API rejects
  • Fixed focus view hiding the reply to your prompt when a scheduled task replied after it
  • Fixed the prompt sometimes missing from a background subagent's view when fullscreen is off
  • Fixed long options in lists and permission prompts being partly overwritten when they wrap, and first-run screens losing lines on narrow terminals
  • Fixed startup warnings about permission rules and the "N MCP servers need authentication" notice being recorded as seen when they were scrolled out of view
  • Fixed the welcome header showing control characters or splitting across lines when an agent's name or the working folder contains them or a line break
  • Fixed the red error shown when Claude tries a command only you can run: a dim line now says it runs only when you type it at the prompt
  • Fixed /stats showing an Active days total that was one day too high
  • Fixed /insights saying a report was ready when no session qualified for analysis, and writing two values into its HTML report without escaping them
  • Fixed /voice saying voice mode changed when managed settings, --settings, or the project's .claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.local.json kept it as it was; it now says what holds it
  • Fixed the IDE welcome dialog showing Cmd+Esc for Quick Launch on Windows and Linux
  • Fixed Slack app tips showing when your organization's policy denies cloud sessions
  • Fixed claude purge hanging silently when there is no terminal to read keys from, and its project picker and -i prompts ignoring the keyboard when stdin is piped
  • Fixed claude plugin eval --output-dir '' writing the report into the current folder; it now exits with an error
  • Fixed claude -p text output on a terminal passing control sequences other than text styling; pipes and files are unchanged
  • Fixed leftover .oauth_refresh.lock.owner.tmp.* files piling up in the config directory
  • Fixed /fast saying "Fast mode has been disabled by your organization" under the keyless Console sign-in, where Claude Code had not asked the server
  • Fixed /model saying that your organization restricts a model when Claude Code could not check that, for example with no network
  • Fixed "Sign in with your Console account" in /login replacing your existing login when you pressed Esc right after the browser step
  • Fixed the browser showing the sign-in success page in some cases where sign-in failed or was canceled
  • Fixed claude auth status and other short commands leaving a lock behind on a Console profile, which made the next session hang for about a minute
  • Fixed background sessions started on your claude.ai login using (and billing) an API key or token from the shell that started the background service
  • Fixed more cases of a session moving to another sign-in in the background; these moves are now refused, with a message saying what works
  • Fixed a second Enter in the exit dialog stopping background work after the move to the background was refused
  • Fixed token counting on Amazon Bedrock sending the conversation to Bedrock when the allowedProviders managed setting does not allow it
  • Fixed AWS credential_process helpers and Google Cloud default credentials failing when Claude Code is started without a HOME environment variable
  • Fixed a session sometimes going back to an earlier permission mode after a subagent's plan was approved
  • Fixed one invalid value in an Agent SDK applyFlagSettings() call silently discarding all settings from earlier calls; a call that would do this is now refused with an error
  • Fixed sessions showing as waiting for input when a finished pull request only needed your own review or merge
  • Fixed an unrecognized teammateMode settings value being ignored without a warning: claude -p, the startup warning and claude doctor now list it as a skipped entry (still not applied)
  • Fixed --worktree skipping a WorktreeCreate hook from a plugin in CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR on the first run in a new home directory
  • Fixed brief-mode sessions, such as Dispatch, sending a reply again after the turn had already replied
  • Fixed Claude saying a working Atlassian, Asana or Sentry connector had failed in cloud sessions when a plugin listed it at a different URL
  • Fixed Claude Desktop and SDK sessions listing a folder's own MCP servers (.mcp.json, local) as host-added or not at all, and not connecting WebSocket ones, after a folder move or pre-warmed start
  • Fixed /mcp still listing a plugin's MCP server after a plugin reload removed it while it was connecting
  • Fixed an MCP server staying "needs authentication", and its mcp_tool hooks being skipped, after a token refresh that was refused only for a moment
  • Fixed MCP elicitation requests being cancelled without asking in headless mode after a server's connection was replaced during a tool call
  • Fixed MCP tool calls from an SDK host answering "Not connected" after a tool call had reconnected the MCP server
  • Fixed an MCP task getting stuck after its question was closed with Esc or asked again: the footer now says it needs your input, and Enter in /tasks shows the question again
  • Fixed background MCP tasks that stopped updating after another call to the same server lost the connection, when a later call reconnects
  • Fixed a background MCP task's question opening over a message you were still typing; it now waits until you send or clear the draft, and the spinner and turn timer keep running
  • Fixed worktree.sparsePaths and sparse plugin and marketplace clones leaving out the repository's root files on older git versions, such as 2.34
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions with several repositories being unable to use a repository added mid-session
  • Fixed Claude asking for permission before reading your own artifact or its data
  • Fixed deny and ask permission rules and hooks for the Artifact tool not applying in some cloud sessions
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts ignoring a worktree entered with EnterWorktree, writing ~ paths into the project, and leaving /mcp showing an MCP server as connected after its sign-in expired
  • Fixed words typed with a Yes at a permission dialog or plan approval not reaching Claude in Code Mode
  • Fixed Claude starting work by itself when you resumed a session that ended during a Code Mode script; it now waits for your next prompt
  • Fixed a missing OpenTelemetry user_prompt event for a message sent while tool calls run. The event has delivery.mode: "mid_turn" and the running turn's prompt.id
  • Fixed the OpenTelemetry user_prompt event leaving out earlier messages' text when queued messages merged into one turn in VS Code, or when one message had an image
  • Fixed a slash command's allowed-tools grants applying to background agents woken during or after its turn
  • Fixed /feedback and /bug to upload other sessions only when they were recorded by the signed-in account or organization
  • Fixed relative deny and ask permission rules (e.g. Read(./.env)) no longer covering the project after a cd; they now also apply in added directories
  • Fixed deny and ask permission rules starting with mcp__plugin_*_ missing a plugin's MCP server or tool spelled in another letter case
  • Fixed deny rules not being applied to a permission approval that arrives after Claude Code restarts, in self-hosted runner and claude remote-control sessions
  • Fixed a case where a committed .claude/settings.local.json could be treated as the user's own when Claude Code was started in certain subfolders of a repository
  • Fixed some deny and ask rules not applying to certain Bash commands
  • Fixed a gap in Bash permission checks where some compound commands could run without asking; these now ask for permission
  • Fixed a case where a Bash allow rule could run a different program than the one it names
  • Fixed a connector tool's approval prompt in cloud sessions being answered automatically while plugins were still loading
  • Fixed some subagents changing an artifact that people outside your organization can see, or uploading files to it, without asking first when an allow rule is set or uploads were approved earlier
  • Fixed some artifact publishes skipping the confirmation for pages that people outside your organization can see when "don't ask again" had been chosen for Artifact
  • Fixed auto mode judging only the first change to an artifact that people outside your organization can see; its yes now covers that change alone
  • Fixed a managed strictPluginOnlyCustomization lock on agents and skills not taking effect in sessions that were already running
  • Fixed sandboxed commands being able to write to the native updater's download folder in some cases
  • Fixed a case where the Bash sandbox did not fully protect a worktree's settings and hooks
  • Fixed a case where the Bash sandbox did not fully protect a linked worktree's shared git folder
  • Fixed /teleport's stash choice in some unusual git states: it now stops and says what to do
  • Windows: Fixed a start-up stall that could last about a second when a PATH entry sits under a folder your account cannot open
  • Fixed /resume on Windows refusing or hiding sessions whose folder was recorded with a different drive-letter case or slashes
  • Fixed an in-session /resume on Windows dropping a project's saved trust when the session was recorded with a different drive-letter case
  • Linux: Fixed sandboxed Bash commands failing with bwrap: Can't create file when the working directory was below an allowRead folder inside a denyRead, such as under a symlinked home directory
  • Fixed Claude Desktop's third-party deployments staying on "Stopping" until a token renewal finished (once it includes this version)
  • Improved subagents cut off at the output token limit: they are now asked for the whole answer again, more briefly, instead of returning only its end
  • Improved startup with a keyless Console sign-in or other Anthropic profile login: a token that is still valid is read without waiting for the credentials lock
  • Improved the account email check: it now also refuses your email as a client's identity in scripts a command runs, file writes, web fetches and MCP calls
  • Improved the HTTPS authentication failed message for private plugin marketplaces: it now says git's terminal prompts and askpass programs are disabled, and it also appears with newer git versions
  • Improved the add-marketplace confirmations, plugin recommendation prompts and plugin install warning to say that plugins can run code on your computer, with access to your files and shell
  • Improved the claude --desktop sign-in error to name the API key, provider or setting that stops a Claude account sign-in from working
  • Improved the /voice "No audio detected" message on macOS and Windows: it now says where to pick your microphone
  • Improved MCP tasks: Claude is now told when a task is waiting for your answer, and can point you to /tasks
  • Improved claude remote-control: it now exits with status 4 when it stops by itself (single-session runs still exit 0) and 69 when it can't register, so a service manager can start it again
  • Improved the messages shown when a background session can't use its session's API key or token: they no longer suggest adding the key to settings
  • Improved the bundled dataviz skill's part-to-whole advice for static images and for parts with a natural order, such as age bands
  • Changed sandboxed Bash commands to follow the normal permission flow by default; set sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true to keep running them without prompts
  • Changed managed settings that turn the sandbox on: to keep commands running without prompts, set sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true in your highest-ranking managed source
  • Changed read-only git commands to ask first in a repository that isn't the project's or one you trusted; name it with --add-dir, not the additionalDirectories setting, to run them without prompts
  • Changed scheduled tasks and /loop to ask before running a skill that declares allowed-tools or hooks; add Skill(name) to permissions.allow to run it unattended
  • Changed "Always allow" in Desktop, IDE and SDK hosts: a rule alone is offered only when saving it would allow that command again, so a scheduled task that relied on one can now wait for you
  • Changed the sandbox to refuse sandboxed writes to .claude settings, skills, agents, commands and hooks in added directories, as it does in the launch folder
  • Changed worktree isolation: an isolated worktree session or agent is now refused git bisect run, git maintenance register|start and scalar's set-up commands, and is told what still works
  • Changed plugin MCP bundles (.mcpb, .dxt) to unpack under the plugins directory, not .mcpb-cache in the plugin's folder, so read-only plugin folders load; one fetched by URL downloads again once
  • Changed plugins of a remote marketplace that managed settings declare, enable and list in prependPlugins or appendPlugins to count as the organization's; pluginDigests is deprecated and ignored
  • Changed plugin loading to skip, and claude plugin validate to report, some unsafe paths and links in a plugin's folder
  • Changed nested skill loading: .claude/skills folders in --plugin-dir plugins no longer load from a session started above them; start Claude Code in the plugin folder instead
  • Changed EnterWorktree to refuse a WorktreeCreate hook path that goes through a symlink inside the project; have the hook print the real path
  • Changed tmux and iTerm2 teammates, and new sessions from the agents view opened with ←, to start in the session's folder instead of where the shell last ran cd
  • Changed prompt suggestions in the terminal to refresh less often after 8 turns in a row started by background or scheduled tasks, saving usage until you press a key or return to the terminal
  • Changed Esc on a background MCP task's question to "answer later": nothing is sent to the server, and the question stays in /tasks
  • Changed CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS to also set the context window of unrecognized model IDs that start with claude-, such as a gateway's claude-sonnet-latest
  • Changed /login to ask for permission to change your privacy settings
  • Changed /cost, $.session.usage(), --max-budget-usd and the cost and token metrics to count a mod's $.model.complete and $.model.classify calls
  • Changed the programs that Claude Code's sandbox starts for its own use, such as its network bridge, to run without Claude Code's sign-in tokens and API keys in their environment
  • Changed ripgrep, local git commands and the sandbox runtime's own helper programs to run without the mTLS client key's passphrase in their environment
  • Remote Control: Changed /resume and /teleport to disconnect first when the connected session has a share link, or when that can't be checked; run /remote-control to connect again
  • Changed Claude Code on the web, cloud scheduled tasks and Cowork cloud sessions to start despite sandbox.failIfUnavailable: the hosted container has no command sandbox
  • Changed requests for settings, permission rules, hooks or status over a cloud or self-hosted session's connection to return less or be refused; what applies in the session is unchanged
  • Changed claude -p with no cached account data to wait for that data before its first request, so a first run in a clean environment can start a few seconds later
  • Changed Claude's instructions to keep files you'll want out of its temporary scratchpad folder, which can be cleared
  • Changed marketplace ref to accept the full ID of any commit on a branch or tag; clients before this version can't clone such a pin, so a marketplace pinned this way stops loading there
  • Changed plugin marketplace and plugin downloads to use a CONNECT tunnel when ALL_PROXY is the only proxy set; a proxy that refuses CONNECT now fails them
  • Changed -p and SDK runs in a worktree or submodule mounted into a container to apply .claude/settings.local.json allow rules only once the folder is trusted
  • Changed self-hosted runners to refuse a session whose session folder or repository path is a symbolic link, other than a checkout hook's checkout
  • Removed "ask your admin to raise it" from spend limit and shared budget errors in cloud sessions and under Remote Control
  • [VSCode] Added prompt suggestions wherever the terminal shows them: Tab accepts the suggested next prompt; promptSuggestionEnabled: false in Claude Code's settings.json turns them off
  • [VSCode] Added a Console sign-in that creates no API key
  • [VSCode] Added a field to paste the redirect URL when signing in to an MCP server from the panel in SSH, WSL and container windows
  • [VSCode] Fixed the model picker's check mark staying on the old model after Claude Code restarted on another model or the model was switched over Remote Control
  • [VSCode] Fixed the effort selector offering levels above the effort cap set by your organization or the maxEffortLevel setting
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen offering sign-ins that the managed allowedProviders setting refuses
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt for MCP tools not saying why Claude Code asks when a safety check raises the question
  • [VSCode] Fixed the message for organization settings that couldn't load saying to run a command again; it now says to try again, matching the tab's Retry link
  • [VSCode] Improved the note shown for an untrusted folder: it now says why the extension is off and how to turn it on
  • [VSCode] Improved the error shown when the system refuses to run Claude Code: it now says your IT team can allow a blocked program
  • [VSCode] Improved the sign-in card to say what to do when the browser shows a connection error for localhost
  • [VSCode] Changed the install link's marketplace confirmation button to "Trust marketplace and continue"
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed new cloud sessions cutting MCP tool descriptions loaded through tool search at 4,096 characters; the limit is now 16,384, as in other Claude Code sessions
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed artifact links pasted in Slack getting no card when the poster's Claude sign-in had expired in a workspace their organization doesn't manage; a plain card now appears

Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon
items.summary:
How Meta's Reality Labs brought Cuttlefish and its QEMU backend to macOS and Apple silicon. [...]

Read More...

The post Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
items.content:
Meta’s Reality Labs builds products such as AI glasses. Emulators provide us with a way to scale development and testing without relying on scarce physical hardware.

Testing software for non-phone Android devices depends on how closely a virtual device reproduces the software behavior of the physical product. While a lightweight emulator like Goldfish gets you part of the way, differences from the real device can hide bugs until later in development. This lack of fidelity also erodes trust in device emulation, increasing reliance on scarce physical hardware.

Cuttlefish is the Android Open Source Project’s (AOSP’s) virtual-device framework for testing Android software against virtual hardware. It boots the same system images as real hardware and runs a realistic software stack against virtual hardware. This enables Cuttlefish to more closely track a physical device’s behavior than a lightweight emulator does.

Unfortunately, Cuttlefish is only supported on Linux, and our application and library developers work on Macs with Apple silicon. This forced us to support Goldfish and Cuttlefish side by side.

We knew if we could consolidate onto a single Cuttlefish-based platform, we could give all of our developers the benefit of the same high-fidelity virtual device. The challenge was porting the stack to make Cuttlefish run natively on macOS.

The Impact of Fragmentation

Maintaining dual emulator platforms imposed a heavy operational burden: It drained computing resources, created confusion for developers, and slowed down the emulator team. Every tool required support for two separate platforms, while infrastructure and engineering capacity were divided between them. Furthermore, developers had to choose an emulator target based on how they worked: Goldfish ran everywhere but had less fidelity while Cuttlefish needed Linux.

The AOSP mirrors this exact divide: Goldfish targets application developers, whereas Cuttlefish serves Android platform developers. So long as we maintained that division, we would suffer the effects of fragmentation.

The Stack and the macOS Gaps

Cuttlefish is the orchestration layer, while the component that actually runs the guest OS is a virtual machine monitor (VMM). On Linux, Cuttlefish normally uses crosvm but previously included support for QEMU as an alternative VMM. That integration had become inactive over time. To enable native Apple silicon support on macOS, we revived QEMU support.

Many of Cuttlefish’s virtual devices use vhost-user backends, separate processes that provide virtio devices to QEMU over a socket. The architecture is clean, but large parts of it were written with a hard Linux assumption. Three of those assumptions break on macOS. The vhost-user machinery is gated to Linux and won’t build or run. The Apple hypervisor imposes resource limits QEMU didn’t expect. Finally, the native display, build, and signing paths didn’t exist. We tackled all three.

Making vhost-user Portable Beyond Linux

The most structurally important changes were in QEMU’s vhost-user path. The frontends, libvhost-user, and the contrib backends such as vhost-user-blk were all gated to Linux. We relaxed those build restrictions so the vhost-user frontends and libraries can build on macOS as well as Linux. This lets Cuttlefish’s device backends hand off to QEMU on a Mac the same way they do on Linux. Without this, the higher-fidelity device model that makes Cuttlefish worth using isn’t available outside Linux.

Living Within Hypervisor.framework

On Apple silicon, QEMU accelerates through HVF (Hypervisor.framework) instead of KVM. QEMU’s HVF backend did not track enough memory regions for larger Cuttlefish configurations. We increased its tracking-slot count so those configurations could run correctly.

A Usable Native Display

Local application development requires an interactive display allowing developers to view and engage directly with the virtual device. To enable direct interaction and bypass reliance on the WebRTC interface, we transitioned to QEMU’s native Cocoa display. The changes include:

  • BGRA Pixel Format Support: Enables accurate display rendering to eliminate visual artifacts on Apple silicon.
  • Mouse-Click-as-Touch: Translates pointer actions into touch input for interacting with touchscreen devices.
  • Custom Geometry Options: Adds the -g flag to graphic_console_init for display configuration.

We also enabled the unstable Rutabaga structs needed to match the Rust-side graphics ABI in gfxstream/rutabaga configurations.

Building and Signing on Apple Silicon

Finally, there was the build and packaging work: initial Darwin build support, building QEMU for arm64 on macOS, and toolchain fixes. The macOS builds also needed the JIT entitlement in addition to support for code signing and notarization. On the Cuttlefish side, we added macOS host support so the framework’s orchestration builds and runs on a Mac instead of assuming a Linux host.

The Benefits

By moving to a unified platform, we cut maintenance requirements, reduced infrastructure needs, eliminated redundant tooling, enhanced fidelity, and ensured developers run the exact same Cuttlefish virtual devices used across CI.

A single platform also made it easier to support capabilities on a shared stack, including:

  • Bluetooth pairing and connectivity.
  • Wi-Fi.
  • Cellular.
  • 3D graphics.
  • Over-the-air (OTA) update testing to exercise over-the-air update flows against a virtual device.
  • Fastboot.
  • Snapshotting to save and restore device state in CI and development flows.

Beyond supporting Reality Labs engineers, this identical virtual device is shared with external developers building for our ecosystem. This alignment guarantees that third-party teams test against the exact same Cuttlefish-based platform we use to develop and validate the OS itself.

With AI agents playing a growing role in Android development, validation execution and runtime behavior is just as essential as code generation. Virtual devices empower both engineers and automated agents to operate concurrently within isolated environments, facilitating application execution and rapid iteration. By enabling instant state resets and repeated test runs, teams eliminate dependencies on shared physical hardware and prevent workflow interruptions. Ultimately, high-fidelity emulation ensures these continuous feedback loops are both rapid and meaningful.

Giving Back to the Community

Although we built this for development within Reality Labs, the macOS support is useful beyond our products. We’re sharing our work with the community so other developers can build on the QEMU and AOSP foundations that enabled our work.

We’re distributing the work in two parts:

  • qemu-wearables: a Meta-maintained fork of QEMU carrying our commits.
  • cuttlefish-wearables: a set of patch files, with instructions for patching Android/AOSP.

The repositories contain our QEMU changes and the Cuttlefish patch series, along with build and patch-application instructions.

We’re also exploring ways to contribute these changes upstream to QEMU and AOSP. In the meantime, developers can use our fork and patch set.

Acknowledgements

This project relies on the foundations laid by the QEMU and Cuttlefish/AOSP communities. We are particularly grateful for the vsock-user implementation created by Stefano Garzarella, which directly enabled our macOS integration.

Special thanks also go to Olya Arkhangelskaia and Tom Care at Meta for their foundational work bringing Cuttlefish to macOS, and to Jeffrey Effendy for improvements to the native Mac developer experience and subsequent productization work.

The post Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon appeared first on Engineering at Meta.

items.summary:
Our Series C Announcement

Today, we’re announcing that LangChain raised $300M at a $3B valuation to advance our mission to enable every company to own its intelligence. The round was led by existing investor CapitalG, with significant participation from new investors GIC and DFJ Growth and existing investors IVP and Sapphire Ventures.

We believe agents will transform the economy. That future will be shaped by domain-specific agents differentiated by their knowledge, data, and UX. These agents will be sold as standalone products and also used to transform internal company operations. The companies that control these systems will build lasting competitive advantages.

To capture that opportunity, every company will need to own its intelligence. Companies should be free to choose the best models for their needs, control their data and infrastructure, and continuously improve their agents, while maintaining the governance needed to operate securely at scale.

That’s why we’ve built LangSmith, the framework-agnostic platform to run, improve, and govern agents. More than 7,000 organizations already rely on LangSmith, from fast-growing startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Listen Labs to Fortune 500 enterprises like NVIDIA, Toyota, and Salesforce. Clay uses LangSmith to monitor hundreds of millions of agent runs per month and improve their agents. Workday uses LangSmith to run and govern agents across the organization, reducing the time to deploy a new agent from five months to under a day.

LangSmith provides the foundation for companies to control their agent systems across three pillars – Agent Runtime, Agent Improvement, and Agent Governance:

Agent Runtime gives teams the architecture and infrastructure to run agents reliably. Deep Agents, LangGraph, and LangChain give developers flexibility across models and control over how context is managed. LangSmith Agent Server and Sandboxes allow teams to deploy and run agents securely at scale, whether in the cloud or in their environment. LangSmith Managed Agents and Fleet provide fully managed services to build, deploy, and run mission-critical agents in production.

Agent Improvement helps teams test, monitor, and improve agent performance. LangSmith Observability and Evaluation give teams visibility into how agents behave and measure quality. LangSmith Engine, our in-platform agent, automates improvement by finding errors, writing code and prompt fixes, and monitoring production traffic for regressions. LangSmith Fine-Tuning helps teams turn agent traces into training data to fine-tune and evaluate specialized models.

Agent Governance gives teams centralized control over how agents use models, tools, and data. Our LLM and Tool Gateways help teams manage model budgets and fallbacks, protect sensitive data, and govern tool access and authentication across teams and agents.

Next Friday, November 20th, we’ll share several new LangSmith capabilities that build on this foundation. Join us for a special release event to see what’s coming next.

LangSmith has been shaped by our fantastic community – from our developer evangelists to the customers we’re lucky enough to partner with. Thank you all for your feedback, insights, and trust.

There’s still so much left to build. Building high performing agents is harder than it should be, and we‘re determined to change that. Come join us in making it easier for every company to own its intelligence.

Harrison

Thank you to our new and existing investors for helping make this journey possible. We’re excited to welcome Salesforce Ventures, Insight Venture Partners, QuantumLight, and MongoDB Ventures, and grateful to Sequoia, Amplify, and Benchmark for doubling down in this round.

How AI Is Helping Care Teams Get Patients the Right Care, Sooner
items.summary: From pediatric research to smart hospitals, AI is helping care teams spend less time on routine tasks and more time with patients.  Health systems and startups are putting it to work across healthcare, from matching patients to clinical trials to supporting radiologists, hospital teams and patients at home. Clinicians stay at the center, reviewing AI […]
items.content:
From pediatric research to smart hospitals, AI is helping care teams spend less time on routine tasks and more time with patients. 

Health systems and startups are putting it to work across healthcare, from matching patients to clinical trials to supporting radiologists, hospital teams and patients at home. Clinicians stay at the center, reviewing AI outputs and guiding decisions, while NVIDIA technologies provide the compute behind the applications.

Read on to learn how healthcare teams are using AI to improve and speed patient care.

Friday, Nov. 13, 5:00 a.m. PT

Dyania Health Uses AI to Turn Decades of Patient Records Into Better Care 

Hospitals hold decades of patient history, most of it written in free text, as physicians’ notes, operative reports, imaging and pathology reads and discharge summaries. To understand one patient’s full story, a clinician would need to read through years of charts. 

Dyania Health, a New Jersey-based clinical AI company, built Synapsis AI to do just that. Synapsis AI is a clinical reasoning engine: It works across every note, report and lab result in a patient’s record, connecting findings that may be years apart to answer clinical questions the way a specialist reviewing the chart would. 

The output is a set of clinical signals, each traceable to its source in the record, that tells care teams which patients need attention and why. Clinicians review the evidence and make every decision. 

Keeping Patient Data Inside the Hospital Walls

Synapsis AI runs on NVIDIA-accelerated computing inside a health system’s own firewall.  The entire health system’s patient records can be processed onsite, so patient data is never shared and never leaves the hospital. 

Processing records this way takes chart review off the desks of clinical teams and lets them spend that time with patients. But Synapsis AI still requires clinician input — it’s an assistive tool that surfaces evidence from medical records that a clinician must still confirm and act on. 

Dyania builds and trains its clinical models with NVIDIA NeMo open libraries, then uses NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM to optimize them to run faster and more efficiently on the hospital’s own GPU servers. 

Synapsis AI in the Real World

Cleveland Clinic used Synapsis AI to support a study of more than 7,800 aortic valve replacement patients between 2005 and 2021. 

Synapsis AI reasoned across each patient’s record, including every echocardiogram added in the years after surgery, and used this information to build a predictive model of valve deterioration and reintervention risk at the three-, five- and ten-year mark after a patient undergoes an aortic valve replacement procedure. The AI platform completed chart review across the full cohort that would have taken clinicians years to complete by hand. 

“Using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help us predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients,” said Dr. Lars Svensson, chief of the Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute at Cleveland Clinic.

The same approach can be applied to any healthcare challenge where the answer sits inside the medical record, such as identifying patients eligible for clinical trials, closing care gaps in cardiology and oncology, and populating clinical registries.

Learn more about Dyania Health.

items.title: BigCodeBench: Benchmarking Code Generation with Diverse Function Calls and Complex Instructions
items.summary:
arXiv:2406.15877v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Task automation has been greatly empowered by the recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) via Python code, where the tasks ranging from software engineering development to general-purpose reasoning. While current benchmarks have shown that LLMs can solve tasks using programs like human developers, the majority of their evaluations are limited to short and self-contained algorithmic tasks or standalone function calls. Solving challenging and practical tasks requires the capability of utilizing diverse function calls as tools to efficiently implement functionalities like data analysis and web development. In addition, using multiple tools to solve a task needs compositional reasoning by accurately understanding complex instructions. Fulfilling both of these characteristics can pose a great challenge for LLMs.To assess how well LLMs can solve challenging and practical tasks via programs, we introduce BigCodeBench, a benchmark that challenges LLMs to invoke multiple function calls as tools from 139 libraries and 7 domains for 1,140 fine-grained tasks. To evaluate LLMs rigorously, each task encompasses 5.6 test cases with an average branch coverage of 99%. In addition, we propose a natural-language-oriented variant of BigCodeBench, BigCodeBench-Instruct, that automatically transforms the original docstrings into short instructions only with essential information. Our extensive evaluation of 60 LLMs shows that LLMs are not yet capable of following complex instructions to use function calls precisely, with scores up to 60%, significantly lower than the human performance of 97%. The results underscore the need for further advancements in this area.
items.author: Terry Yue Zhuo, Minh Chien Vu, Jenny Chim, Han Hu, Wenhao Yu, Ratnadira Widyasari, Imam Nur Bani Yusuf, Haolan Zhan, Junda He, Indraneil Paul, Simon Brunner, Chen Gong, Thong Hoang, Armel Randy Zebaze, Xiaoheng Hong, Wen-Ding Li, Jean Kaddour, Ming Xu, Zhihan Zhang, Prateek Yadav, Naman Jain, Alex Gu, Zhoujun Cheng, Jiawei Liu, Qian Liu, Zijian Wang, Binyuan Hui, Niklas Muennighoff, David Lo, Daniel Fried, Xiaoning Du, Harm de Vries, Leandro Von Werra

items.title: Astraios: Parameter-Efficient Instruction Tuning Code Large Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2401.00788v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The high cost of full-parameter fine-tuning (FFT) of Large Language Models (LLMs) has led to a series of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods. However, it remains unclear which methods provide the best cost-performance trade-off at different model scales. We introduce Astraios, a suite of 28 instruction-tuned OctoCoder models using 7 tuning methods and 4 model sizes up to 16 billion parameters. Through investigations across 5 tasks and 8 different datasets encompassing both code comprehension and code generation tasks, we find that FFT generally leads to the best downstream performance across all scales, and PEFT methods differ significantly in their efficacy based on the model scale. LoRA usually offers the most favorable trade-off between cost and performance. Further investigation into the effects of these methods on both model robustness and code security reveals that larger models tend to demonstrate reduced robustness and less security. At last, we explore the relationships among updated parameters, cross-entropy loss, and task performance. We find that the tuning effectiveness observed in small models generalizes well to larger models, and the validation loss in instruction tuning can be a reliable indicator of overall downstream performance.
items.author: Terry Yue Zhuo, Armel Zebaze, Nitchakarn Suppattarachai, Leandro von Werra, Harm de Vries, Qian Liu, Niklas Muennighoff

items.title: Fake News Detectors are Biased against Texts Generated by Large Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2309.08674v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The spread of fake news has emerged as a critical challenge, undermining trust and posing threats to society. In the era of Large Language Models (LLMs), the capability to generate believable fake content has intensified these concerns. In this study, we present a novel paradigm to evaluate fake news detectors in scenarios involving both human-written and LLM-generated misinformation. Intriguingly, our findings reveal a significant bias in many existing detectors: they are more prone to flagging LLM-generated content as fake news while often misclassifying human-written fake news as genuine. This unexpected bias appears to arise from distinct linguistic patterns inherent to LLM outputs. To address this, we introduce a mitigation strategy that leverages adversarial training with LLM-paraphrased genuine news. The resulting model yielded marked improvements in detection accuracy for both human and LLM-generated news. To further catalyze research in this domain, we release two comprehensive datasets, \texttt{GossipCop++} and \texttt{PolitiFact++}, thus amalgamating human-validated articles with LLM-generated fake and real news.
items.author: Jinyan Su, Terry Yue Zhuo, Jonibek Mansurov, Di Wang, Preslav Nakov

items.title: When to Rethink: Learning Multi-Perspective Self-Verification for Vision-Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.07018v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in multimodal reasoning, yet they remain prone to generating plausible but incorrect answers. Self-verification offers a practical way to improve answer reliability without relying on external judges, but existing methods typically depend on a single verification criterion or fixed prompt, resulting in incomplete and unstable reliability estimates. We first systematically analyze how verifier capability and prompt design affect verification performance. Our findings show that stronger verifiers provide more reliable judgments, while verification performance is highly sensitive to prompt choice, with no single prompt consistently dominating across tasks. Guided by these findings, we propose \texttt{MOTIVE}, a \textbf{M}ulti-View Self-Verificati\textbf{O}n wi\textbf{T}h Rel\textbf{I}ability-Guided Selecti\textbf{VE} Rethinking framework for reliable multimodal reasoning. \texttt{MOTIVE} evaluates each candidate answer from complementary verification perspectives and learns a correctness-aligned reliability score through correctness-grounded multi-view verification learning. During inference, this score governs an accept-or-rethink decision, allowing reliable answers to be returned directly while uncertain ones trigger history-guided rethinking. Extensive experiments across diverse multimodal benchmarks and VLM backbones demonstrate that \texttt{MOTIVE} consistently outperforms strong self-verification and self-correction baselines. Further results show that reliable verification improves accept-or-rethink decisions and reduces unnecessary reasoning turns, enabling more reliable and efficient self-verification without an external judge.
items.author: Ziquan Zhu, Hanruo Zhu, Si-Yuan Lu, Morris Yu-Chao Huang, Yicheng Lin, Wei Han, Tianlong Chen, Mingyuan Wu, Hanchao Yu, Gaojie Jin, Lu Liu, Bo Sun, Tianjin Huang

items.title: Proof-Grounded Patient-Specific Clinical Explanations from Knowledge-Graph Reasoning
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.06549v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Clinical decision support can lack auditable links from observations and encoded knowledge to conclusions and recommendations. Downstream of a frozen, training-free clinical knowledge-graph reasoner, the CKG Clinical Explanation Engine converts patient inference states and disease knowledge into typed facts, explicit rule traces, provenance-linked conclusions, and policy-licensed recommendations. Separate availability, representation completeness, and disease-specific activation distinguish observed zero-activation and partial evidence from unobserved evidence. Language-generation evaluation remains future work. Across six usable workbooks (11,289 patients, 33,867 patient-disease traces, 1,715,928 feature-evidence rows), IG-range validity, knowledge provenance, cross-sheet numerical fidelity (203,202/203,202), and exported fact/report field presence (33,867/33,867) reached 100.00%. Availability-representation consistency reached 99.29% (1,703,811/1,715,928), with 12,117 disagreements across five systematic feature-cohort patterns.
