  • Fixed WebFetch not rechecking organization policy and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_WEB_FETCH at each call
  • Fixed file titles, app names and session names in @-mentions from claude.ai and the desktop app sometimes being treated as text you typed
  • Fixed a multi-row status line being pushed off screen by a long prompt in the fullscreen renderer
  • Fixed a case where certificate errors behind a TLS-inspecting proxy persisted when the proxy itself is reached over https://
  • Fixed Pro and Max accounts being offered feedback drafts that their organization would refuse
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome's policy message telling people to contact their admin when no admin setting can turn it on
  • Fixed the artifact preview sometimes opening a different artifact than the one Claude just published
  • Fixed certificate name-constraint errors being retried for minutes; they now fail at once with a message that says what to fix
  • Fixed claude --teleport opening an empty session when the server could not find the session's history, and claude -p --teleport exiting without an error when the resume failed
  • Fixed a misspelled keybinding modifier, such as ctl+k, binding the bare key; the binding is now ignored
  • Fixed /btw answers and recaps sometimes including earlier replies from the conversation
  • Fixed start-up requests switching from an organization's managed proxy and CA settings to user-set ones when a read of the managed settings file failed
  • Fixed Claude giving a wrong reason when a new message interrupted a file it was sending you
  • Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN re-running a turn that a hook's continue: false had stopped
  • Fixed Claude being told that automatic model switching is off when safeguards stopped a subagent whose model had no other model to switch to
  • Fixed the changed-files list of remote sessions leaving out files added with git add -N before the first commit
  • Fixed some Claude in Chrome tool calls, such as browser_batch, not showing the tool's name in the fullscreen transcript (ctrl+o) or in a subagent's progress
  • Fixed subagent progress summaries skipping an update when the reply took between 10 and 20 seconds
  • Fixed claude doctor and /status saying a linked managed settings file is still read when it could not be read
  • Fixed an interactive --chrome session giving no reason for starting without Claude in Chrome when your organization's policy turns it off: a line now says so
  • Fixed the /rewind list on network paths and hung folders: it named every tracked file as changed, was slow to show labels, and showed none at all when a file read never returned
  • Fixed --debug and --debug-file replacing a file named latest in the debug log's folder
  • Fixed a timed-out feedback send being reported as too large; it now says the request timed out
  • Fixed screen reader mode cutting off an announcement when the system clock moved forward while it was being read
  • Fixed screen reader mode dropping dictated or pasted text, and emoji, typed into an answer to a question or permission prompt
  • Fixed the name label under permission and plan dialogs hiding part of some agent names
  • Fixed a case where pressing Ctrl+C just as claude update finished removed the claude command
  • Fixed the fullscreen header naming the session's effort level for a viewed subagent on a different model, which that subagent doesn't use
  • Fixed the model picker and /model showing a picked effort level that CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL overrides
  • Fixed the tip after a slow worktree creation suggesting a sparsePaths list without .claude, which left worktrees without your project settings and rules
  • Fixed the newest model's highlight missing from the /model picker
  • Fixed /upgrade and Ctrl+clicked links in fullscreen failing silently when no browser can open: the address is now shown
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway's JSON logs escaping newlines and other control characters in a message twice
  • Fixed terminal control sequences in a subagent's message taking effect instead of showing as plain text when the message is expanded
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome setup saying /chrome finishes the connection; it now tells you to restart with claude --chrome
  • Fixed the Option-key hint appearing while typing ø or π inside words on Danish, Norwegian, Faroese and Greek keyboard layouts
  • Fixed a Claude Desktop session getting stuck as busy after another of your sessions sent it the same message twice or many messages at once
  • Fixed long tool results staying on disk after a session run with --no-session-persistence; they are now removed on normal exit, Ctrl+C or SIGTERM
  • Fixed PreCompact, PostCompact and post-compaction SessionStart hooks not receiving agent_id and agent_type when a subagent compacts
  • Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_TRANSCRIPT_LOCAL_GC dropping messages from the saved transcript when another process rewrote the file while it was being trimmed
  • Fixed the "Now using usage credits" notice repeating or not showing past the weekly Fable limit when Claude Code made a quick side request on a smaller model, such as naming the session
  • Fixed Fable's weekly limit showing no reset time and no options menu in the terminal
  • Fixed a wait chosen in the usage limit menu silently moving to a later reset when its request was refused; the menu now opens

  • Fixed /usage hiding limit bars for setup tokens and CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN: it keeps the session and weekly bars and says why the rest are missing

  • Fixed a cloud session's history becoming unreadable if its machine stopped just after the history was rewritten
  • Fixed scheduled tasks from an ended session sometimes not running after another session in the same folder used /clear, /resume or /branch
  • Fixed an approved plan being answered with "You are not in plan mode" when the approval arrived after the session's process had restarted, in cloud, self-hosted runner and SDK sessions
  • Cloud sessions: Fixed an answer to Claude's question being lost after a restart in a long conversation
  • Fixed a message dropping out of a cloud session's conversation when the session restarted before Claude replied
  • Cloud sessions: Fixed Claude saying an attached image is missing when the message names its file
  • Fixed a resumed cloud session making a model call nobody asked for when files arrived right after a chat's first reply
  • Fixed streamed replies in cloud sessions missing text from the middle when the session's container shut down partway through a reply
  • Fixed skill files sent from Cowork cloud sessions sometimes failing to upload on the first try

What's changed

  • Added Code Mode, an experimental opt-in in which Claude writes JavaScript to call its tools; see https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-mode to turn it on, or to turn it off for an organization
  • Added engines["claude-code"] to plugin.json: plugins outside their stated Claude Code version range are not installed, updated or loaded, and install and update pick the newest version that fits
  • Added type checking of a plugin's TypeScript hooks module to claude plugin validate; each finding is a warning, and --strict fails on it
  • Added to claude plugin validate the $ nouns a mod's engine.create hook adds, withholds or replaces
  • Added support for CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_MODEL in managed settings for Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers (takes effect once Claude Desktop includes this version)
  • Added an options menu (stop, switch to usage credits, upgrade) when a model needs usage credits that are turned off or used up
  • Added a progress heartbeat every 30 seconds while hooks run long in claude -p and SDK sessions, so a host such as Claude Desktop won't end the turn as hung (once it includes this version)
  • Added .docx support to Artifact tool asset uploads
  • Added a /diff to close hint to the diff panel, and the keys that focus and close a panel to the ? shortcut guide
  • Added a start-up warning for Bash allow rules with a * in a variable's value, such as Bash(PORT=* npm run dev)
  • Added a warning when a plugin's language server can't start, naming the server and what to check
  • Added a one-time startup notice naming CLAUDE_CODE_PERFORCE_MODE when Perforce settings are found and the mode is off
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES (available since 2.1.318): set it to 1 to turn off subagent progress summaries and the requests that write them (#86879)
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_HINT_COMMAND, which a program that starts Claude Code can set to have the exit hint name its own resume command
  • Added unsetOptionCount to the claude plugin install --json result: how many userConfig options are not yet set
  • Added isPromptCovered to the props a mod's pane is drawn with, telling it when a dialog or a field above the prompt covers the prompt
  • Fixed running /compact again, or after a command such as /context, summarizing away a message that Claude had not answered yet
  • Fixed a resumed session joining your next message to an old interrupted message that was not resumed
  • Fixed a memory spike at the next prompt after Claude changed a very large file
  • Fixed a setting saved in a running session undoing a hand edit made to settings.json moments earlier; a settings file you delete during a session now stays deleted
  • Fixed claude plugin commands and claude mcp list signing you out of a Console profile when they ended while the token was being renewed
  • Fixed Edit and Bash running out of memory on certain /proc files, and Edit hanging or running out of memory on devices and named pipes
  • Fixed Claude Code failing to start, or to clear stored credentials at sign-out, when saving its configuration file failed with "Out of memory"

items.title: Microsoft Research Focus – Edition #98
items.summary:
What's new in research at Microsoft? Host Anson Ho explores the latest, including AI-powered universal translation, a breakthrough in a 31-year-old mathematics challenge, and advances making AI coding agents faster and more efficient. 

The post Microsoft Research Focus – Edition #98 appeared first on Microsoft Research.
items.content:
What’s new in research? 

In this edition of Microsoft Research Focus, based on the Research Focus newsletter (opens in new tab), host Anson Ho shares some of the latest news and cutting-edge research from across Microsoft—from bringing AI-powered universal translation closer to reality and solving a 31-year-old mathematical challenge to making AI coding agents faster and more efficient. 

Catch up on the ideas, tools, and discoveries researchers are exploring today and get a quick look at what’s coming next. 

Related links:

  • A research intern’s journey from computer vision to physical intelligence at Microsoft Research Asia – Tokyo
  • Breaking the Language Barrier — How AI Speech Translation Is Rewriting Our Digital Lives
  • Solving a 31-year-old grand challenge in mathematics – the KLS conjecture
  • Benchmarking Long-Horizon Agent Context Compaction with CompactionBench
  • Latent Core Tokenizer: Compress, but Meaningfully

Chapters 

0:35: Internship: Growing expertise, building community  (opens in new tab)

1:28: Breaking the language barrier with AI (opens in new tab)

2:10: Solving a 31-year-old mathematics challenge (opens in new tab)

2:56: Making AI coding agents more efficient (opens in new tab)

3:57: Improving AI tokenization across 104 languages (opens in new tab)

Subscribe to the Microsoft Research Podcast:

  • Apple Podcasts
  • Email
  • Android
  • Spotify
  • RSS Feed

Transcript 

[MUSIC]

This is Microsoft Research Focus, your quick look at news and cutting-edge research from across Microsoft. 

I’m Anson Ho, and these are some of the latest advances we’re tracking. 

Coming up in this edition: how AI is bringing the possibility of a universal translator closer to reality; a breakthrough that solves a 31-year-old mathematical challenge; a new approach to make AI coding agents faster and more efficient; and more. 

Here’s what’s new. 

[MUSIC FADES]

Internship: Growing expertise, building community

At the Microsoft Research lab in Tokyo, research intern Lilika Makabe found opportunities to grow her expertise while helping to shape a new research community. 

Makabe joined the lab with a background in computer vision and worked alongside researchers exploring robotics and physical intelligence, AI systems that can interpret information and act in the physical world. 

Her experience highlights how research internships can offer more than technical training. Through hands-on experimentation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and everyday conversations with colleagues from different backgrounds, Makabe expanded her research perspective while contributing to the lab’s growing community. 

You can read about her experience on the Microsoft Research blog. 

[TRANSITION MUSIC] 

Breaking the language barrier with AI 

For decades, science fiction has imagined a world where language barriers no longer stand in the way of communication. 

For example, in 1967, Star Trek introduced the fictional Universal Translator. Now, advances in AI are bringing that possibility closer to reality. 

In a new conversation, Microsoft Applied Science Manager Jinyu Li explores how AI is advancing the prospect of communication across languages, the progress researchers have made, and the challenges that remain. 

To learn more, catch the full episode of the podcast Our Digital Life, available to listen or watch on YouTube and podcast platforms. 

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Solving a 31-year-old mathematics challenge 

For the last 31 years, the KLS conjecture has been one of the central open problems in high-dimensional geometry. But not anymore.

New research has resolved the conjecture. This removes a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. 

The breakthrough establishes a universal principle for log-concave distributions: simple flat cuts can identify their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. The results have been independently validated, and the proof has also been formally verified using computer-assisted methods. 

Learn more about this breakthrough on the Microsoft Research blog.

[TRANSITION MUSIC] 

Making AI coding agents more efficient

Coding agents can help when writing and modifying code, but long sessions can max out the amount of information an AI model can process at once. As a result, coding agents will summarize earlier interactions in a resource-intensive process known as context compaction.

A new study looked at 13.5 million coding sessions and found fewer than 8% required context compaction. Yet those sessions accounted for 44% of total AI processing costs. 

To address this challenge, researchers developed COMPACTIONBENCH.

COMPACTIONBENCH is a benchmark for evaluating context compaction during long-running coding tasks. They also introduced APEC, a method that prepares summaries in the background instead of interrupting an agent’s work. 

In evaluations, APEC improved coding performance while reducing costs by up to 25.4% and execution time by 9.6%. 

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Improving AI tokenization across 104 languages

Before AI models can process text, they break it into smaller units called tokens. How that text is divided can affect both efficiency and performance, especially across different languages. 

Most tokenizers are designed to compress text as efficiently as possible. But a new study suggests that compression alone isn’t enough. 

Researchers introduced the Latent Core Tokenizer, or LCT, which identifies reusable components of words before building a shared vocabulary across languages. 

In evaluations spanning 104 languages, LCT produced more linguistically meaningful tokens than leading alternatives while maintaining comparable efficiency across languages. It also improved model performance across four multilingual benchmarks. 

The findings suggest that better tokenization depends not just on how much text can be compressed, but on how well the underlying structure of language is preserved. 

[MUSIC]

And that’s your Microsoft Research Focus. 

From the research culture and the collaborations driving discovery to producing more linguistically meaningful tokens, these are just a few of the developments researchers are exploring across Microsoft. 

Want to learn more and stay connected? Explore the latest research, discover the people behind it, and keep tabs on the ideas shaping what’s next by visiting aka.ms/MicrosoftResearch (opens in new tab) and follow Microsoft Research on all major social platforms. 

I’m Anson Ho, and thanks for tuning in. 

We’ll see you at the next Microsoft Research Focus. 

[MUSIC FADES] 
Opens in a new tab

A New Dawn in the Cloud: ‘Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV’ Is Coming to GeForce NOW
items.summary: Rally the ranks this GFN Thursday. Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV is coming to GeForce NOW, allowing players to experience the battle for Kronus through cloud gaming. There’s more on the horizon, with NVIDIA DLSS 5 technology coming to War Thunder and Where Winds Meet. Meanwhile, Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen brings new tales […]
items.content:
Rally the ranks this GFN Thursday. Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV is coming to GeForce NOW, allowing players to experience the battle for Kronus through cloud gaming.

There’s more on the horizon, with NVIDIA DLSS 5 technology coming to War Thunder and Where Winds Meet. Meanwhile, Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen brings new tales and encounters, alongside 10 games joining the GeForce NOW library this week.

Kronus Calls for Reinforcements

Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV, developed by KING Art Games and published by Deep Silver, is coming to GeForce NOW. Launching on Steam Thursday, Dec. 3, the real-time strategy game returns to the series’ roots with large-scale battles, base building and a renewed fight for planet Kronus.

Command the Space Marines, Orks, Necrons or the Adeptus Mechanicus, which makes their series debut. Build a base, secure resources and customize squads to the conflict across more than 70 campaign missions, playable solo or in co-op mode. The Last Stand, Skirmish and multiplayer modes offer more ways to put tactics to the test.

GeForce NOW will bring the action to supported PCs, Macs, handhelds and other devices, with game downloads and updates handled in the cloud. Save the storage space for everyday essentials and planning for the next offensive. Wishlist the game on Steam, and stay tuned to GFN Thursday to prepare for launch.

DLSS 5 Keeps on Coming

NVIDIA DLSS 5 continues to evolve, with Gaijin Entertainment’s War Thunder and Everstone Studio’s Where Winds Meet next to receive support for the technology with the 3D-Guided Neural Rendering feature.

Arriving in mid-November, War Thunder’s Eagle’s Shadow major update adds DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, dozens of new planes, ships and tanks, along with cluster bombs for planes and visual-effects enhancements increasing the realism and dynamism of battle.

In Where Winds Meet, DLSS support arrives Monday, Nov. 23, enhancing the environments and characters of its wuxia open-world action role-playing game.

Both titles will use the latest DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering model, released in October, which doubles model performance compared with the previous version. Since its initial announcement in March, model performance has improved tenfold, bringing the technology to more gamers, including GeForce NOW Ultimate members streaming with GeForce RTX 5080 cloud rigs.

Get a closer look at the DLSS updates and find more details. 

A New Tale for the Arisen

Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is streaming on GeForce NOW, expanding the deep, explorable fantasy world of Dragon’s Dogma 2 with new tales and encounters. Travel to the long-abandoned region of Norgan, join the enigmatic Eir and uncover the secrets of the undying Fallen Dragon.

Unearth forgotten relics to unlock powerful weapons and skills, take on Lost Rites’ 12 dungeon challenges and explore new hairstyles and tattoos for Arisen and Pawn customization. 

Delicious in Dungeon also arrives in the world of Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen with a special collaboration.

GeForce NOW keeps all the new downloadable content available across supported devices — without a single download claiming local storage on a gamer’s hardware of choice.

In addition, members can look for the following games joining the GeForce NOW library this week:

  • Worst Class Ever (New release on Steam, Nov. 9)
  • Ashes of the Singularity II (New release on Steam, Nov. 10)
  • Cyberpunk 2077 (Xbox Play Anywhere, new release on Battle.net, Nov. 10)
  • DreamWorks Shrek 2 Remastered (New release on Steam, Nov. 10)
  • Warhammer Survivors (New release on Steam and Xbox, available on Game Pass, Nov. 10)
  • Main Sequence (New release on Steam, Nov. 12)
  • Deadly Days: Roadtrip (Steam)
  • GeForce 8800 GTX – 20 Years of a Legend (Steam, Ultimate members)
  • Graveyard Keeper (Steam)
  • Tape to Tape (Steam)

Also this week, Ultimate members can take a trip back to 2006 with GeForce 8800 GTX – 20 Years of a Legend, a playable demo celebrating the iconic GPU’s 20th anniversary with DLSS 4.5 and path tracing in the cloud.

Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after release and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates on announced titles.

Those ready to put the next game plan into action can grab a day pass to try Performance or Ultimate, with the cost applicable toward a first monthly membership.

What’s on the gaming lineup this weekend? Let us know on X or in the comments below.

items.title: Intelligent Delivery: Making Every Unit of Compute Serve Better Ads
items.summary:
Ads ranking models are growing toward LLM scale faster than the hardware to run them can keep up. An extra unit of compute has more impact on some ad requests, models, and chips than on others. The challenge is deciding where to allocate it to get the best outcome for the entire system. We built [...]

Read More...

The post Intelligent Delivery: Making Every Unit of Compute Serve Better Ads appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
items.content:
• Ads ranking models are growing toward LLM scale faster than the hardware to run them can keep up. An extra unit of compute has more impact on some ad requests, models, and chips than on others. The challenge is deciding where to allocate it to get the best outcome for the entire system.
  • We built Intelligent Delivery, an ML-driven system that allocates resources across the serving stack toward the system-wide optimum. It has delivered ~10% incremental ranking performance on top of model and system advancements since 2017.
  • We’re sharing a few of Intelligent Delivery’s capabilities: how we build ML models to predict the marginal utility of compute, multi-layered mechanisms to move resources across the system, and how we increasingly leverage agentic AI to continuously detect and respond to system shifts. 

As frontier ads ranking systems advance toward larger models, broader candidate sets, and richer delivery architectures, they also place greater demands on serving efficiency. Compute resources do not scale at the rate that models and system complexity do. The challenge is not just how to build more powerful models, but how to operate them efficiently across a heterogeneous system, with finite serving capacity, and under a tight latency budget. We recently shared how we put idle inference capacity to work. This post covers how we decide where each unit of compute goes to achieve globally optimal system efficiency.

Intelligent Delivery is our approach to the problem, and it has contributed an additional ~10% improvement in ads ranking performance on top of model and system advancements across major surfaces, from 2017 through the first half of 2026. It introduces an ML-driven, increasingly AI-operated adaptive optimization layer that continuously directs resources toward the requests, models, hardware fleets, and ranking stages with the highest marginal utility. This helps us run advanced ads ranking models efficiently in production, getting more out of every unit of compute to serve better ads for people who use our apps and services.

The Goal and What Makes It Difficult

One of our goals is to create a delivery system that continuously converges on its global optimum, regardless of how user behavior changes, models evolve, and the serving stack grows more complex. 

Three fundamental properties of ads delivery systems make this challenging:

The marginal impact of compute is highly heterogeneous and context-dependent: The same additional unit of compute can generate very different returns depending on the product surface, user intent, candidate quality, and system state. Request-aware signals alone are not sufficient; allocating well means estimating, for every request, the return on every available tunable system parameter, where each knob behaves differently at each stage of the funnel. We need to produce a per-request result calculation across a vast decision space within milliseconds.

Local optimality does not translate to global optimality: Result estimation is just the start; the serving stack must also be dynamically controllable. Ads delivery spans multi-stage ranking, hundreds of models, generations of hardware, and many data centers. Resources cannot be shifted freely and reliably across these boundaries without adaptive controls that account for complex dependencies throughout the stack. 

The global optimum is a moving target: The optimization landscape is continuously shifting. Every new model, hardware generation, or new architecture changes the landscape and can invalidate previously optimal allocation decisions. The system needs to adapt quickly enough to retain its optimality. 

Intelligent Delivery includes three capabilities, each designed to address one of these fundamental system challenges.

Capabilities of Intelligent Delivery

1. Request Understanding: A Shared ML Intelligence Layer for Compute

Some ad requests benefit more from additional computation than others. Initially, we captured these differences through coarse segments: Requests were grouped by attributes such as surface, context, and ad creative representation, with engineers creating policies to allocate resources for each group. This approach delivered improvements but did not scale. Every new signal multiplied the rules, making the effort unsustainable, and independent segments could not capture the nonlinear interactions among thousands of signals, which limited accuracy.

We achieved about a 20% improvement in identifying the highest-impact ad requests in offline benchmarks on major surfaces, relative to our previous production model, after reframing this into two ML problems: Which ad requests are most likely to benefit from additional compute? And how will different resource settings affect their outcomes and serving performance?

To answer the first question, we built the Resource Core Model, deep learning models with 6B sparse parameters and 20M dense parameters that run once before candidate retrieval and are shared across the delivery funnel. Learned embeddings and deep feature interactions capture nuanced request patterns that manually defined segments cannot.

We then fine-tune the Resource Core Model into a set of specialized models, each generating incremental signals about outcome, compute consumption, and latency impact. Together this forms a shared ML intelligence layer for resource allocation: The Resource Core Model understands each request and its serving behavior, while individual mechanisms determine how to translate those predictions into actions.

2. Allocation Mechanisms: A Hierarchy of Decision Engines

Ads serving runs on a globally distributed, heterogeneous fleet with many data center regions, several hardware generations, and millions of hosts, all shared by a multi-tier serving stack. A single allocation mechanism cannot control the complex resource distribution end to end. So we decomposed the problem into a hierarchy of layers and built a dedicated decision engine for each. The easiest way to see the hierarchy is to follow a single request through it.

Someone opens their feed. An ad request is created, and over the next few hundred milliseconds it passes through a chain of resource allocation decisions. This leads us to three important questions and answers.

Which region serves it? Traffic and capacity are not colocated, and each region carries a different hardware mix and a different amount of headroom — so the same unit of compute is more efficient in some places than in others. We built real-time infrastructure to dynamically shift traffic between regions in a cycle of minutes, driving toward the point where every region achieves the same level of efficiency on its marginal unit of capacity.

What hardware does it land on? Our fleet spans CPUs from Intel, AMD, and Arm and accelerators from NVIDIA, AMD, and our own Meta Training and Inference Accelerator (MTIA), across several generations of each. The hard part isn’t the variety; it’s that capacity isn’t interchangeable. Our stages are bound by different resources — retrieval by memory capacity, ranking by compute, and model inference by accelerator throughput — so there is no single fastest SKU, only a best match per workload. We benchmark measured efficiency for every workload-SKU pair, then solve the assignment so that scarce hardware goes to the workloads that convert it into the most useful work. 

Inside the host, how much of this machine does the request get? Concurrent requests differ in latency budget and impact, under a hard tail-latency SLO. We predict each request’s expected outcome and its compute and latency cost in real time using our advanced deep learning models, and solve a constrained optimization that maximizes impact delivered within the host’s latency budget — as the host load increases, the performance trade-off rises and resource-intensive low-impact work is trimmed first. Enforcing those decisions takes control across the whole stack, so the framework spans from kernel-level scheduler up to application-level thread pools.

These three steps are just a subset of the allocation decisions we make during a request’s lifecycle. Following this, we optimize the number of ads to rank for each request in each ranking stage, what ad candidates enter the pool, and much more.

These allocation decisions are tightly coupled, so a resource change in any one of them ripples across the whole system. Shifting traffic between regions changes per-host load, which drives the feedback controller that sets how much work each request gets. We validate these changes in an end-to-end, closed-loop hardware testing environment to make sure we are optimizing for the global optimum instead of a local optimum.

3. Optimization Loop: Self-Optimizing Serving with Agentic AI

As our ad system advances, productionizing a new model, a new mechanism, or new hardware into the system requires a lot of effort to achieve seamless integration. We can’t brute-force every single configuration across millions of tunable dimensions built in our system for a new change. That would require too much time and far more hardware resources than we have. 

We relied heavily on human expertise and engineers’ prior knowledge to identify promising configurations. But this approach didn’t scale, because every new model, mechanism, and hardware generation expanded the search space faster than engineers could explore it.

We tried automating this with a constrained optimization approach, which delivered improvements but remained inflexible and slow. We found that it lacked the ability to generalize (it could only cover a few key knobs) and couldn’t effectively incorporate human intuition from prior experience.

Instead of doing a blind search, AI agents continuously monitor the entire system landscape, identifying changes and inefficiencies to address. In a long context window, an agent reads mechanism source code, design documents, and a decade of experiment logs and narrows that to a handful of changes worth testing. Engineers review and approve the final change before it ships.

Today, agents can already propose well-reasoned changes and design and run rigorous experiments. In the first half of 2026, agents contributed to about 20% of Intelligent Delivery optimizations. On our most automated mechanism, they now contribute to about 80% of the engineering effort, from understanding the system landscape and forming hypotheses to running experiments and converging on the final change. This shortens the optimization loop from months to weeks while keeping people firmly in control. And it steadily captures the expertise engineers have built over the years.

The Next Frontiers for Intelligent Delivery

End-to-end real-time optimization: Today, understanding a request and deciding how to serve it are still two separate steps. We’re building toward fusing them into a single model that reads a request and serves it in real time, without months of experiments. There’s established work in varying compute per request with learning-based methods. However, doing it jointly across every serving stage at once — under shifting traffic, hard capacity limits, and tight inter-stage dependencies — is the part that’s still open, and it’s what we’re pushing on.

Serving state-of-the-art models on GPUs: Large ranking models, like Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM), are growing toward LLM scale and increasingly run on GPUs, which opens a different optimization space. GPU capacity doesn’t divide the way CPU time does — it comes in whole, fixed blocks, and throughput, batching, and memory all behave differently. The levers we built for a CPU world have to be reimagined, and much of our work now goes into understanding those mechanisms and turning them into new levers. The more useful work we get out of each accelerator, the more people we can serve with strong models under the same capacity.

Acknowledgements

Sowji Adavi, Karthik Alle, Tao Cai, Olivier Chaine, Jianhao Du, Antonio Frigo, Gayatree Ganu, Chao Li, Chao Ma, Bennet Matazzoni, Riddhi Mehta, Saurabh Pohnerkar, Sudhir Pokhrel, Yuehui Qian, Liang Qiao, Yitao Qiu, Rob Schwartzberg, Sanketh Shetty, Ganlin Song, Samuel Tatipamula, Xueqi Wang, Ye Wang, Wei Wei, Jing Xu, Haomin Yu, Jiayi Yu, Jay Zang, Caijie Zhang, Shengjie Zhang, Tong Zhang, and Wei Zheng.

  • Most of the quality comes from the context we gave the agent rather than from prompt tuning. Because GTM Agent also knows where each deal stands, it can suggest the right document before a customer call.
  • You can replicate this work on top of the Deep Agents harness, and Managed Deep Agents already includes the sandbox, skills, and memory it depends on.
  • Deals where a rep sent one of these documents to the customer moved to a later stage 47% of the time, compared with 16% for matched deals without one.

Over the last 12 weeks, our internal GTM Agent has saved LangChain's sales reps thousands of hours across its workflows. In that time, it generated 1,540 sales artifacts, which reps used to build by hand, one account at a time. These artifacts include customized account plans, proof-of-value documents, proposal decks, and onboarding plans.

A powerful model can speed up artifact creation, one of the biggest time sinks in any deal, but can only take automation so far. What makes the biggest difference is everything built around the model:

  • Taste from our sales leadership
  • Context from real customer calls
  • Business logic, like company sales stages
  • Concrete requirements for moving through each stage

This post walks through how we used business context to build artifact generation with our GTM agent, and how we shaped it to fit the way LangChain sells.

You can replicate this work on top of the Deep Agents harness. The primitives it depends on (a sandbox, skills, memory, and scheduled runs) are available in our managed version, Managed Deep Agents, so a team building something similar can get straight to capturing how its business runs.

Key results

  • 47% of deals with a sent artifact moved to a later stage, compared with 16% of matched deals without one
  • 46% of artifacts were followed by a customer call within 14 days
  • Over 100 artifacts / week generated over the last 12 weeks
  • Artifacts that got sent to customers accounted for 337 hours of saved rep time

Why we added artifact generation to GTM agent

Earlier this year we wrote about how we built LangChain’s GTM Agent, which now runs a wide range of our sales and marketing workflows. It researches new leads and drafts personalized outreach for reps to approve in Slack, and every week it surfaces account signals like expansion opportunities and deal risks. Since reps were already using it every day, it was the natural place to take on one of the most time-consuming parts of their job: building sales collateral.

That work was overdue for a fix. Inconsistent versions of the same document were showing up across the org. Account executives built proposal decks by pulling usage data into a chat assistant and assembling the deck themselves. The same work got repeated on every deal, and it looked different every time. We needed a way to standardize our hard-won lessons on what works without slowing anyone down.

We were solving for three things at once:

  1. Keep a high bar for everything a customer sees
  2. Stop repeating work that every rep was doing by hand
  3. Follow a consistent process on every deal

The third goal was the hardest to get right. Every stage of a deal has gates, or things that must happen before the deal can move forward, like naming an economic buyer or agreeing on success criteria. We track which stage every deal is in and which artifact helps clear each gate. But when this work was all manual, a skipped step usually came to light in a pipeline review, weeks after the rep could have asked the customer. Now that artifacts are filed through the GTM Agent, it can spot a missing one while the deal is still active.

This workflow also gives our sales leaders a natural place to weigh in. They can tell us what is working best across the org, and we can use that as guidance for the agent to scale those best practices to everyone.

Handing our context to the agent

The agent is highly customized to how we run our business. The GTM Agent holds the context for how LangChain runs a deal at every step, including the template for every document, which follow-up questions will come up, and the right source for every piece of information. You can build the same system with our tools by customizing the context of your agent.

Most of what makes the agent useful is context the model wouldn't have on its own:

  • Process knowledge: Which artifacts we need, when we need them, and what good looks like gives the agent a backbone to work from
  • Customer context: The agent reads the Salesforce record, product usage, call transcripts, risks, decision criteria, and next steps. This helps ground our salespeople and lets them scale to handle more deals than a rep without AI assistance
  • Voice and brand: LangChain's brand assets and style guide make sure everything that comes out looks polished and consistent

Most of our effort goes into providing the agent with context. We spend very little time on prompts that compensate for the model and instead focus on capturing how our business runs. Each integration was refined over time by our reps using the product, and tuned to the preferences of our power users.

Building this system required assembling a handful of primitives:

  • Skills and instructions that hold our sales process, templates, and stage rules, versioned separately from the code
  • A sandbox with Office tools installed, so the agent can build a file, render it, look at the result, and fix it
  • A Slack interface, where reps already ask for help
  • Scheduled runs that power the pre-meeting briefs and make the agent proactive
  • Memory that carries context across a deal, not just a single conversation
  • Tracing in LangSmith, which shows every render, tool call, and review step, and is how we diagnosed the latency problem described below

Any team building a similar agent will need all of these. If you’re starting today, Managed Deep Agents provides them as building blocks, including sandbox orchestration with no extra steps, so you can go straight to the part that matters: your context.

Brand as code

The artifacts go out under our brand or a rep’s name, so GTM Agent works from the same brand rules all teams use. Our brand kit (logos, color and type tokens, fonts, and style/taste guidelines) is built into the sandbox image, so brand changes go through a reviewed pull request. After each render, the agent looks at its own pages and checks them against that guidance. You can learn more about this self-review loop here.

Self-review raises quality, but without a stopping rule, it also raises latency. Early versions of artifact generation were painfully slow. We found cases of the agent re-reviewing pages that were already fine, sometimes dozens of times. To fix this, we added a simple rule to ship once one review finds no real defect, which cut cost and wait time. On a one-pager, the rule took a run from 18 minutes down to 7 minutes.

Artifacts across the sales cycle

GTM Agent has to cover a deal end to end, which calls for a variety of different artifacts. We map artifacts to five stages of the sales cycle, each with its own standard documents.

How an artifact gets generated

An artifact is a collaboration between the agent and the rep. The agent fills a template with as much as it can reasonably retrieve, then hands off a document with flags on anything a human still needs to fill in. Every artifact follows the same path:

  1. Trigger: A rep asks for an artifact in Slack, or the agent offers the artifact during meeting prep
  2. Read the account: The agent resolves the account in Salesforce and reads its Drive folder before building anything
  3. Capture missing inputs: If the artifact needs context the account doesn't have, like success criteria or an economic buyer, the agent asks the rep first
  4. Fetch the template: A tool copies the leadership-owned template into the agent's sandbox
  5. Build: The agent fills the template in the sandbox with python-pptx, using the brand kit baked into the sandbox image
  6. Render and review: LibreOffice converts the file to PDF, the pages are rasterized, and the agent reads the images back to check the layout. It fixes what it finds and renders again
  7. File and hand off: The finished file is converted to native Google Slides, Docs, or Sheets in the account folder, and the rep gets a PDF preview and a link in Slack, with flags on whatever still needs a human edit

Each account has one Google Drive folder that the rep and the agent share. Reps add call notes and edit what the agent built, and the agent reads all of it before building the next artifact. Leadership’s templates live in the same drive. This means when a leader updates one, every rep gets the new version.

Building a proactive agent

Most reps wouldn’t ask for an artifact they didn’t know existed, so the agent had to offer help at the right moment. We drove adoption through proactive agent capabilities.

Pre-meeting briefs: The agent watches reps' calendars and sends a short brief before customer calls. Because we know where the deal is in the sales cycle, the agent can spot a meeting for a stage that doesn't have the right artifacts filed yet, and tell the rep which one to bring.

Tasks: We can assign a task to the account executive on a deal to prepare the right artifact, whether the GTM Agent builds it or they make it by hand. This keeps deals moving through the stages with the artifacts our leaders expect, in the order they expect them.

All of this comes together in our artifact hub, a web interface that shows every deal, where it sits in the sales cycle, which artifacts exist, and which should come next.

The result is that the agent has become a distribution channel for enablement and for process at the same time. The scorecard described below tells us whether that’s working.

Learning loops

Often, human taste is the truest signal of whether your agent is doing its job. If we had only checked the artifacts against the agent's own instructions, using other agents or our own judgment, we'd never have known whether those instructions captured the business process correctly or left things out.

So we kept people in the loop constantly. Our main sources of truth were:

  • Weekly meetings with the leaders of each org that owns an artifact
  • Weekly presentations and office hours for the whole sales org
  • Slack channels where we gathered regular feedback from every rep using the artifacts

Each artifact had an owner whose taste was a constant input to the design. We'd record long conversations going through every minute detail with an owner, every checkbox, every button, and every word on the page, then hand that transcript straight to our coding agents to scope improvements. That let us make fast improvements across a large suite of artifacts and ship a useful artifact generation agent.

Human feedback tells us whether an artifact meets our standards, but not whether reps are actually using it. To quantify the agent’s impact, we track what happens to every generated artifact and watch those numbers as we change the agent.

  • Volume: How many artifacts is the agent generating?
  • Utilization: How many of them are shared with someone outside the company?
  • Leverage: How many hours of rep time does that save, relative to what it costs to run?
  • Outcomes: How much pipeline do those artifacts touch?

We use the same framework for every job the GTM Agent does, and it keeps us honest about how well the system is performing. A job can look busy on volume and still go mostly unused. Closing that loop, from what the agent produces to what actually makes it into a deal and why the rest doesn’t, is a big part of what we’re building toward in the next version of the GTM Agent. We’ll go deeper on how the GTM Agent measures outcomes in an upcoming post.

Context is the moat

We’re already seeing measurable impact across 100+ weekly generated artifacts created by GTM Agent. It’s a clear example of how much more useful an agent becomes once it knows how your business runs, and how much of that comes from the context around the model rather than the model itself.

To build your own, get started today with Managed Deep Agents. For another example of agents in our GTM stack, read about our design agent.

items.title: BRQGen: Towards Adaptive Completeness Assessment and Follow-Up Question Generation for Bug Reports
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.15903v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Many bug reports lack the necessary information required to reproduce issues. In early studies, large language models have been employed to generate follow-up questions to enhance incomplete reports. However, they ask a fixed number of questions regardless of whether the report is incomplete. We propose BRQGen, an iterative framework that identifies missing or ambiguous information in bug reports and generates targeted follow-up questions, only if necessary. Reports with no identified gaps are classified as sufficient. When the author responds, BRQGen evaluates whether the answers provide the requested information and generates further questions for any exposed gaps. We curated a novel dataset of 429 incomplete bug reports from Home Assistant and Brave Browser, each containing at least one maintainer follow-up question. Each question is mapped to the author's answer and assigned a label indicating whether the requested information could have been provided directly through the issue template. Earlier maintainer requests were associated with author responses, whereas delayed requests were associated with no response. Among responding authors, requests within one hour received median replies after 0.52 hours in Home Assistant and 1.45 hours in Brave, versus 9.76 and 13.49 hours after four hours. BRQGen covered 35.4% (Qwen 3.8 Flash) to 51.8% (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) of the 1,073 ground-truth follow-up questions. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash managed to ask 45.7% of all detailed questions and 63.9% of all generic questions. Gemini 3 Flash Preview reached the highest macro-F1 for completeness assessment of 49.3%, but with a post-hoc analysis by getting only the gaps with high severities, Qwen 3.8 Flash reaches 73.6% macro-F1 score. Completeness assessment improved when at least one identified gap had high severity, and nearly all ground-truth questions were captured within the first two iterations.
items.author: Tevfik Emre Sungur, Akif Emre K\"o\c{s}\"u\c{s}, U\u{g}urcan Do\u{g}ru\c{c}am, Eray T\"uz\"un

items.title: The Import Tax: A Longitudinal Measurement of Startup Cost in the Python Ecosystem
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.02753v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Python programs pay for their imports at every process start, a cost that is invisible in steady-state benchmarks but dominant for command-line tools, test workers, and serverless cold starts. Python 3.15 adds explicit lazy imports (PEP 810) on largely anecdotal evidence. We measure the import cost of the 500 most-downloaded PyPI packages, every quarterly release since mid-2021, under six CPython versions (3.9-3.14) on two platforms (Apple M5/macOS and Intel Xeon/Linux), 66,816 cells in all, with targeted experiments that isolate individual effects. Values are for macOS (Linux in parentheses). Import cost is heavily skewed (median 12.3 ms, 99th percentile 400 ms). Among packages that import in more than 2 ms, namespace distributions excluded, the median package spends 68% of its import time in the standard library (68% on Linux with the interpreter on local storage, 79% on network storage). Precompiling bytecode removes almost all of the cold-start penalty on Linux and 92% of it for the median package on macOS, but only a third of the summed macOS penalty: packages with native libraries pay a security assessment of each library that the system has not seen before, again in every fresh environment. A package's own import code grows by a median 4.0% (5.0%) per year; installing each release with the dependencies of its time changes its trend by a median of only 0.15 (0.35) percentage points (CPython 3.9). CPython 3.14 runs package code faster than 3.9 but imports more and slower standard-library modules, a net 1.16x (1.07x) slowdown. Submodules that dependents import beyond the top level add nothing for the median package and at most 11.7 (49.5) ms for nine packages in ten. On CPython 3.15, global lazy mode cuts the imports that dependents perform to 0.41x (0.39x) of their cost, and 38 of 461 packages fail under it, many only on first use of a name. Harness, code, and dataset are public.
items.author: Trinath Sai Subhash Reddy Pittala

items.title: SACS: A Code Smell Dataset using Semi-automatic Generation Approach
items.summary:
arXiv:2602.15342v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Code smell is a great challenge in software refactoring, which indicates latent design or implementation flaws that may degrade the software maintainability and evolution. Over the past of decades, the research on code smell has received extensive attention. Especially the researches applied machine learning-technique have become a popular topic in recent studies. However, one of the biggest challenges to apply machine learning-technique is the lack of high-quality code smell datasets. Manually constructing such datasets is extremely labor-intensive, as identifying code smells requires substantial development expertise and considerable time investment. In contrast, automatically generated datasets, while scalable, frequently exhibit reduced label reliability and compromised data quality. To overcome this challenge, in this study, we explore a semi-automatic approach to generate a code smell dataset with high quality data samples. Specifically, we first applied a set of automatic generation rules to produce candidate smelly samples. We then employed multiple metrics to group the data samples into an automatically accepted group and a manually reviewed group, enabling reviewers to concentrate their efforts on ambiguous samples. Furthermore, we established structured review guidelines and developed a annotation tool to support the manual validation process. Based on the proposed semi-automatic generation approach, we created an open-source code smell dataset, SACS, covering three widely studied code smells: Long Method, Large Class, and Feature Envy. Each code smell category includes over 10,000 labeled samples. This dataset could provide a large-scale and publicly available benchmark to facilitate future studies on code smell detection and automated refactoring.
items.author: Hanyu Zhang, Tomoji Kishi

items.title: Autonomous Cyber Operations Gym for Training and Evaluating AI Models for Defence
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.18594v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: This paper proposes an Autonomous Cyber Operations (ACO) gym, a unified framework integrating high-fidelity network emulation, realistic user behaviour modelling for benign network traffic and adversarial profiles, and the generation of cybersecurity scenarios through open toolkits. By supporting live and deferred feature extraction at the packet and flow levels, the gym facilitates the creation of labelled synthetic datasets for training Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs), as well as developing and evaluating modular components for autonomous defence agents through emulated interactions. While evaluation of a DNN classifier within the gym shows high in-domain performance, achieving near-perfect recall on adversarial network flows, our experiments reveal a significant sensitivity to domain shift, showing that even minor changes in network composition, such as variations in traffic protocol distribution, can lead to a catastrophic collapse in model transferability and detection performance.
items.author: Tobias H\"urten, Johannes F. Loevenich, Florian Spelter, Erik Adler, Laurin Holz, Maxime Schwarzer, Thies Moehlenhof, Roberto Rigolin F. Lopes

items.title: Small area learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.15953v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Small area estimation (SAE) traditionally borrows strength across domains through a prespecified working model. We introduce small area learning (SAL), a novel learner-agnostic framework that formulates SAE as a multi-target semi-supervised learning problem and treats outcome prediction as a nuisance task. Areas may differ through unrestricted covariate shift and structured conditional shift, with information shared through common and area-specific components. We develop estimators with and without cross-fitting, accommodating low-complexity and flexible learners and unifying synthetic, model-based, and semi-supervised estimators. For area means, we establish a unified asymptotic theory for these estimator families, characterizing conditions for consistency, asymptotic normality and providing variance estimators and confidence intervals without prescribing a particular learning algorithm. We extend the theory to settings with only aggregated population covariates and characterize the resulting aggregation bias. SAL reveals clearly a bias-variance trade-off: partial residual correction in classical estimators can reduce mean squared error, whereas full correction yields estimators robust to the misspecification of working models, potentially at higher variance. Simulations yield RMSE reductions of 34%-49% relative to direct estimation, with the best configuration varying across settings. The numerical studies also illustrate how shrinkage can produce overly optimistic confidence intervals at the expense of strong modeling assumptions.
items.author: Katarzyna Reluga, Nicola Salvati, Setareh Ranjbar, Nikos Tzavidis, Mark van der Laan

items.title: Pro-t-VAE: Closed-Form Student's t Mixtures for Robust Prototype Discovery
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.14894v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We present a robust deep generative framework for unsupervised image prototype discovery, built on a heavy-tailed Student's t mixture prior, that bridges statistical robustness and mathematical tractability. Existing generative approaches typically rely on noise-prone Gaussian priors or computationally intensive diffusion models; neither simultaneously provides explicit latent structure nor exact analytic optimization. While diffusion models can yield strong priors, iterative sampling and intractable likelihoods limit scalability and interpretability for prototype discovery. We address these issues by constructing a Student's t latent space via a Bayesian scale-mixture formulation. This yields a fully closed-form augmented ELBO for unsupervised Student's t mixture variational autoencoders, which, to our knowledge, is the first such objective applied to robust image prototype discovery, avoiding biased variational approximations and high computational costs in prior heavy-tailed or diffusion-based frameworks. Treating precision as a latent variable automatically modulates each data point's influence, downweighting outliers to learn a data-dependent measure of trust. The result is improved robustness, accuracy, and efficiency, with well-separated latent representations and more stable manifold learning than state-of-the-art methods. We validate our model on standard vision benchmarks and challenging neuroimaging tasks. In brain MRI-driven neurodegenerative disease analysis, our model recovers clean, anatomically coherent prototypes where clinical noise often collapses rare subtypes. These results highlight the ability of our framework to preserve anatomy-associated patterns for precise discovery in clinical settings. Our code is available at: https://github.com/xuzhikangnba/torch-tvae.
items.author: Zhikang Xu, Jiarui Xing, Jian Wang

items.title: Rethinking Floorplan Generation with Space Syntax: From Design Theory to Model Improvement
items.summary:
arXiv:2602.22507v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Architectural design increasingly adopts generative AI (GenAI) for floorplan generation, an early-stage design task exploring how spaces should be organized for use. Yet fidelity objectives inherited from native visual and geometric generators do not automatically capture this design purpose. This organization remains largely implicit in generated representations, limiting direct evaluation and feedback. Drawing on space syntax, an established architectural design theory, the Space Syntax Integration Operator (SSIO) recovers convex-space access graphs across heterogeneous formats. This theory-grounded shared intermediate representation, which we call a design container, supports evaluation and model understanding of spatial design. Applying SSIO to four residential corpora spanning 15 countries reveals public spaces' integration levels are highest, with corpus-dependent distributions. These patterns underpin the RPLAN-SSI benchmark, an empirical design reference system assessing population-level functional-profile alignment (IPD) and distributional alignment of within-plan public-space advantage (PIAD). Comparison with this residential reference reveals a design gap: public spaces in generated floorplans have a smaller integration advantage over other spaces. To address this gap, Space Syntax-Guided Post-Training (SSPT) provides a plug-and-play design-learning interface: SSIO-derived RL feedback reduces IPD and PIAD across five heterogeneous diffusion backbones while preserving native mechanisms. We further discuss how this approach may inform GenAI applications in other design domains.
items.author: Zhuoyang Jiang, Dongqing Zhang, Qingxiang Liu, Yuxuan Liang

items.title: Governing Copyright Responsibly in the Era of Generative AI
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.17002v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models are trained on collections that may include scholarly works, while authors generally lack work-level information about whether and how their works were used. This paper asks how copyright governance frames and operationalises the protection of such authors, and what a responsible alternative would require. Forty legislative, judicial and soft-law instruments issued between 2019 and 2026 were coded deductively against a framework derived from Responsible Research and Innovation theory, yielding 1,337 category assignments across 835 segments. The European Union and the United States are the primary cases; the United Kingdom, China and international bodies serve as comparators. Normative orientation and the distribution of responsibility dominate the corpus, while reflexivity is the least represented category and reaches its minimum in the US sub-corpus. Both primary jurisdictions frame protection procedurally rather than as an entitlement, and no instrument in the corpus creates a general author-facing attribution duty for the use of works in AI training. From the coded gaps, the paper derives a six-instrument governance design and a capacity-based allocation of responsibility among developers, publishers, collecting societies, funders, institutions, regulators, and individual authors.
items.author: D. Kochetkov

items.title: A Scaled-Up Empirical Study of Syntactic Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.16837v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Syntactic language models (SLMs) that generate sentences along with their syntactic tree structures have shown promise in both syntactic generalization and downstream tasks. Prior studies, however, have mostly evaluated smaller models trained on less pretraining data and tested on narrower task suites. In addition, the design space of tree linearization and attention masks remains underexplored. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of 12 controlled configurations---one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants spanning different linearizations and masks---at scales up to 1B parameters and 100B training tokens, evaluated across 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. The experimental results show that SLMs with standard causal attention match or exceed structural-mask variants across downstream and syntactic benchmarks. They require no architectural modifications and remain compatible with FlashAttention. We also observe that when scaling up to the 1B-parameter scale, the top-performing SLM variant no longer shows a clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline, suggesting that SLMs may become less competitive with scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/qlwpc/TG-Interpolation.
items.author: Pengcheng Wang, Zhexuan Zhang, Chao Lou, Kewei Tu

items.title: Where Polanyi Meets Galois: Tacit Knowing as an Algebro-Deterministic Operation, Toward Re-rooting AI-Generated Science
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.16102v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Tacit knowing is an operating regime of one memory substrate, not a separate kind of content. In VaCoAl (CASRAM, PyVaCoAl), an algebro-deterministic hyperdimensional memory over GF(2), one DAG of bound records is read in two ways. With every collision repaired (Rescue), the trace is exactly auditable but no path outranks another; with collisions tolerated (Don't Care), a path-integrated confidence $CR_2$ ranks direct over circuitous routes without being stated. This audit-valuation complementarity formalizes Polanyi's claim that tacit and explicit knowledge are not sharply divided. (1) Polanyi's from-to structure reads as non-commutative binding. (2) Full explication destroys the valuation (Lemma 1), as with Polanyi's pianist; tacitness is contingent or regime-bound, placing Polanyi, Nonaka, Tsoukas and Collins on one substrate. (3) The same lemma answers the popular dual-process moral ("train slow System 2 to tame fast System 1"), which mirrors the two-store reading of knowledge Polanyi rejected; Mercier and Sperber's reply, that reasoning is intuitive inference about reasons, matches his. (4) To know a large DAG is to cull it. Simon answered Polanyi's Meno argument: a test and a generator suffice. The AlphaGo-to-AlphaProof lineage builds that answer, yet a checker audits an endpoint and values no path: the tacit is relocated, not removed, and results are verified yet rootless. (5) Collins's three tacit knowledges map to bound structure, substrate valuation and value binding. (6) Our mentor-student DAG charts tacit transmission. (7) AI-solved problems with few follow-ups (Tao) are rootless explicit knowledge, re-rooted when LLMs generate, VaCoAl keeps the trace and the community values. (8) On Mercier and Sperber's theory an LLM is a sophist; truth-seeking lies in collective tacit knowing, Polanyi's conviviality, which we conjecture extends beyond humans. Testable predictions follow.
items.author: Hiroyuki Chuma, Kanji Otsuka, Yoichi Sato, Kodo Yamauchi

items.title: HarnessNet: Feedback-driven Hierarchical Joint Harness Evolution for Multi-agent Systems
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.15221v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: AI agents can evolve by using environment feedback to revise their harnesses, the software managing model inputs, tool use, memory, and execution, while keeping foundation models frozen. Existing studies focus on single agents, leaving joint harness evolution in multi-agent systems (MAS) underexplored. A single global optimizer faces growing context and workload as the system scales, while access restrictions may prevent sharing agent internals or system-wide feedback. We propose HarnessNet, a framework for hierarchical harness evolution in MAS. Its basic unit, Agentron, comprises an evolvable forward harness, a foundation model, and a local optimizer that can observe and modify only that harness. Agentrons form a layered graph through which environment feedback propagates backward, with upstream optimizers receiving node-specific feedback from the downstream layer. This decomposes joint harness evolution into smaller, coordinated tasks with separate contexts, reducing individual optimizers' context and workload while keeping access local. Optimizers need not access all agent trajectories or raw environment feedback. Experiments on AgentBench with multiple foundation models demonstrate the feasibility of training HarnessNet. Compared with a single global optimizer, HarnessNet achieves comparable performance gains while respecting local privacy and requiring fewer tokens and less time per optimizer call. A migration study shows that the evolved harnesses remain jointly effective after replacing the foundation models, suggesting transferability across models.
items.author: Zhaoyuan Qiu, Sachith Seneviratne, Yu Xia, Saman Halgamuge

items.title: Four conditions for composing plugin-based agents without a host agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.28553v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language model agents now run long-horizon, multi-tool, autonomous sessions, and the infrastructure must keep the current assembly of capabilities, the progress of execution, and the basis for recovery after a fault. A single-process host holds this information in its own running state, so its death takes the session record and the assembly with it. This paper gives four conditions under which a plugin-based agent needs no host process, one each on state placement, record carriers, recovery coordination, and provider resolution. The store, writer, and delivery disciplines keep the conditions in force, and each carries formal support from the spatiotemporal-composability calculus and from the proofs in the supplementary materials. An agent that meets them can be constructed with its assembly on a bus of peer processes and its record in an append-only carrier owned by no process, and removing any one part makes the assembly need a host again. The conditions themselves are the contribution, and every implementation that meets them inherits the same advantages. Such an agent keeps its session through the death of any process, wastes no calls after a fault, loses no records, recovers locally, changes its capability set while it runs, and carries its undo semantics across processes. This paper builds one SDK of the conditions, Logos, and measures whether it fulfills their promise against the single-process reference and a configuration over MCP under one fault in each of 200 tasks, realized in 197. The reference lost all 197 faulted sessions, the MCP configuration kept its sessions but issued 1,212 wasted calls, and the SDK kept every session, wasted no call, lost no record, and fulfilled the promise of the conditions in every faulted task, with task performance preserved. The conditions give builders a tested route from single-process hosts to peer processes.
items.author: Hanzhang Jia, Liheng Zeng, Hao Cheng, Yi Gao, Bo Ma, Guolong Xu

items.title: ASAP: Assembly-Source Aligned Pseudocode Refinement For Binary Decompilation
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.06900v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in binary decompilation to refine the C-like pseudocode produced by traditional rule-based decompilers. While this pseudocode is useful, it is a heuristic and lossy abstraction rather than a faithful copy of the source code. It often contains decompiler errors, especially for aggressively optimized binaries where critical low-level details are obscured. We present ASAP, an Assembly-Source Aligned Pseudocode refinement framework for binary decompilation. ASAP learns source-aligned assembly representations from paired source and binary functions using joint function-level and snippet-level contrastive alignment. A Q-Former then compresses chunk-level assembly features into a fixed number of assembly tokens. These tokens and the decompiler-produced pseudocode jointly condition the decompilation LLM. During refinement, we use stochastic pseudocode masking and a relative assembly-advantage loss to discourage the model from relying solely on pseudocode. On two decompilation benchmarks across multiple compiler optimization levels, ASAP improves the average re-execution rate from 64.7% to 71.9% and the average recompilation rate from 91.6% to 96.6% compared with the strongest baseline. Our approach offers both a new perspective and a practical solution to binary decompilation.
items.author: Yujian Zhuang, Dehong Gao, Qichao Zhang, Qijing Lai, Jiaxin Wang, Libin Yang, Xiaoyan Cai

items.title: Scentree: a framework for generating scenario trees for multistage stochastic programming
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.21495v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We present scentree, an open-source Python package for constructing scenario trees for multistage stochastic programming models using either historical data or samples drawn from a probability distribution. It combines machine learning and multivariate time series models to obtain a scenario fan that captures dependencies in the stochastic processes. This scenario fan is subsequently reduced into a scenario tree that preserves representativeness of the stochastic process, providing a flexible and extensible framework for uncertainty modeling in stochastic programming problems. The framework can also be naturally applied to two-stage stochastic programming problems. Key contributions are the joint modeling of the stochastic process, preserving correlations between all random variables, and the automation of the complete workflow, including forecasting model selection, parameter estimation, scenario fan generation, and scenario tree construction. In addition, scentree does not assume any underlying data distribution, reducing the statistical expertise required to produce a scenario tree, and is modular by design, allowing external forecasts and other partial executions of the workflow.
items.author: Cristian Pach\'on-Garc\'ia, Albert Sol\`a Vilalta, F. -Javier Heredia

items.title: Insights from GitHub Community on the Matter Standard: Developer Perspectives and Challenges
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.01494v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Matter seeks to resolve longstanding interoperability problems in the Internet of Things (IoT), yet little is known about how developers experience the standard in day to day work. This paper examines over 13,000 issues from the official Project CHIP GitHub repository to understand the kinds of problems contributors report when implementing and integrating Matter. Using topic modeling and qualitative analysis, we identify four recurring areas of concern, Testing, Interoperability, Development, and Platform and Network, and describe how they manifest in the evolution of the codebase and tooling. The findings reveal systematic technical and integration challenges and point to concrete opportunities to refine Matter's test infrastructure, cross vendor guidance, and documentation as the standard continues to mature.
items.author: Muhammad Hassan, Carl Gunter, Susan Landau, Masooda Bashir

items.title: Automated Code Review Assignments: An Alternative Perspective of Code Ownership on GitHub
items.summary:
arXiv:2512.05551v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Code ownership is central to ensuring accountability and maintaining quality in large-scale software development. Yet, as software supply chain attacks threaten project health and quality assurance, mechanisms for assigning and enforcing responsibility have become critical. In 2017, GitHub introduced the CODEOWNERS feature, a file in the repository that names the developers responsible for specific files and automatically requests them as reviewers, to strengthen accountability and protect critical parts of the codebase. Little is known about how CODEOWNERS is adopted and practiced. We present the first large-scale empirical study of CODEOWNERS usage across over 844,000 pull requests with 1.9 million comments and over 2 million reviews. We identify 10,287 designated owners, the developers named in CODEOWNERS files, track their code review activities, and compare them with contribution-based owners, the developers who contributed at least 5% of a file's lines. Results indicate that designated owners take part in a moderate share of the pull requests that touch their files, that their collaborative behavior resembles that of contribution-based owners, and that after adoption merge time and review effort grow more slowly, or fall, relative to their pre-adoption trend. Using regression discontinuity design analysis, we further find that designated owners' review, decision (approval and merge), and authoring activity jumps upward at adoption, and that over the following year they do more review and decision work per pull request than before, whereas contribution-based owners do less review work per pull request. Our results position CODEOWNERS as a promising yet sparsely adopted mechanism for improving software governance and resilience. We discuss how projects can leverage this alternative ownership method to enhance security and accountability in open-source development.
items.author: Jai Lal Lulla, Raula Gaikovina Kula, Christoph Treude

items.title: Architectural Degradation: Definition, Motivations, Measurement and Remediation Approaches
items.summary:
arXiv:2507.14547v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Architectural degradation, also known as erosion, decay, or aging, impacts system quality, maintainability, and adaptability. Although widely acknowledged, current literature shows fragmented definitions, metrics, and remediation strategies. Our study aims to unify understanding of architectural degradation by identifying its definitions, causes, metrics, tools, and remediation approaches across academic and gray literature. We conducted a multivocal literature review of 108 studies extracting definitions, causes, metrics, measurement approaches, tools, and remediation strategies. We developed a taxonomy encompassing architectural, code, and process debt to explore definition evolution, methodological trends, and research gaps. Architectural degradation has shifted from a low-level issue to a socio-technical concern. Definitions now address code violations, design drift, and structural decay. Causes fall under architectural (e.g., poor documentation), code (e.g., hasty fixes), and process debt (e.g., knowledge loss). We identified 54 metrics and 31 measurement techniques, focused on smells, cohesion/coupling, and evolution. Yet, most tools detect issues but rarely support ongoing or preventive remediation. Degradation is both technical and organizational. While detection is well-studied, continuous remediation remains lacking. Our study reveals missed integration between metrics, tools, and repair logic, urging holistic, proactive strategies for sustainable architecture.
items.author: Noman Ahmad, Ruoyu Su, Matteo Esposito, Andrea Janes, Valentina Lenarduzzi, Davide Taibi

items.title: Preserve the Vulnerability, Break the Alert: Testing the Robustness of CodeQL Taint Tracking with Natural Rewrites
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17123v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Static application security testing (SAST) tools such as CodeQL serve as security gates in continuous integration and code review, and a gate is also read in reverse. When a previously reported alert disappears after a change, developers and the tools around them often take the vulnerability to be gone. That inference holds only if the analyzer is robust to changes that keep the vulnerability. We test this robustness for CodeQL's JavaScript taint tracking with natural, vulnerability-preserving rewrites. A large language model, given only the alert CodeQL exposes and no knowledge of its implementation, rewrites one function along a reported flow as a plausible maintenance change, and we verify by manual audit and controlled experiments that the flaw survives and the alert does not. On 172 flows that CodeQL detects in real npm vulnerabilities, three rewrites per flow silence 26.2% of them, at about USD 0.51 per silenced flow. The same generator, asked only to refactor the same functions with no knowledge of the alert, silences none of them. Every silencing rewrite traces to one of seven gaps at the library-modeling boundary, and 64 of the 70 rewrites cross a gap inside an API CodeQL already models. The largest is the WHATWG URL constructor, which propagates taint to a URL's query components but not to its pathname. The boundary is not specific to CodeQL. 74% of the silencing rewrites also silence an independently built taint analyzer, and 53% escape three analyzers combined. A disappearing alert after an ordinary-looking change is therefore weak evidence that a vulnerability has been fixed, the gaps point SAST developers to narrow and concrete repair targets, and robustness to natural rewrites belongs alongside detection rate in how taint analyzers are evaluated.
items.author: Zhezhen Cao, Weiyuan Ding, Bowen Xu

items.title: A Code-Level Audit of X
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.16800v1 Announce Type: cross
