Across five settings spanning Who&When and LongRCA and three backbone models, CoLFA achieves the highest exact step-localization accuracy with the lowest token consumption. Compared with individual baselines in each setting, CoLFA improves accuracy by up to 37.50% and reduces token consumption by up to 97.6%.
items.author: Yufei Luo, Yuchen Ling, Chunrong Fang

items.title: ToolTurns: Benchmarking LLM Agents in Multi-Turn Dialogue
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.14925v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-using language models are increasingly deployed in conversational settings, yet most large-scale tool-use benchmarks focus on isolated requests. We introduce ToolTurns, a benchmark of 2,620 problems spanning 1,827 tools and 11,004 API endpoints across 47 categories. Each dialogue begins with an intentionally underspecified request and continues through two context-dependent follow-ups, testing clarification, tool use, and retention of conversational context. We also introduce an open-source user simulator that reveals withheld context through dialogue and generates follow-up requests, with a checker--fixer pipeline for improving its turns. Across nine language models, the best agent resolves 69.6% of individual requests but completes only 39.8% of full dialogues. Under this evaluation protocol, every evaluated model receives lower success scores on follow-up requests than on the initial request, and dialogue-quality rubric scores and task success can rank models very differently. Paired turn-level evaluation shows that the checker--fixer reduces detected dialogue defects, and blind human evaluation favors the revised turns. ToolTurns provides a testbed for evaluating whether agents sustain task success across multi-turn dialogue with tools.
items.author: Milad Gholami, Brendan King, Jeffrey Flanigan

items.title: Hy ASR 3.0 Technical Report
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.14908v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present Hy ASR 3.0, a large language model (LLM)-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) system that delivers strong recognition accuracy, supports flexible contextual conditioning, and maintains robust recognition performance across diverse speech conditions. Hy ASR 3.0 supports Mandarin Chinese, English and 13 Chinese dialect groups, including Cantonese. Among the evaluated systems, it achieves the lowest aggregate error rates on public Mandarin Chinese, English, and Cantonese benchmarks and the lowest error rates on the corresponding internal test sets, alongside first-tier dialect recognition performance. Beyond audio-only transcription, Hy ASR 3.0 supports multiple forms of external context, including hotword lists, question--answer dialogues, and summaries, enabling the use of task-relevant information during recognition. The model also leverages intra-utterance context to disambiguate homophonic and phonetically similar keywords using information from other parts of the same utterance, without requiring a separate contextual input. Evaluations demonstrate strong contextual recognition in both external-context and intra-utterance settings, as well as robust recognition of long-form speech, children's and older adults' speech, low-volume speech, and speech in noisy environments. This report describes the model architecture and training methodology and presents evaluations across recognition accuracy, context utilization, and robustness.
items.author: Aoxiong Yin, Auden Li, Chao Huang, Chuanyang Hu, Eitan Wang, Ethan Zou, Fangming Feng, Guangyu Chen, Guinan Li, He Wang, Jiahong Li, Meng Yu, Mingyu Cui, Peng Wang, Rongjie Li, Steve Yves, Teddy Sun, Tian Zheng, Wei Liu, Yang Zhou, Yixuan Zhang, Zhennan Lin, Zhihang Xu, Zhuohao Li, Ziqiang Zhang, Anji Zhang, Bang Wang, Caisheng Ouyang, Chengqi Zhu, Chong Li, Conglian Xie, Dongdong Wang, Edward Wang, Evelynn Liu, Ferman Yang, Feng Lu, Gang Zhang, Jathon Zhang, Jaxl Liu, Jiachen Luo, Jian Li, Jingxi Gui, Kysun Wang, Liang Dong, Longsha Zhou, Na Hu, Qi Chen, Rilin Chen, Rui Yuan, Shanshan Sang, Siyu Yan, Steven Hong, Taihui Wang, Weiwei Li, Xiangyu Zhang, Xiaotong Yang, Xue Hu, Xue Jiang, Yameng Li, Yifu Sun, Yuhuan Zhou, Zhiang Chen, Zhibin Wang

items.title: Is Jev a Good Multilingual Judge?
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.14861v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative large language models are widely used for multilingual text evaluation, yet whether decision models that directly output judgment probabilities can serve as multilingual judges has received limited attention. We evaluate Jev against generative LLM judges on four multilingual benchmarks with human annotations, covering up to 47 language varieties and three evaluation formats: binary decisions, pairwise comparisons, and graded ratings. At approximately $1/31$ to $1/61$ of GPT-6.1's evaluation cost, Jev is competitive on most multilingual judging tasks, but falls behind GPT-6.1 on knowledge-intensive answer verification. Further analysis shows that Jev is more likely to accept incorrect answers in low-resource languages than in English and that its probability outputs help identify errors across tasks. Based on these findings, we offer recommendations on evaluation instructions, confidence-based selection, and model routing, providing empirical guidance for using Jev as a multilingual judge.
items.author: Wei Liu, Yi Fan, Xiyan Fu

items.title: LLMs and the Homogenization of Teaching
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.14828v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known to lack diversity in open-ended text generation, a limitation that is especially consequential in education, where homogeneity can narrow the kinds of thinking and disciplinary work students are invited to do. We study diversity in two educational generation tasks: math items and essay feedback. We compare frontier and open-weight models with human-authored reference distributions using lexical, semantic, and domain-grounded measures. For math, we examine the mathematical activities students are asked to perform; for feedback, we examine the revision work requested and the rhetorical strategies used to communicate it. We evaluate direct prompting, two diversity prompting methods, and post-training. Across both tasks, directly prompted model outputs are markedly less diverse than human-authored content--78% higher on lexical (Self-BLEU) and 51% higher on semantic (embedding) similarity--and represent a narrower range of instructional forms. Diversity prompting and post-training increase variation largely through surface features without broadening the instructional repertoire. Models inherit and amplify the most normative routines of human instruction. Overcoming mode collapse in education will require richer instructional data and investment in teachers' creative capacity and professional judgment.
items.author: Mei Tan, Hyunji Nam, Hari Subramonyam, Dorottya Demszky

items.title: Distributionally Robust BEST-RQ For Speech Representation Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.14801v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: BEST-RQ, based on random projection and quantization, has been a well-established self-supervised learning approach to learn speech representations from large-scale unlabeled audio due to its high performance and efficiency. However, in BEST-RQ representations learned by random quantization can be sensitive to the choice of quantization targets. To address this issue, we propose a distributionally robust extension of BEST-RQ that seeks representations robust across multiple quantization configurations. Specifically, we define groups by codebooks and formulate the training as a group Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) problem. Rather than optimizing solely for the average loss across groups, our approach adaptively reweights groups to emphasize those performing poorly. Additionally, we regularize DRO with a Kullback-Leibler divergence to prevent excessive distribution deviation. We evaluate our approach on the Multilingual LibriSpeech dataset and show that the distributionally robust BEST-RQ achieves superior performance over the conventional uniform average across multiple codebooks.
items.author: Muhammad Khan, Xiaodong Cui, Brian Kingsbury, George Saon

items.title: An LLM Is All You Need: Data-Efficient Adaptation to Full-Duplex, Word-Level Spoken Dialogue
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.14774v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue, in which a system listens while it speaks and can backchannel, yield the floor, and be interrupted, is usually obtained by training on hundreds of thousands to millions of hours of speech. This is costly, rewrites the language model that supplies the system's knowledge, and still leaves turn-taking either implicit or decided coarsely rather than word by word. We show that a frozen, general-purpose multimodal LLM can instead be adapted into a word-level full-duplex system with little data. Our system is a thinker-talker cascade on an 80 ms frame clock. The thinker keeps the LLM frozen and trains only lightweight adapters and a few new token embeddings (97M parameters); at every frame it emits one token of agent text, with pauses, yields, and onsets represented as tokens of the same vocabulary and kept legal by a finite-state machine. A four-stage curriculum, each stage anchored to the model's own behavior under the previous format, performs the conversion in about 30 GPU-hours. The talker reads only the thinker's discrete tokens, so the two halves are trained independently. On Full-Duplex-Bench and InteractionBench, the system is competitive with open-source full-duplex systems built through large-scale speech training: among them, it is the least likely to take the floor when the user merely pauses, backchannels most often, and leads in spoken-task accuracy, groundedness, and coherence over long conversations.
items.author: Tairan Chen, Richard Yucheng He, Yihang Liu, Baodong Cao, Chen Xu

items.title: Probe What-If Worlds Before You Ship: Persona Simulation for Real-World Decision Making
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.14700v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: User research and system testing reveal whether products and services meet user needs, yet recruiting specialized participants, designing controlled what-if comparisons, and repeating studies as designs evolve often bottleneck design iteration and data-driven decision-making. We present a framework and execution infrastructure that translates real-world industry inquiries into controlled experiments with simulated users. Our methodology formally defines the target cohort, experimental stimuli, and decision-relevant metrics, while the pipeline supports large-scale concurrent runs over cohort-stimulus-environment combinations (survey, web, chatbot, and OS app), auditable trial-level logging, cohort-level outcome aggregation, and cross-cohort and cross-variant statistical reports. Across twelve industry partner cases spanning five domains, we show how constructing hard-to-reach or what-if persona cohorts supports exploratory studies and distills simulated responses into testable design hypotheses. Cross-model comparisons on selected cases largely preserve primary conclusions, whereas perturbing or ablating persona attributes alters service outcomes, effect sizes, and inter-group differences, indicating that grounding target cohorts in detailed personas materially shapes simulation results. Together, these studies show that persona-enabled agents can test specified cohorts at design speed, diagnose systems under test, and deliver directional evidence that focuses problem definition, steers design and strategic decisions, and guides further study.
items.author: Julie Zhu, Jianheng Hou, Zhixu Silvia Tao, Shi Bo, Yilan Fan, Yixuan He, Zhiyuan Hu, Shirley Huang, Fangyu Liu, Yijun Wang, Zibu Wei, Haimingyue Xu, Zhen Xu, Zichen Yuan, Jierui Zuo, Jintao Huang, Yifan Wang, Qianfeng Wen, Jiahan Li, Zhejian Peng, Bowen Yang, Shushu Liang, Yuexing Hao, Xiaomin Li

items.title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Bellman Tournaments
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.35748v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Model selection and hyperparameter tuning pose a central challenge in off-policy evaluation (OPE) because estimation errors in fitted $Q$-functions and occupancy ratios cannot be directly evaluated using held-out transition data. Existing Bellman-residual-based validation methods often require auxiliary regressions, while many minimax-based methods require optimization over separate critic classes. We propose pairwise Bellman validation (PBV), a family of penalized Bellman tournament methods that reduces validation to computing held-out sample averages. PBV constructs critics from pairwise candidate differences, on the log scale for occupancy ratios, and selects the candidate with the smallest worst-case penalized score. This construction approximates oracle critics given by $Q$-function errors and log ratios of candidate to true occupancy ratios, whose Bellman and adjoint Bellman moments control estimation error. Critic penalties account for approximation error under candidate-class misspecification. We establish finite-sample oracle inequalities relative to the best available candidate, even under candidate-class misspecification. For $Q$-function selection, unweighted PBV avoids importance weighting but requires a coercivity condition on a quadratic form induced by the Bellman operator. Importance-weighted PBV (IW-PBV) uses marginalized importance weighting to exploit Bellman contraction under the target-policy occupancy measure, avoiding this condition. For occupancy-ratio selection, adjoint PBV (A-PBV) exploits KL contraction of the adjoint Bellman operator to obtain oracle guarantees under the offline data law. On Hopper and DeepOPE, unweighted PBV is competitive with LSTD-Tournament, often achieving higher accuracy on Hopper, while importance weighting can further improve performance under controlled overlap.
items.author: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus

items.title: Controlled Block Proximal Linearized Method for Nonconvex and Nonsmooth Optimization
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.34390v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In this paper, we consider multiblock nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization without assuming bounded iterates or coercivity of the original objective. We propose the Controlled Block Proximal Linearized (CBPL) method, whose control potentials establish boundedness while retaining the original objective, constraints and variables. We prove finite length and whole-sequence convergence to an effective critical point of the original objective, where one limiting subgradient annihilates all effective feasible directions. We establish finite total variation of the original objective and block functions, summable original effective residuals, and finite termination and linear or sublinear convergence rates for the original objective values. Scale orthogonality further gives full original criticality and, for homogeneous balancing controls, summable absolute objective errors with an $o(1/K)$ best-iterate bound. We establish a complete degeneracy theory for graph-regularized nonnegative factorizations: scale criticality is equivalent to graph collapse, and full criticality eliminates graph action; our controls prevent this collapse while retaining genuine reconstruction changes. Furthermore, our proposed method provides the practical, simple, and effective schemes for these applications, combining guaranteed convergence with explicit closed-form updates that can be applied directly to solve the original problems. We apply CBPL to graph-regularized sparse nonnegative matrix factorization with $\ell_0$-constraints ($\ell_0$-GSNMF), graph-regularized sparse nonnegative canonical polyadic (CP) decomposition with $\ell_0$-constraints ($\ell_0$-GSNCP), and graph-regularized sparse nonnegative independent-core matrix tri-factorization with $\ell_0$-constraints ($\ell_0$-GSNMTF). Numerical experiments demonstrate effectiveness, convergence and structural control.
items.author: Weifeng Yang

items.title: Beyond Spatio-Temporal Priors: A Generalizable Approach for Dense Correspondence Matching
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.12421v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Dense correspondence matching has historically been bounded by simplifying spatio-temporal priors, such as smooth motion and rigid geometry. While effective for classical tasks, these assumptions break down in image editing and reference-guided generation (IEG), where transformations can preserve visual identity while breaking physical continuity. To establish identity-preserving correspondence across such transformations, we introduce FreeMatching, a generalizable framework combining generative and semantic foundation representations with heterogeneous supervision from classical datasets, tracked videos, and synthetic scenes. Teacher-guided iterative refinement further improves correspondence in IEG without dense correspondence annotations. Experimentally, a single FreeMatching model substantially improves correspondence quality on challenging IEG image pairs while retaining competitive performance on classical benchmarks. Furthermore, we demonstrate its utility as a quantitative metric for evaluating identity preservation, with scores that correlate with human judgment. The code is available at https://github.com/luping-liu/FreeMatching.
items.author: Luping Liu, Bingyi Kang, Yifan Wang, Dong Xu

items.title: Bias-Aware Adjoint Calibration and Optimal Control of Stochastic Multiscale Bioprocess Digital Twins
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.09505v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We develop a bias-aware digital-twin calibration and control framework for multiscale bioprocess models within a biological systems-of-systems (Bio-SoS) paradigm. The digital twin is represented by a stochastic differential equation (SDE) model and calibrated from sparse observations using quasi-likelihood estimation and adjoint sensitivity analysis. SDE generator-based moment expansions characterize truncation-induced parameter bias, while forward-backward adjoints quantify how calibration uncertainty propagates to value functions and policy performance. The resulting parameter-error distribution supports both policy-directed data acquisition and uncertainty-aware policy optimization through a second-order Gaussian-averaged objective. We characterize the asymptotic behavior of the resulting exploration criterion and derive a physical-system performance under the optimized policy. To implement these ideas, we develop an Actor-Simulator algorithm that jointly updates model parameters, selects informative experiments, and optimizes control policies. Numerical studies demonstrate improved calibration accuracy, sample efficiency, and control performance relative to state-of-the-art baselines.
items.author: Keilung Choy, Wei Xie

items.title: BiGym 2.0: Benchmarking Learned and Agent-Developed Policies for Humanoid Household Manipulation
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.07594v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Humanoid household manipulation requires the arms to act while the body balances, steps and changes posture. We present BiGym 2.0, an adaptation of BiGym for the Unitree G1 across 20 household tasks using a unified whole-body controller for demonstration and evaluation. The suite provides 60 native human virtual-reality demonstrations per task with synchronised multi-camera views and full-body execution records. We benchmark vision-language-action fine-tuning, imitation learning, demo-driven reinforcement learning, and cold-start coding agents given the interaction budget of online reinforcement learning. With the same onboard views, proprioception and whole-body controller for every method, vision-language-action fine-tuning has the highest nine-task mean, and agent-developed programs outperform every demo-driven reinforcement learning baseline on this mean and lead on bimanual reaching. Cross-workspace stacking remains open, $\pi_{0.5}$ stays low on pick-box, and multi-object transport is hard for imitation learning, demo-driven reinforcement learning and coding agents. All environments, human demonstrations, and evaluation traces are open-sourced at https://github.com/swirl-uk/BiGym2.
items.author: Zexi Zhang, Zecheng Zhu, Zidong Chen, Zulkhuu Tuya, Stephen James

items.title: Quantum Machine Learning Protection of Military Quantum Key Distribution Against Cryptographically Camouflaged Attacks
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.04543v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Quantum key distribution proves its protocol secure and says nothing about the hardware beneath it, so military and government operators fielding it for command-and-control keys monitor the channel for implementation attacks, and that monitoring has a blind spot. An adversary with a kleptographic foothold in the generator of a public per-block value \(x=g^v \pmod p\) can hide attacked blocks in honest noise, gating them on a predicate of its discrete logarithm, making detection a discrete logarithm problem that defeats every efficient classical monitor yet yields to a quantum kernel recovering \(v\) through Shor's algorithm. I formalise these cryptographically camouflaged attacks, reduce their hardness to an established learning separation, prove a single-frequency fidelity kernel cannot represent an interval predicate, and test them on Ghillie, a decoy-state BB84 simulator with a positive key rate to 142 km. From 10- to 14-bit groups over two seeds, a classical monitor reads 0.458 to 0.516 on camouflaged attacks while the quantum kernel reads 1.000, and both catch overt attacks above 0.99. Finite-precision recovery under depolarising noise and a hardened predicate lower the quantum result to 0.916 through 0.983 with the classical monitor at chance, and a feasibility probe on IBM Heron processors tracks the exact kernel within 0.034. A defender can therefore discard precisely the compromised key material, although the advantage is asymptotic, awaits fault tolerance, and holds only when the feature map matches the adversary's predicate, since a low-frequency map reads 0.545 on a residue pattern and 0.982 once aligned.
items.author: Muhammad Shaheer Bin Junaid

items.title: LieDiscover: Adaptive Symbolic Library Construction for Explicit Open-form Symmetry Discovery
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.33663v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Discovering symmetries from observational data provides interpretable insights into dynamical systems and priors for scientific machine learning. However, existing symmetry discovery methods face two limitations. Many methods represent symmetries implicitly, making it difficult to obtain explicit infinitesimal generators that can serve as physical priors for learning dynamical systems. Meanwhile, methods that explicitly identify generators often rely on predefined function libraries, limiting their ability to capture complex symmetries involving high-order polynomials or transcendental functions. To address these limitations, we propose LieDiscover, a framework that explicitly identifies infinitesimal generators through an iterative symbolic search process that dynamically expands the symbolic function library to capture complex functional forms. Specifically, at each search step, we design an encoder-decoder architecture to generate a candidate symbolic expression. An adaptive singular value decomposition (SVD)-based evaluation is introduced to assess how each candidate contributes to the recoverable symmetry subspace. The resulting evaluations are incorporated into step-wise rewards to guide reinforcement learning toward discovering richer symmetry structures with concise symbolic representations. Experiments on eight partial differential equation (PDE) benchmarks demonstrate that LieDiscover recovers explicit generators involving higher-order polynomial, exponential, and trigonometric terms, while achieving more accurate symmetry subspace recovery and improved robustness to noise. Furthermore, the recovered generators enable effective symmetry-based data augmentation, improving the accuracy of downstream neural PDE solvers.
items.author: Xinxin Li, Jianming Ma, Xingyu Cui, Da Li, Juan Zhang, Junping Yin

items.title: JAREX: An Acquisition Function for Multi-Objective Algorithmic Process Characterization
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.24954v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Pharmaceutical process characterization is central to Quality by Design because it defines how variations in process parameters affect the ability to meet product quality specifications, thereby supporting proven acceptable ranges and robust manufacturing. In practice, however, characterization still relies largely on factorial design of experiments (DOE) approaches, which are inefficient for resolving multivariate pass/fail boundaries in higher-dimensional spaces. While Bayesian optimization has transformed process optimization, adaptive methods for multi-objective process characterization remain lacking. Here, we introduce JAREX (Joint Acceptable Region EXploration), a Bayesian active-learning acquisition function for multi-objective process characterization. JAREX formulates characterization as a joint boundary-learning problem and adaptively selects experiments to recover the joint pass region defined by simultaneous satisfaction of threshold criteria across multiple objectives. JAREX combines an optimistic joint-feasibility mask with a multi-objective extension of randomized straddle, focusing sampling on the joint edge of failure. Our benchmark study suggests that JAREX provides more accurate and sample-efficient recovery of the joint pass region than factorial DOE, space-filling designs, and greedy objective-wise strategies over the full experimental budget range. For batched experimentation, it reduces the number of iterative process characterization experiments by more than half while preserving high accuracy for the boundary-identification task. Implemented in the open-source obsidian package, JAREX provides a modular framework for adaptive, data-efficient multi-objective algorithmic process characterization, supporting sample-efficient range finding in high-dimensional spaces.
items.author: Xinyang Li, Kevin Stone, Ajit Vikram

items.title: When Does Low-Bit Quantization Preserve the Decisions of Vector Search?
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.09854v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: An orthogonal rotation improves the distance rank correlation of two-bit Cohere codes from 0.75 to 0.91, yet increases nearest-neighbour comparison flips by 51%. We analyse quantization through the comparisons made by graph search. A comparison changes only when its quantization error exceeds its exact margin, giving a flip bound that separates close calls from large errors. Shared endpoints induce correlated distance errors that partly cancel within a comparison. An exact replay identity connects candidate-level actions to the output of neighbour selection. A Gaussian model gives coordinate-code errors in closed form, and a rare-spike construction exposes heavy tails in the population-radius error. Held-out blocks give model-free certificates for acceptance rules based on exact or quantized margins. Across 24 dataset-code configurations, calibration-estimated risk correlates with held-out ranking and pruning flips at 0.97 and 0.99, compared with 0.91 and 0.99 for a margin-to-noise summary and 0.74 and 0.05 for distance rank correlation. Paired builds of 200,000-vector graphs connect rotation, query scoring, and topology to end-to-end recall and search work.
items.author: Wenxuan Xiao, Xu Cao

items.title: The microscope is the mask: privileged views and labels from a cryo-ET forward model
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.04325v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We explore the use of simulated data for training a model for protein annotation in crowded cryo-electron tomography volumes reconstructed from images collected at limited tilt angles and severely corrupted by the measurement operator. Firstly, we leverage the corruptions imposed by the forward model to generate domain-specific augmented paired views of the exact same scene for an invariance objective integrated into the LeJEPA self-supervised training framework. Secondly, we use additional information from the simulation pipeline such as the positions and identity of proteins in the simulated volumes to inform the architecture of the model and the loss function, so that semantic information is localised at protein positions in the resulting dense feature volume. The resulting model, CARNIVAL, is evaluated without finetuning on classification and detection tasks in real tomograms, using a benchmark dataset containing multiple protein types and two tomogram processing types. We show that CARNIVAL outperforms a state-of-the-art model trained using a contrastive objective on simulated data but without forward model-based paired views or privileged information.
items.author: Bogdan Toader, Kiarash Jamali, Tanmay A. M. Bharat, Sjors H. W. Scheres

items.title: MoTE: Mixture of Task Experts for Multi-Task Video Understanding
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.24763v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Procedural video-language models must solve heterogeneous tasks from the same visual evidence, including action recognition, forecasting, and procedure prediction. Dense transformer decoders share the same feed-forward networks across tasks, which can entangle task behavior and make controlled capability expansion difficult. Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) decoders provide conditional computation, but token-level learned routing is not naturally aligned with task-level procedural objectives. We propose MoTE (Mixture of Task Experts), a decoder architecture that converts large language model feed-forward networks into task-specific experts while keeping the multimodal backbone shared. Each example follows one sample-level task route, so active task-expert computation remains independent of the number of stored task experts. We instantiate this design as VideoLLM-MoTE and evaluate it on five COIN benchmarks using explicit task routes. The five-expert model activates ~2B LLM parameters per sample and achieves higher average top-1 accuracy than recent VideoLLM baselines. Under the same expert topology, it improves over dense all-expert activation and learned sparse-routing controls. These results show that task-structured routing provides an interpretable and compute-efficient decoder alternative for multi-task video-language learning.
items.author: Muhammad Asad Ali, Umar Khan, Nadia Robertini, Didier Stricker

items.title: Addressable Memory for Video World Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.07408v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study visual persistence in interactive video world models. These models rely on a Key-Value (KV) cache as a growing visual memory to carry forward previously generated frames. However, we find that models can no longer reliably address stored content once rollouts extend beyond the training horizon, because temporal Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) offsets can exceed the training range and the model struggles to retrieve the relevant visual information through attention. Moreover, naively compressing the cache in the RoPE-rotated space degrades memory by averaging keys with incompatible positional phases. To address this, we propose WorldTrace, a training-free memory framework for long-horizon visual persistence. WorldTrace keeps compressed memory addressable by assigning each summary slot a distinct, in-distribution virtual position. Within this cache, WorldTrace uses the model's own attention to decide which observations to retain verbatim and which redundant ones to merge into compressed summaries, all within one bounded addressable memory bank. We evaluate this ability with LoopBench, a benchmark that tests whether a compressed cache can reconstruct a previously visited scene after a long detour. On LoopBench, WorldTrace improves average DINOv2 recall similarity by 32.6% over a sliding window at the same cache budget, extending visually persistent generation without retraining.
items.author: Xindi Wu, Sven Elflein, James Lucas, Olga Russakovsky, Laura Leal-Taix\'e, Despoina Paschalidou, Jonathan Lorraine, Aljo\v{s}a O\v{s}ep

items.title: Beyond Co-Movement: Locality by Exposures Enables a Joint Factor-Graph Framework for Portfolio Diversification
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.06618v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Current portfolio construction methods are either agnostic to the effects of idiosyncratic shocks (standard factor models) or to the latent data structure driving systematic returns (recent graph-based approaches). This presents an opportunity to combine the complementary market aspects captured by the factor and graph domains, allowing asset allocations to operate directly on the underlying market structure, rather than on its observed co-movement or its finite-sample artefacts. In this work, we introduce the Mutually-INformed Graph-Locality and Exposures framework (MINGLE), which mutually regularises the factor and graph domains by redefining graph locality through systematic factor exposure profiles, rather than via observed co-movements. This is formalised through a unified Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) framework that jointly learns a latent factor representation and its induced graph topology directly from market returns. The resulting exposure-similarity graph aligns more closely with established economic sectors than conventional correlation-based graphs. Portfolios constructed from this representation are shown to consistently outperform their correlation-based counterparts across a range of volatility regimes and transaction cost levels. For rigour, paired statistical testing confirms that these gains stem from the reconciliation of the graph and factor domains.
items.author: Sara Chehab, Giorgos Iacovides, Parisa Yazdanparast, Danilo Mandic

items.title: TIDE: A Physically Diverse 3D Turbulence Benchmark Dataset for Advancing Scientific Machine Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.04222v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Turbulence is a central testbed for machine learning on physical dynamics because its governing laws are known exactly. However, most existing studies remain in 2D, while 3D turbulence has fundamentally different physics and is far more costly to simulate. Existing 3D resources also typically provide only one realization per configuration, making it difficult to distinguish learning the dynamics from fitting the statistics of a single flow. In this paper, we introduce TIDE (Turbulent Incompressible DNS Ensembles), a 256^3 DNS corpus and benchmark for 3D incompressible turbulence, with 15 configurations on eight controlled axes, independent ensembles, pressure fields, and equation-level verification. The benchmark includes five tasks, standardized learned baselines, controlled generalization splits, and physical-fidelity metrics alongside pointwise error. Across the main forecasting configurations, current learned models trained under a fixed reference recipe barely outperform persistence and still make about twice the error of a spectral solver given the true equations. Moreover, lower pointwise error can coincide with severely distorted small-scale dynamics, showing that accuracy alone does not ensure physical fidelity. Rollout stability depends on the configuration, the training seed, and how densely training samples each trajectory. Joint training across neighboring regimes does not close the transfer gaps we test, and the forced-to-decay contrast bounds a conditioning limit: an estimate of the current forcing state removes 20-41% of the error a spectral solver makes without forcing input, while history or forcing inputs help only some learned architectures. Closing these accuracy, fidelity, and conditioning gaps is the central open problem made measurable by TIDE. https://github.com/Dyloong1/TIDE-dataset-benchmark
items.author: Yilong Dai, Yiming Sun, Yiheng Chen, Shengyu Chen, Peyman Givi, Xiaowei Jia, Runlong Yu

items.title: Learning-enabled Acceleration of Scenario-based Model Predictive Control
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.12775v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Scenario-based model predictive control (SBMPC) is a variant of model predictive control (MPC) that explicitly accounts for uncertainty by optimizing control actions over multiple predicted scenarios. However, its computational complexity increases rapidly with the number of scenarios and prediction horizon, limiting its applicability to real-time planning and control. This paper presents a learning-accelerated Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) algorithm for efficiently solving SBMPC problems by leveraging parallel computing and Moreau envelope learning, while maintaining high solution accuracy. We reformulate the SBMPC problems into consensus forms that can be decomposed via ADMM, separating the scenario-dependent dynamics from non-anticipativity constraints and enabling parallel updates across scenarios and time steps. Building on this decomposition, we utilize a learning-to-optimize scheme that leverages Moreau envelope learning of the cost function to accelerate the primal update in ADMM, thereby reducing computation time. The proposed framework is evaluated on a microgrid energy management problem subject to load and renewable generation uncertainties. Comparisons with IPOPT and MadNLP, two popular and modern nonlinear programming solvers, demonstrate substantial computational speedups while maintaining reliable closed-loop control performance.
items.author: Trinh Tran, Binh Nguyen, Truong X. Nghiem

items.title: Physically-Relevant Information Learning in High-Dimensional Time-Derivatives Spaces
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.05127v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Understanding the physics of many-body complex dynamical systems may be a non-trivial task. High-dimensional analysis approaches are often deemed necessary to prevent losing important information. Typically, these use order parameters or descriptors capturing information related to, e.g., relative positions, symmetries, etc., of the units in the studied system. However, in many cases, gaining information related to the relative positions of the constitutive units (or their velocities) alone may be insufficient, and to reach a more complete physical knowledge, one should ideally learn and correlate with each other both structure and dynamics. Here we demonstrate how to achieve such a goal efficiently by building and navigating high-dimensional Time-Derivatives (TiDe) spaces. A TiDe space can be generated for virtually any type of system/phenomenon from the time-series data collected along its observation over time. Each TiDe's dimension corresponds to a growing-order time-derivative of the extracted data, thus containing information related to different physical phenomena/events, which can be easily extracted via unsupervised approaches. We demonstrate how, by definition, TiDes can be directly analyzed without a need for prior dimensionality reduction, providing results that are intrinsically intuitive to interpret. We show the potential of the method by analyzing two prototypical example datasets extracted from molecular dynamics simulations or experimental tracking of different types of complex dynamical systems. Our results demonstrate how efficiently one can navigate and learn in information-rich TiDe spaces, which provide a robust general framework for data analysis and for studying complex dynamical systems from the data collected along their observation over time.
items.author: Domiziano Doria, Matteo Becchi, Giovanni M. Pavan

items.title: Graph-Based Nearest-Neighbor Search with Recall Guarantees Using Graph Spanners
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.02338v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Graph-based indexes such as Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs make nearest-neighbor retrieval efficient, but a high average recall can hide queries whose results fall below an application's quality requirement. We introduce Certify-then-Rectify (CTR), which returns an initial graph-search result when a calibrated rule accepts it and searches for missing neighbors otherwise. The recovery search reuses the existing graph and the distances already evaluated by the initial search. To determine how far this search should proceed, we relate metric distances to graph-path lengths through graph stretch. We develop Stretch-Bounded Expansion from Query (SBE-Q), together with Metric Bound Verification (MBV) to prune unnecessary work, and estimate its budget from paths to the fraction of true neighbors needed for the requested recall. Finite-sample tolerance bounds support this recall-aligned estimate; paths recorded during proposal recovery offer a conservative alternative to separate shortest-path computations. Independent tests certify initial acceptance and recovery outcomes, giving an end-to-end population recall guarantee even when the estimated stretch does not cover every relevant path. If recovery cannot be certified, rejected queries use exact scan. Experiments on HNSW compare five stretch estimators, assess recovery efficiency, and evaluate compliance and throughput on databases of up to 100 million vectors. CTR is not specific to HNSW, and we also evaluate it on another graph index.
items.author: Minghao Li, Raghav Mittal, Sanjivni Rana, Suraj Shetiya, Gautam Das, Nick Koudas

items.title: Fast approximation and learning of binary classification tasks in o-minimal structures using ReLU neural networks
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.01266v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study binary classification tasks whose decision sets are given by definable sets in o-minimal expansions of the real field. Motivated by the cell decomposition theory of definable sets, we introduce traceable sets that isolate the analytical properties of definable sets used for fast approximation by ReLU neural networks. Under uniform bounds on the number of cells and a suitable extension assumption for the boundary functions, we prove that classifiers can be approximated in $L^p$ up to accuracy $\varepsilon>0$ by ReLU neural networks of size $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-p(n-1)/m})$, with depth independent of $\varepsilon$ and polynomially bounded weights. This establishes quantitative approximation rates for suitable definable collections in o-minimal structures using ReLU neural networks. Furthermore, the stated approximation rates are also derived for definable maps under similar geometric assumptions on their smoothness domains. We then obtain statistical learning rates for empirical risk minimization with hinge loss over the approximating ReLU neural network classes. For $N$ uniformly distributed samples, the predicted classifiers achieve expected misclassification error of order $N^{-m/(m+n-1)}$ up to an arbitrarily small polynomial loss.
items.author: Clemens Kinn, Philipp Petersen

items.title: The Decomposition Is the Fingerprint: Per-Component Identity for Agent Skills
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.31272v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: AI agents increasingly acquire and execute skills at runtime: bundles of prompt instructions, executable code, and tool declarations fetched from marketplaces and other agents. Governing them needs a stable notion of skill identity, yet cryptographic hashing is engineered to destroy the very similarity we need, as a one-character edit scrambles the digest. We present a compact, locality-sensitive fingerprint that embeds each component of a skill and projects it to bits with a multi-bank SimHash, giving a fixed 120-byte signature compared in constant time by Hamming distance. Our central claim is that keeping the fingerprint as a per-component triple (prompt, code, tools), rather than a single score, is what makes it useful: the triple recovers skill-family identity through paraphrase, renaming, refactoring, and controlled code translation when another component remains shared, while independent multilingual reimplementation is not recovered; it also localizes which component carries the reuse. We claim lineage, not behavioral equivalence: identity supplies the structural axis of a registry and leaves safety to behavioral verification. The fingerprint reaches an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.974 (95% CI [0.956, 0.994]) over 4,950 pairwise comparisons while using 77x fewer bits than the embedding it approximates, with ranking preserved in expectation and finite-bit concentration; the per-component split turns one number into relationship classification, families, novelty, and a portable "SkillBOM" for a skill registry. On a 906-skill injection benchmark the fingerprint recognizes injected skills as tampered copies of a known base and localizes the change, but recognition is not trust: it remains, by design, an identity signal complementary to behavioral verification rather than a safety verdict.
items.author: Hongliang Liu, Yuhao Wu, Tung-Ling Li

items.title: Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.31248v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Kilometer-scale convection shapes precipitation extremes, tropical organization, and cloud feedbacks, but most global atmospheric models approximate these processes at 25-100 km resolution. Global storm-resolving physics models resolve convective systems explicitly, but at a cost (roughly one MWh per simulated day on exascale supercomputers) that limits long-duration simulation. We introduce STRATA (Storm-resolving Tile-based autoRegressive Atmosphere Transformer Architecture), the first autoregressive AI emulator for global storm-resolving atmospheric dynamics. STRATA is trained on the highest-resolution atmospheric dataset yet used for global AI emulation: 17 days of SCREAM physics-model output at 4.9-km resolution (~25 million grid cells) sampled every 10 minutes. Our central premise is that on 10-minute timescales atmospheric dynamics are predominantly local, so training on small spatial tiles trades scarce global temporal samples for abundant local spatial samples and enables global rollout via overlapping-tile blending. STRATA combines 3D patch embedding and local 3D neighborhood attention, a novel Stereographic Rotary Position Embedding (StereoRoPE) for grid-invariant encoding, and a pixel-space de-aliasing decoder that suppresses patch-scale rollout artifacts. An iso-FLOP scaling study reveals that km-scale emulation requires ~10x more FLOPs per grid point than coarse-resolution AI weather models, consistent with the higher information density of convective-scale dynamics. Trained on only 17 days of data, STRATA produces stable 24-hour global rollouts with realistic km-scale dynamics across diverse regimes, though large-scale biases develop with lead time. It achieves 48 simulated days per megawatt-hour (more than 50 times better energy efficiency than the SCREAM physics model) and 741 simulated days per wall-clock day at 512 H100 GPUs.
items.author: Zeyuan Hu, Akshay Subramaniam, Noel Keen, Tao Ge, Jaideep Pathak, Mohammad Shoaib Abbas, Suman Ravuri, Karthik Kashinath, Naser Mahfouz, Peter Caldwell, Mike Pritchard, Noah Brenowitz

items.title: Streaming Interventions: Can Video Large Language Models Correct Mistakes as They Occur?
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.09547v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Learning everyday skills, like cooking a dish, relies increasingly on instructional media such as online videos. This opens the door to the use of video (and multimodal) large language models (LLMs) as task guidance assistants. A crucial capability for the real-world success of a prospective task guidance assistant is it's ability to intervene proactively as soon as a mistake is apparent in order to guide the user. To evaluate this crucial capability, we introduce Ego-MC-Bench (Mistake Corrections), a benchmark for evaluating reactive, step-by-step task guidance in realistic cooking scenarios. Extensive experiments show that Ego-MC-Bench is highly challenging for state-of-the-art video LLMs. We argue that a key reason is the limited availability of training data for fine-tuning models on this task. Although there exists a wide range of cooking video datasets, existing datasets lack examples of mistakes along with appropriately timed interventions. To help address this data limitation, we also introduce Ego-CoMist, a counterfactual synthetic dataset created by transforming non -interactive cooking videos into supervised training examples showing proactive interventions. We show that fine-tuning on Ego-CoMist yields performance gains especially for smaller and more efficient video LLMs that are well suited for delivering assistance on edge devices.
items.author: Apratim Bhattacharyya, Shweta Mahajan, Sanjay Haresh, Rajeev Yasarla, Reza Pourreza, Litian Liu, Risheek Garrepalli, Roland Memisevic

items.title: Environment-Robust Representation Learning with Empirical Bayes
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.05365v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We consider multi-environment prediction problems. We assume the environments change the distribution of a latent variable, while the mechanisms generating observed covariates and targets remain stable conditional on that variable. For example, hospitals or clinical cohorts may differ in the prevalence of latent patient states, even though the relationships between those states, physiological measurements, and outcomes remain unchanged. Given a dataset from multiple environments, we formulate a Bayesian model for such problems and derive the corresponding variational objective. We show that this objective decomposes into per-environment terms and an additional cross-environment balancing term induced by the model's structure. We use an empirical Bayes method to set the prior and incorporate it into the objective. Based on this objective, we develop an amortized variational algorithm for posterior approximation, and use the resulting learned latent variables to form predictions in new environments.We study our approach through simulations and real-world studies of astronomical source identification, microbiome-based disease detection, and ICU sepsis prediction. Across these settings, our method outperforms previous approaches for prediction in new environments.
items.author: Yuli Slavutsky, Matthew Shen, Bohan Wu, David M. Blei

items.title: Visual Instruction Tuning Aligns Modalities through Abstraction
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.03871v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Visual instruction tuning effectively adapts a pre-trained Large Language Model (LLM) to process image information alongside text. Yet it remains unclear how visual features are embedded within the layer-wise hierarchy of abstractions in the LLM backbone. Across a diverse set of vision-language architectures, we show that instruction tuning primarily serves as a bridge, embedding visual features directly into the intermediate semantic layers of the LLM, bypassing the early layers devoted to unimodal processing. With probing analyses and causal interventions, we show that these intermediate layers constitute the semantic core of vision-language processing and play a critical role in performance across a broad set of multimodal benchmarks. In addition, by comparing the geometry of semantically equivalent visual and textual representations, we find that fine-tuning extends and strengthens the existing abstraction phase, aligning visual features with pre-existing textual ones. Finally, we confirm the functional role of this localized alignment by restricting fine-tuning to intermediate layers alone: this strategy preserves the performance of full fine-tuning on vision-centric benchmarks while reducing training time. Our results suggest that multimodal integration is a localized phenomenon driven by the repurposing of the internal abstraction engine of the LLM.
items.author: Luis Palacios, Lorenzo Basile, Diego Doimo, Alberto Cazzaniga

items.title: Learning Sparse Compositional Functions with Norm-Constrained Neural Networks
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.25608v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The ability of deep neural networks to learn hierarchical features is widely regarded as a key mechanism underlying their success in high-dimensional learning. Existing theory partially supports this view by establishing approximation rates based on parameter counts and sample complexity guarantees for compositional models without incurring the curse of dimensionality (CoD). To study overparameterized regimes, where the number of parameters exceeds the sample size, we develop a framework that measures complexity via the parameter norm. Within this approach, we establish approximation rates and excess risk bounds for learning sparse compositional functions whose compositional structure is represented by directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), using Frobenius norm-constrained deep neural networks. Our results have broad applicability since every function that is efficiently Turing computable admits sparse compositional representations. In particular, we cover a range of representative models, including multi-index models, binary tree structures, and general compositional architectures. The rates we derive show that deep networks can exploit the compositional structure of the target functions, effectively avoiding the CoD through hierarchical representations.
items.author: Shuo Huang, Lorenzo Fiorito, Lorenzo Rosasco, Tomaso Poggio

items.title: Corrected Integrated Laplace Approximation for Bayesian Inference in Latent Gaussian Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.20345v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Latent Gaussian models (LGMs) are a popular class of Bayesian hierarchical models that include Gaussian processes, as well as certain spatial models and mixed-effect models. Efficient Bayesian inference of LGMs often requires marginalizing out the latent variables. For LGMs with a non-Gaussian likelihood, exact marginalization is not possible and a popular approach is to do approximate marginalization with an integrated Laplace approximation (ILA). Using ILA produces an approximate posterior which, in some settings, can differ significantly from the correct posterior, which impacts downstream applications. We propose an importance sampling scheme to correct the error introduced by ILA. By increasing the number of samples in importance sampling, the posterior with ILA converges to the correct posterior. This idea is realized with various techniques, including pseudo-marginalization, quasi-Monte Carlo and randomized quasi-Monte Carlo. We implement our methods in an automatic differentiation framework to support gradient-based algorithms when doing inference on the hyperparameters. For the latter, we specifically consider the use of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. We demonstrate the benefits of reduced error in various applied models.
items.author: Jinlin Lai, Charles C. Margossian, Daniel Sheldon

items.title: PrivacySIM: Evaluating LLM Simulation of User Privacy Behavior
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.12147v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but their ability to simulate individual privacy decisions is not well understood. In this paper, we evaluate whether a core set of user persona attributes can drive LLMs to simulate individual-level privacy behavior across various contexts. We introduce PrivacySIM, an evaluation suite that benchmarks LLM simulation of user privacy behavior against the ground-truth responses of 1,000 real users. These users are drawn from five published user studies on privacy behavior spanning LLM healthcare consultations, conversational agents, and chatbots. Drawing on these user studies and prior work in privacy behavior, we hypothesize three persona facets as plausible predictors of privacy decision-making: demographics, previous experiences, and stated privacy attitudes. We condition nine frontier LLMs on subsets of these three facets and measure how often each model's response to a data-sharing scenario matches the user's actual response. Our findings show that (1) zero-shot conditioning on these facets consistently improves simulation quality, but the performance of the best model (40.4% accuracy) suggests that richer and more nuanced persona facets are needed to reliably align with users' mental models for privacy decisions. (2) A user's stated privacy attitudes alone are often not the best predictor because they can diverge from the user's actual privacy behavior. (3) Users with high AI/chatbot experience are the most challenging to simulate. PrivacySIM is a first step toward understanding and improving the capabilities of LLMs to simulate user privacy decisions. We release PrivacySIM to enable further evaluation of LLM privacy simulation.
items.author: James Flemings, Murali Annavaram

items.title: Exact Fixed-Point Constraints in Neural-ODEs: Injecting Prior Knowledge into the Network Parameters
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.10613v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Neural ordinary differential equations (Neural-ODEs) learn a velocity field from data. Often, however, additional information on the target field is available, such as the location of some of its equilibria or, more generally, its values at given points. We introduce a method to inject this information directly into the parameters of a Neural-ODE, so that a finite set of prescribed fixed points holds exactly throughout training, with no penalty terms and no post-hoc projection. The output matrix is parametrized through the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, implemented by a thin QR factorization of the hidden features at the prescribed points. This splits the output matrix into a component determined by the constraints and a free one, which shapes the field away from the prescribed points without altering its values there. As a result, the constrained Neural-ODE remains a universal approximator of the continuous vector fields compatible with the constraints. We test the method on a two-dimensional Lotka-Volterra competition model with four equilibria. In vector field regression, the constrained model keeps the fixed-point residual at single-precision round-off, and its test error is up to about five times lower than that of an unconstrained network of the same architecture. A soft penalty on the equilibria lowers the residual only at the cost of accuracy, and still leaves it at least an order of magnitude above that of the constrained model. Trained to convergence on datasets of increasing size, the unconstrained and penalized networks saturate already on small datasets, while the constrained model keeps improving over a wider range. Close to the equilibria and over long time horizons, the constrained model is the most accurate at every dataset size considered. This also holds when the models are trained on observed trajectories, by backpropagation through the ODE solver.
items.author: Feliciano Giuseppe Pacifico, Duccio Fanelli, Lorenzo Buffoni, Lorenzo Chicchi, Diego Febbe, Raffaele Marino

items.title: Penalty-Based First-Order Methods for Bilevel Optimization with Minimax and Constrained Lower-Level Problems
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.08006v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study a class of bilevel optimization problems in which both the upper- and lower-level problems have minimax structures. This setting captures a broad range of emerging applications. Despite the extensive literature on bilevel optimization and minimax optimization separately, existing methods mainly focus on bilevel optimization with lower-level minimization problems, often under strong convexity assumptions, and are not directly applicable to the minimax lower-level setting considered here. To address this gap, we develop penalty-based first-order methods for bilevel minimax optimization without requiring strong convexity of the lower-level problem. In the deterministic setting, we establish that the proposed method finds a lifted $\epsilon$-KKT point with $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$ oracle complexity. We further show that bilevel problems with convex constrained lower-level minimization can be reformulated as special cases of our framework via Lagrangian duality, leading to an $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$ complexity bound that improves upon the existing $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-7})$ result when the lower-level Slater's condition holds. Finally, we extend our approach to the stochastic setting, where only stochastic gradient oracles are available, and prove that the proposed stochastic method finds a nearly lifted $\epsilon$-KKT point with $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-9})$ oracle complexity.
items.author: Yiyang Shen, Yutian He, Weiran Wang, Qihang Lin

items.title: Debiased Counterfactual Generation via Flow Matching from Observations
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.07665v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Estimating the full counterfactual distribution under an intervention is central to treatment risk assessment and counterfactual generation tasks. Existing approaches model the counterfactual distribution as a standalone generative target, without exploiting its relationship to the observational data. In this work, we show that under standard assumptions, observational distributions and marginal counterfactual distributions over outcomes are tightly linked: they have identical support and tail behavior, remain statistically close under weak confounding, and share any outcome features which are invariant to confounders. These properties motivate learning counterfactual distributions not from scratch, but via a deconfounding flow from the observational distribution. We formulate this problem via flow-matching and derive a semiparametrically efficient estimator based on a novel efficient influence function correction. We subsequently extend our estimator to target minimal-energy flows in high-dimensions, which we show can be especially simple targets between observational and counterfactual distributions. In experiments, deconfounding flows outperform existing debiased counterfactual distribution estimators, while also mitigating known failure modes of flow-based methods.
items.author: Hugh Dance, Johnny Xi, Peter Orbanz, Benjamin Bloem-Reddy

items.title: The Interplay of Data Structure and Imbalance in the Learning Dynamics of Diffusion Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.06367v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Real-world datasets are inherently heterogeneous, yet how per-class structural differences and sampling imbalance shape the training dynamics of diffusion models---and potentially exacerbate disparities---remains poorly understood. While models typically transition from an initial phase of generalization to memorizing the training set, existing theory assumes homogeneous data, leaving open how class imbalance and heterogeneity reshape these dynamics. In this work, we develop a high-dimensional analytical framework to study class-dependent learning in score-based diffusion models. Analyzing a random-features model trained on Gaussian mixtures, we derive the feature-covariance spectrum to characterize per-class generalization and memorization times. We reveal the explicit hierarchy governing these dynamics: class variance is the primary determinant of learning order---consistently favoring higher-variance classes---while centroid geometry and sampling imbalance play secondary roles. Specifically, sampling imbalance acts as a modulator that can reverse this ordering and, under strong imbalance, forces minority classes to acquire distinct, delayed inference times during backward diffusion. Together, these results suggest that diffusion models can memorize some classes while others remain insufficiently learned. We validate our theoretical predictions empirically using U-Net models trained on Fashion MNIST.
items.author: Flavio Nicoletti, Chenxiao Ma, Enrico Ventura, Luca Saglietti, Stefano Sarao Mannelli

items.title: TRACED-X enables in vivo imaging of cellular microstructure, intrinsic extracellular diffusivity, tortuosity, and membrane permeability in human glioma patients
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.02615v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The lack of analytical models describing diffusion time dependence at intermediate time scales in complex tissue microstructure limits accurate quantification of extracellular diffusivity and tissue microstructure. Cell membrane water permeability modulates the signal in complex ways and is often disregarded in tumor microstructure models. We introduce TRACED-X, a Monte Carlo-based model that incorporates diffusion time dependence and membrane permeability in cell distributions to quantify pathologically-relevant properties in solid tumors. Monte Carlo simulations of water diffusion in semipermeable spheres were used to train neural network regressors for parameter estimation. A separate neural network was trained to predict the extracellular effective diffusivity, enabling the estimation of extracellular space tortuosity. Diffusion data from eight mixed-grade glioma patients were fitted with TRACED-X and analyzed in conjunction with clinical images. Simulation results demonstrate improved parameter estimation compared to comparator models. TRACED-X enabled the simultaneous in vivo quantification of intracellular volume fraction, cell size distribution, intrinsic extracellular diffusivity, tortuosity, and membrane permeability in glioma patients. Parameter maps show coherence with radiological findings and expected tumor phenotypes. TRACED-X permits the rapid estimate of unique biophysical properties in solid tumors, such as intrinsic extracellular diffusivity, tortuosity, and membrane permeability, in addition to cell microstructure. TRACED-X maps show promise in identifying heterogenous tumor subregions before and after treatment. Neural network implementations of diffusion time-dependence and tortuosity showed behavior consistent with coarse-graining and effective medium theory, respectively. Future work will explore the clinical utility of TRACED-X parameters in additional patients.
items.author: Joshua K. Marchant, Hong-Hsi Lee, Elizabeth R. Gerstner, Susie Y. Huang, Bruce R. Rosen

items.title: Equation-Free Digital Twins for Nonlinear Structural Dynamics
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.00950v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Monitoring floating offshore wind turbines (FOWTs) under stochastic excitation and sensor failure requires computationally efficient and physically interpretable estimators. This paper introduces an equation-free, output-only digital twin framework combining Hankel dynamic mode decomposition (Hankel-DMD), sparse-sensor reconstruction, and a stochastic Kalman extension. A sufficient identifiability condition is derived for modal amplitudes recovered from delay-embedded measurements, while Tikhonov regularization addresses ill-conditioned sensor layouts. Correlation-domain identification improves damping estimates under stochastic forcing and distinguishes structural modes from rotor harmonics.
  The framework is validated using OpenFAST simulations of an NREL 5-MW spar turbine and experimental basin-test measurements from a 1:70-scale IEA 15-MW semi-submersible. In simulations, the identified tower modes agree with established operational modal analysis methods (MAC at least 0.99), while the Kalman estimator achieves R-squared values of 0.91 to 0.99 under severe sensor sparsity. Experimental results identify tower modes at 0.430 and 0.415 Hz with MAC of 1.00 against SSI-COV and reconstruct tower-base bending moments on unseen runs with R-squared values of 0.83 to 0.89 using three of four sensors. The framework provides a computationally efficient, sensor-failure-resilient structural-state estimation layer for digital twins.
items.author: Mohammad Mahdi Abaei, Ahmad BahooToroody, Arttu Poloj\"arvi, Heikki Remes, Ulf Tyge Tygesen, Mikko Suominen, Michael Beer

items.title: MARS: Towards High Goodput and Low KV Thrashing in Agent Serving under GPU Memory Constraints
items.summary:
arXiv:2604.26963v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Self-hosted LLM agents offer greater control over sensitive data and model customization while avoiding per-request API fees. However, serving concurrent, multi-turn workflows within limited GPU memory makes it difficult to achieve high workflow-level goodput. In particular, as workflows accumulate context, their reusable key-value (KV) caches can easily outgrow GPU capacity, triggering repeated eviction and recovery, known as KV cache thrashing. This process consumes resources and delays workflow completion. Although existing approaches propose various methods, our motivation study shows that the evaluated baselines still incur substantial thrashing overhead or fail to address the workflow-level goodput issue.
  We present MARS, an agent serving system that coordinates workflow admission and in-engine scheduling to achieve high workflow-level goodput on memory-constrained devices while avoiding KV cache thrashing. Specifically, outside the engine, an admission controller selects root workflows using initial prefix footprint estimates and live KV availability, adapting admissions to memory pressure. Inside, an agent-centric scheduler prioritizes turn completion and coordinates prefill allocation with KV reclamation to reduce disruptive evictions. Across two models and three GPU configurations, MARS achieves 1.59x-7.56x mean end-to-end latency speedups over the fastest baseline. Integrated as the serving backend for OpenCode, Codex, and OpenHands, MARS further improves mean workflow completion time by 1.17x-1.87x.
  Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Afterglow231/MARS_preview .
items.author: Yifei Wang, Tsun-yu Yang, Hancheng Ye, Yechen Xu, Cong Guo, Chiyue Wei, Qinsi Wang, Dongting Li, Tingjun Chen, Hai "Helen" Li, Danyang Zhuo, Yiran Chen

items.title: There Will Be a Scientific Theory of Deep Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2604.21691v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In this paper, we make the case that a scientific theory of deep learning is emerging. By this we mean a theory which characterizes important properties and statistics of the training process, hidden representations, final weights, and performance of neural networks. We pull together major strands of ongoing research in deep learning theory and identify five growing bodies of work that point toward such a theory: (a) solvable idealized settings that provide intuition for learning dynamics in realistic systems; (b) tractable limits that reveal insights into fundamental learning phenomena; (c) simple mathematical laws that capture important macroscopic observables; (d) theories of hyperparameters that disentangle them from the rest of the training process, leaving simpler systems behind; and (e) universal behaviors shared across systems and settings which clarify which phenomena call for explanation.
  Taken together, these bodies of work share certain broad traits: they are concerned with the dynamics of the training process; they primarily seek to describe coarse aggregate statistics; and they emphasize falsifiable quantitative predictions. We argue that the emerging theory is best thought of as a mechanics of the learning process, and suggest the name learning mechanics. We discuss the relationship between this mechanics perspective and other approaches for building a theory of deep learning, including the statistical and information-theoretic perspectives. In particular, we anticipate a symbiotic relationship between learning mechanics and mechanistic interpretability.
  We also review and address common arguments that fundamental theory will not be possible or is not important. We conclude with a portrait of important open directions in learning mechanics and advice for beginners. We host further introductory materials, perspectives, and open questions at learningmechanics.pub.
items.author: Jamie Simon, Daniel Kunin, Alexander Atanasov, Enric Boix-Adser\`a, Blake Bordelon, Jeremy Cohen, Nikhil Ghosh, Florentin Guth, Arthur Jacot, Mason Kamb, Dhruva Karkada, Eric J. Michaud, Berkan Ottlik, Joseph Turnbull

items.title: Cloning is as Hard as Learning for Stabilizer States
items.summary:
arXiv:2604.15269v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The impossibility of simultaneously cloning non-orthogonal states lies at the foundations of quantum theory. Even when allowing for approximation errors, cloning an arbitrary unknown pure state requires as many initial copies as needed to fully learn the state. Rather than arbitrary unknown states, modern quantum learning theory often considers structured classes of states and exploits such structure to develop learning algorithms that outperform general-state tomography. This raises the question: How do the sample complexities of learning and cloning relate for such structured classes. We answer this question for an important class of states. Namely, for $n$-qubit stabilizer states, we show that the optimal sample complexity of cloning is $\Theta(n)$. Thus, also for this structured class of states, cloning is as hard as learning. To prove this result, we relate stabilizer state cloning to a variant of the sample amplification problem for probability distributions that was recently introduced in classical learning theory. This allows us to obtain our cloning lower bounds in analogy to new sample amplification lower bounds for classes of distributions with an underlying linear structure. Our results provide a more fine-grained perspective on No-Cloning theorems, opening up connections from foundations to quantum learning theory and quantum cryptography.
items.author: Nikhil Bansal, Matthias C. Caro, Gaurav Mahajan

items.title: Conformal Risk Control under Non-Monotone Losses: Theory and Finite-Sample Guarantees
items.summary:
arXiv:2604.01502v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Conformal risk control (CRC) provides distribution-free guarantees for controlling the expected loss at a user-specified level. Existing theory typically assumes that the loss decreases monotonically with a tuning parameter that governs the size of the prediction set. However, this assumption is often violated in practice, where losses may behave non-monotonically due to competing objectives such as coverage and efficiency.
  In this paper, we study CRC under non-monotone loss functions when the tuning parameter is selected from a finite grid, a setting commonly arising in thresholding and discretized decision rules. Revisiting a known counterexample, we show that the validity of CRC without monotonicity depends critically on the relationship between the calibration sample size and the grid resolution. In particular, reliable risk control can still be achieved when the calibration sample is sufficiently large relative to the grid size.
  We establish a finite-sample guarantee for bounded losses over a grid of size $m$, showing that the excess risk above the target level $\alpha$ scales on the order of $\sqrt{\log(m)/n}$, where $n$ is the calibration sample size. A matching lower bound demonstrates that this rate is sharp for the CRC selection rule under the same population-safe endpoint condition. We also derive refined guarantees under additional structural conditions, including Lipschitz continuity and monotonicity, and extend the analysis to settings with distribution shift via importance weighting.
  Numerical experiments on synthetic multilabel classification and real object detection data illustrate the practical implications of non-monotonicity. Methods that explicitly account for finite-sample uncertainty achieve more stable risk control than approaches based on monotonicity transformations, while maintaining competitive prediction set sizes.
items.author: Tareq Aldirawi, Yun Li, Wenge Guo

items.title: HRIR-Former: Grid-Free Time-Domain Reconstruction of Head-Related Impulse Responses with a Spatially Encoded Transformer
items.summary:
arXiv:2603.27998v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Individualized head-related impulse responses (HRIRs) enable binaural rendering, but dense per-listener measurements are costly. We address HRIR spatial up-sampling from sparse per-listener measurements: given a few measured HRIRs for a listener, predict HRIRs at unmeasured target directions. Prior learning methods often work in the frequency domain, rely on minimum-phase assumptions or separate timing models, and use a fixed direction grid, which can degrade temporal fidelity and spatial continuity. We propose HRIR-Former, a time-domain, grid-free binaural Transformer for reconstructing HRIRs at arbitrary directions from sparse inputs. It uses sinusoidal spatial features, a Conv1D refinement module, and auxiliary interaural time difference (ITD) and interaural level difference (ILD) heads. On SONICOM, it improves normalized mean squared error (NMSE), cosine distance, and ITD/ILD errors over prior methods; ablations validate modules and show minimum-phase preprocessing is unnecessary.
items.author: Shaoheng Xu, Chunyi Sun, Jihui Zhang, Amy Bastine, Prasanga N. Samarasinghe, Thushara D. Abhayapala, Hongdong Li

items.title: Pseudo-Labeling for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation with Kernel GLMs
items.summary:
arXiv:2603.19422v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We propose a principled framework for unsupervised domain adaptation under covariate shift in kernel Generalized Linear Models (GLMs), encompassing kernelized linear, logistic, and Poisson regression with ridge regularization. Our goal is to minimize prediction error in the target domain by leveraging labeled source data and unlabeled target data, despite differences in covariate distributions. We partition the labeled source data into two batches: one for training a family of candidate models, and the other for building an imputation model. This imputation model generates pseudo-labels for the target data, enabling robust model selection. We establish non-asymptotic excess-risk bounds that characterize adaptation performance through an "effective labeled sample size", explicitly accounting for the unknown covariate shift. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate consistent performance gains over source-only baselines.
items.author: Nathan Weill, Kaizheng Wang

items.title: Functional Stochastic Localization
items.summary:
arXiv:2602.03999v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Eldan's stochastic localization is a probabilistic construction that has proved instrumental to modern breakthroughs in high-dimensional geometry and the design of sampling algorithms. Motivated by sampling under non-Euclidean geometries and the mirror descent algorithm in optimization, we develop a functional generalization of Eldan's process that replaces Gaussian regularization with regularization by any positive integer multiple of a log-Laplace transform. We further give a mixing time bound on the Markov chain induced by our localization process, which holds if our target distribution satisfies a functional Poincar\'e inequality. Finally, we apply our framework to differentially private convex optimization in $\ell_p$ norms for $p \in [1, 2)$, where we improve state-of-the-art query complexities in a zeroth-order model.
items.author: Anming Gu, Bobby Shi, Kevin Tian

items.title: Hippasus: Accurate and Cost-Efficient Feature Augmentation over Relational Tables
items.summary:
arXiv:2602.02025v3 Announce Type: replace-cross
